appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
Volume Two of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography came out in 1888, running from Crane to Grimshaw. Editors Wilson and Fiske kept the pace of a life for nearly every notable name. The set was sold by subscription across the country.

This volume's span covers many founders, Civil War officers, and men of letters of the young republic. Each entry gives birth, career, works, and death in tight, factual prose. Steel portraits mark the most famous names. Read across the six volumes, Appletons' forms a portrait gallery of the nation as the Victorian age wished to remember it.

Volume Three of Appletons' Cyclopaedia, also from 1888, continues the alphabet from Grinnell to Lockwood. Wilson and Fiske's dictionary was halfway done, with thousands of American lives already in print. The work's scale was unmatched in its day.

Governors, judges, explorers, and divines fill these pages, each weighed in a column or two. The editors include Canadians and Latin Americans whose lives touched the United States. Family details and lists of writings make the entries useful for tracing kin and careers. The volume carries the national biography through the middle letters with steady, encyclopedic calm. The print is dense, but the facts are laid out in a steady, clear order.

Volume Four of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography appeared in 1888, covering Lodge to Pickens. The dictionary had become a fixture in American libraries. Wilson and Fiske drew on family papers and earlier collections for their facts.

This stretch of the alphabet holds many Revolutionary officers, senators, and college presidents. Entries balance public deeds with private character sketches drawn from obituaries and memoirs. A few lives were polished by the families themselves, a flaw later readers learned to discount. Even so, the volume preserves facts about hundreds of figures that survive nowhere else in print. Many entries rest on obituaries clipped from the newspapers of the day.

Volume Five of Appletons' Cyclopaedia came out in 1888, running from Pickering to Sumter. The set was nearing its end, and the editors' net had caught most of the nation's notable dead and living. Subscribers received the volumes year by year.

Revolutionary statesmen, Civil War generals, and leading clergy crowd this part of the alphabet. The entries keep the house style: dates, posts, battles, books, and a closing judgment. Charles Sumter's contemporaries and Charles Sumner both appear in these pages. For students of nineteenth-century America, the volume is a dense quarry of names, dates, and careers.
army-letters-from-an-officer-s-wife-1871: Frances Roe's letters home from frontier army posts paint a vivid woman's picture of the post-Civil War West — long marches, isolated forts, and encounters with a vanishing frontier. Candid and observant, they preserve daily life that official reports never captured. A gem of Western Americana.
arxiv-2512-00088:
Mohammad Zare proposes a new way to feed text into convolutional neural networks, in a 2025 study called SemImage. Instead of treating a document as a one-dimensional string, the method turns it into a two-dimensional semantic image. Such networks are usually built for pictures, so text must first be reshaped.

In a SemImage, each word becomes a pixel, rows stand for sentences, and an extra boundary row marks where sentences change. The layout is meant to keep linguistic features separate and readable for the network. The idea offers a fresh route for text classification and other tasks that usually rely on word sequences.
arxiv-2512-00188:
Ring oscillators are simple circuits whose steady pulsing underlies clocks in modern chips. Ashwin Gopal, Massimiliano Esposito, and Jan Meibohm analyze CMOS ring oscillators near the point where coherent oscillations begin, in a 2025 study. Their model is built to stay consistent with thermodynamics.

For driving voltages close to the critical value, the authors derive the normal form of the Hopf bifurcation behind the transition. They study both dissipation and fluctuations in that regime. The results speak to engineers and physicists who need to know how much energy tiny oscillators waste and how noisy their timing becomes. Ring oscillators are also test beds for how circuits behave near instability.
arxiv-2512-00388:
Chirality, the asymmetry between a structure and its mirror image, drives many useful material properties. Okamoto and a large team study how altermagnetism boosts chiral phonons in 2025. Phonons are vibrations of a crystal lattice, and they can carry magnetization under the right conditions.

In crystallographically chiral materials, phonons with nonzero momentum can acquire a longitudinal magnetization. Helical spin order breaks all mirror symmetries and therefore carries magnetic chirality of its own. Combining the two effects could give engineers new control over heat, sound, and spin in quantum materials. Phonons carry heat, so chiral phonons may eventually steer heat flow itself. The boost in the title refers to magnetic order strengthening the phonons' chirality.
arxiv-2512-00588:
The Virasoro algebra governs conformal symmetry in two-dimensional physics, and the Sugawara construction builds it from currents. Armin Ghazi and Ahmad Moradpouri study an equivariant Virasoro algebra through alternative Sugawara constructions in 2025. Their starting point is a Kac-Moody algebra with two U(1) factors.

Besides the standard invariant tensor, this case offers a second, antisymmetric invariant tensor. That extra tensor enables an infinite family of genuinely new realizations beyond the conventional one. New realizations can expose hidden symmetries in conformal field theories and string models built on them. The extra invariant tensor exists only because the algebra has two current factors. Equivariance ties the construction to a cyclic symmetry between those factors. For folks who build such nets, the gain is a stock of new forms to try. Each one can be checked in the same clean way as the old forms.
arxiv-2512-00788:
Anupam, Sheryl Mathew, and Sibasish Ghosh study quantum batteries in a 2025 physics paper. A quantum battery stores energy in a quantum system, and researchers hope quantum effects can charge it faster than any classical device. Many charging schemes claim such an advantage, called superextensive charging power.

What physical ingredients that advantage truly needs is still unclear. The authors examine whether it can appear without global operations, the costly controls that act on the whole system at once. Their answer shapes how realistic quantum batteries might be built. If local control suffices, lab devices become much more plausible.
arxiv-2512-00888:
Ishaan Gangwani and Aayam Bansal measure the hidden hardware cost of tabular foundation models in a 2025 paper. These models promise train-free prediction on table data: you show them a table, and they predict without fitting a new model. That promise says little about the machines needed to run them.

The authors present a lightweight benchmark that pairs accuracy with cost. They track wall-clock latency, peak CPU memory, and peak GPU memory on four public tables, including income, housing, and wine quality data. Two open foundation models are tested. Honest cost numbers help teams judge whether train-free prediction is worth its hardware bill.
arxiv-2512-01088:
Jingxiang Huang and Samer Lahoud analyze LoRa wireless links under interference in a 2025 paper. The Internet of Things is filling the sub-gigahertz unlicensed bands with protocols like LoRa, Sigfox, and LR-FHSS. They must share the same frequencies, so they interfere with each other.

The authors study LoRa's robustness at the physical layer when narrowband interference is present. Physical-layer analysis looks at the raw signal, before any protocol fixes are applied. Knowing how much interference LoRa can tolerate helps planners deploy sensors in crowded spectrum. Their results inform choices about channels, spreading settings, and expected range.
arxiv-2512-01188:
Edward Hu and a team of roboticists teach robots to look for information on purpose in a 2025 paper. A robot's current sensory view does not always reveal the facts it needs for a task. Under such partial observability, the best behavior often means acting to gain the missing information, like moving to see behind an object.

Standard robot learning techniques struggle to produce such active perception behaviors. The authors propose a simple real-world learning recipe that efficiently trains active perception policies on physical robots. Robots that deliberately gather information could handle cluttered homes and warehouses where the needed facts are rarely in plain sight.
arxiv-2512-01288:
Abhimanyu Susobhanan and a large team revisit how to time pulses from spinning stars. Pulsars send out beams that sweep past Earth like a lighthouse. Each pulse has a shape that shifts with radio tone. Wideband timing reads the pulse time and the gas shift at once.

The team gives a new way to do that joint read. Their method deals with noise in a strict, clean way. Clean timing matters because tiny shifts can hint at huge waves in space. Better pulse times help teams hunt for those waves with sets of pulsars spread across the sky.
arxiv-2512-01388:
Hidemasa Ishii and Hiroshi Kori study how noise can push linked units out of a stable state. Each unit has two stable states. Units are linked so each feels its neighbors. Noise, link strength, and the bend of each unit all play a part.

The pair show that mix yields three clear escape routes. Which route fires rests on how strong the links are. Weak, mid, and strong links each give a distinct path out. Knowing the routes helps predict flips in power grids, nerve cells, and other linked bistable sets. The three routes give modelers a map for when a whole set flips at once and when it escapes in parts instead.
arxiv-2512-01588:
Number theorists often need the class group and unit group of a number field, two structures that reveal how arithmetic works inside it. A 2025 paper by Koen de Boer, Alice Pellet-Mary, and Benjamin Wesolowski presents the first method that provably computes both for any number field in subexponential time.

Earlier fast methods either handled only imaginary quadratic fields or leaned on heuristic assumptions that resisted proof for decades. The new algorithm assumes the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, a famous unproven claim, but needs no other leaps of faith. That guarantee matters because class group computations sit underneath both pure number theory and widely used cryptographic systems.
arxiv-2512-01688:
Naoki Tsukamoto studies light bending near unstable photon spheres in general spacetimes. Photon spheres trap light rays in loops around black holes. Rays bent just inside or outside can shape shadow images. The Event Horizon Telescope reads those shadows now.

Near-future space views may catch rays near the spheres with more detail. Tsukamoto works out lensing traits for a general static, spherical case. His results cover exotic spacetimes as well as black holes. They give observers a guide to tell object types apart by their light rings. Static spherical symmetry keeps the math general yet tractable, a middle ground between toy cases and full numeric relativity runs.
arxiv-2512-01788:
Christian Molliere and co-authors test learned image compression for Earth observation with segmentation in mind. Satellite data volumes grow fast. Sending and storing it all strains links and archives. Learned compression can shrink files a lot, but it may drop details that later tasks need.

The team scores compression by downstream segmentation quality. Maps of land, water, and crops are the end use. A codec that keeps segmentation sharp while files shrink wins. That trade-off decides if learned codecs can serve real satellite pipelines. Segmentation-aware training bakes the end task into the codec, a shift from generic fidelity scores that often mislead archive planning.
arxiv-2512-02188:
AI systems that outline organs and tools in surgical video usually train on images from one hospital and one camera type, then falter elsewhere. Mansoor Ali and co-authors present RobustSurg in 2025, aimed at surgical scene segmentation that keeps working on unseen hospitals and imaging modalities.

The failure mode is domain shift: lighting, equipment, and practice differ across centers, and performance drops out of distribution. The authors tackle that generalization gap directly for surgical scenes. Reliable segmentation across hospitals is a precondition for surgical AI leaving the lab, since an assistant that only works where it was trained helps few patients.
arxiv-2512-02488:
Koshiishi and a large team of co-authors probe a puzzle inside iron based superconductors. In these materials, electrons favor one direction over another, breaking four fold symmetry in a phase called nematic. Why that happens has been argued about since the effect was first found.

One open question is how the nematic phase links to stripe like magnetic order and to a slight stretch of the crystal lattice. Both appear at lower temperatures, in the antiferromagnetic orthorhombic phase. Sorting out which effect drives which could guide the search for better superconductors and clearer theory. Each clear link in the chain cuts the guess work for the next round of lab tests.
arxiv-2512-02588:
Nurimangul Nurmamat and eight co-authors tally the strength of fast radio bursts caught by the CHIME telescope. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of radio energy, mostly from far beyond our galaxy. What triggers them, and how they shine, remain largely unknown.

The team studies four hundred fifteen bursts that did not repeat, after careful manual filtering for completeness. They chart how fluence and energy are distributed across the sample. Such distributions test ideas about burst sources: a shape that fits one source class may rule out another, guiding future observing time. More bursts of this clean kind will let the team split the set by sky spot and strength next.
arxiv-2512-03188:
Factorials grow fast, and their products rarely match exactly. Joshua Cooper and Joseph Preuss study the equation where two factorials multiply to a third in this 2025 work. The problem goes back to Erdős, and few nontrivial solutions are expected.

The authors ask how sparse the smaller number in such solutions can be. Sparse here means the values spread thin as numbers grow. Their results add to work on whether only finitely many solutions exist. Such questions test deep tools in number theory, even when the equation looks simple. Sparsity results narrow where hunters for new solutions should spend their search effort.
arxiv-2601-06988:
Research by Yue Ban and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with counter-diabatic driving for fast spin control in a two-electron double quantum dot. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The techniques of shortcuts to adiabaticity have been proposed to accelerate. The “slow” adiabatic processes in various quantum systems with the applications in quantum information processing.

The authors study the counter-diabatic driving for fast adiabatic spin manipulation in. A two-electron double quantum dot by designing time-dependent electric fields in the presence of spin-orbit coupling. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07488:
Ayush Bidlan, Dipanjan Dey, and Parth Bambhaniya study how a star-like object might collapse under an alternative theory of gravity. Their 2026 preprint uses Brans-Dicke gravity, where a scalar field joins the usual geometry of spacetime. Here the collapse is driven by that scalar field alone, with no ordinary matter present. The field carries a self-interaction potential and couples directly to the Ricci scalar.

Gravitational collapse is the process that can form black holes and singularities. Testing it in Brans-Dicke gravity shows whether the outcomes match Einstein's theory or differ. The setup is deliberately clean, so the scalar field's role stands out. Readers get a focused probe of singularity formation beyond standard gravity.
arxiv-2601-07788:
Liberty Kent, Nilufer Tuptuk, and Ingolf Becker study how cybersecurity teams hand over work between shifts. Incident response runs around the clock, so handovers are constant. Effective transitions are crucial, yet guidance on managing them is limited. Their 2026 preprint reports an exploratory study to build such guidance. The authors reviewed existing literature and online resources, then consulted practitioners.

Two draft guidelines, labeled A and B, came out of the literature work. Practitioner input then tested and refined them. A poor handover can drop an active attack from view for hours. Clear rules for what to pass on, and how, reduce that risk. The paper serves security operations managers and scholars of teamwork under pressure. It treats the handover itself as a security control.
arxiv-2601-07988:
Adithya V Ganesan and colleagues argue that longitudinal text data need new modeling habits. Standard NLP treats documents as independent, unordered samples. In longitudinal studies that assumption rarely holds. Documents are nested within authors and ordered in time. Together they form person-indexed, time-ordered behavioral sequences. Their 2026 preprint adapts modeling and evaluation ideas from word sequences to these behavioral sequences.

The shift matters for mental health, social science, and any field tracking people over time. Order carries signal: change itself can be the outcome of interest. Evaluation must also respect the nesting, or results leak between a person's documents. The authors span several universities and research groups. The paper serves computational social science and clinical NLP scholars. It asks the field to model people through time, not piles of text.
arxiv-2601-08588: Jacob Paul Simpson, Efstratios Palias, and Sharu Theresa Jose study sample complexity in composite quantum hypothesis testing. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats symmetric binary testing, where an unknown state lies in one of two uncertainty sets. Asymptotic error exponents for this problem are well studied. The finite-sample regime remains poorly understood, though. Knowing how many copies of a state suffice for a target error matters for real quantum sensors. The work helps set honest sample budgets for quantum detection tasks.
arxiv-2601-08988:
Ananya Mantravadi, Shivali Dalmia, and Abhishek Mukherji build a test for health AI agents that must act, not just chat. Safe care needs steps: read a chart, check a cut off, sum past values, then act if a rule is met. Past tests lean on quiz style asks. They miss those step and rule skills in full.

Their test is called ART. It runs agents on tasks drawn from real health charts. Each task needs a chain of steps with checks at set points. A slip in one step fails the task, as in real care. A reader in health AI gets a strict, act based scale. It shows which agents can be trusted with chart work.
arxiv-2601-09088:
Shaotian Yan and a team from Alibaba Cloud give a small open chat model built for step thought. The model is called DASD-4B-Thinking. Small here means four billion set values, lean next to top models. Yet the team says it tops open peers of its size on hard tests in math, science, and code. It can beat some far large models too, they say.

Their key is how they pass skill from a big model to the small one. They match the spread of the big model's steps, not just its last reply. That match keeps the small model's thought path in line. A reader who needs cheap step thought gets a lean model with a clear train trick.
arxiv-2601-09388:
Felix Rupprecht and Sabine Wölk study how to build sparse quantum states at lower cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper improves state preparation, one of the most basic tasks in quantum computing. A sparse state has only a few nonzero entries among its basis states, yet it is a key input for many algorithms.

The authors cut the Toffoli gate cost of preparing such states. Sparse states matter most in quantum simulation and in solvers for linear systems. Cheaper preparation means those algorithms spend less of their budget just loading data. The paper gives circuit builders a leaner primitive to work with.
arxiv-2601-09788:
Giulia Brunelli and a large team take a fresh X-ray look at a candidate PeVatron near the galactic center. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the pulsar wind nebula G0.9+0.1 with hard X-ray and multiwavelength data. The nebula is powered by the energetic pulsar PSR J1747-2809 inside a composite supernova remnant.

PeVatrons are rare sources that push particles to petaelectronvolt energies. The team models the nebula's full spectral energy distribution. NuSTAR, XMM-Newton, and Chandra supply the X-ray views. Pinning down how this nebula accelerates particles helps explain where the galaxy's most energetic cosmic rays come from.
arxiv-2601-10188:
Jincheng Guo and a large team profile a rare white dwarf star. The star is named TMTS J0006, in short. A white dwarf is the dense core left when a star dies. This one is both ultra massive and highly magnetic. It also spins at a fast rate.

Its spin period is just a short span, seen in sharp light curves. Three sky surveys caught the same beat. That cross check makes the beat firm. Fast spin in such a dense star is rare. The team works out its mass, field, and heat from the data. Such stars test how stars die and merge.
arxiv-2601-10488:
Louise Gassot, Patrick Gérard, and Peter Miller prove a long held claim for the Benjamin Ono equation. The law rules waves on deep water with a non local term. The claim is named soliton resolution. It says each wave ends as a sum of lone waves plus a fading tail.

Each lone wave moves at its own speed. The tail spreads and dies out in time. The claim needs the start wave to be smooth and to fade at the tails. The proof in this paper closes the claim for that case. Such proofs are a peak aim in wave math.
arxiv-2601-10688:
Rubel Hassan Mollik, Vamsi Krishna Kosuri, Hans Djalali, Stephanie Ludi, and Aboubakar Mountapmbeme work on access to block-based coding for blind and low-vision learners. Tools like Scratch and Code.org are now standard in school computer science classes. Yet they remain mostly out of reach for blind students. Their visual blocks demand sight at every step.

Past fixes changed the Blockly library itself, which made them hard to add to live platforms. The team's framework works as an extension instead, leaving the base library alone. That choice could help schools adopt it without rebuilding their tools. The goal is coding classes where blind learners build programs on equal terms.
arxiv-2601-10888:
Arjun Maniyar studies the cross-ratio degree for eight points on the projective line. The cross-ratio is the basic invariant of four points on a line. The degree problem asks how many configurations of n points meet a set of cross-ratio conditions. For n points, n minus three conditions are specified.

Maniyar computes the maximal cross-ratio degree in the eight-point case. Silversmith's work points to several connections and uses for this degree. Such counts live in enumerative geometry, where each number answers: how many shapes fit the rules? Exact values at small n anchor the theory and hint at patterns for larger point sets.
arxiv-2601-11088:
Yuki Arai and co-authors report a large anomalous Hall effect in the antiferromagnet NbMnAs at room temperature. Some antiferromagnets share symmetry breaking with ferromagnets and can give strong ferromagnetic-like responses. The anomalous Hall effect is a transverse voltage that tracks such a response. NbMnAs shows it at zero applied field.

The effect appears despite the material's small net magnetization. Room temperature and zero field are the conditions devices need. Antiferromagnets are robust against stray fields and can switch fast. A strong Hall signal makes their state easy to read electrically. The result points toward spintronic memory and logic built on antiferromagnets that behave, usefully, a little like ferromagnets.
arxiv-2601-11188:
Lucas Happ studies a rare kind of three-body state in this 2026 preprint. The states are bound, yet they sit inside a range of free motion. He asks how such states form as system settings change. His tool is the path of poles in the plane of complex energy.

Happ uses a simple one-line model for the test. Two bosons are the same, and a third particle is distinct. The parts pull on each other through smooth Gaussian wells. He then varies the pull strength, the range, and the mass ratio one step at a time. The pole paths show how loose states turn into bound ones.
arxiv-2601-11288:
P. Oliva studies an old bronze figure from Sardinia with neutron beams. The 2026 preprint looks at a Nuragic figurine in close detail. Nuragic figures are rare works of early Iron Age craft. Sardinian smiths made them with great skill for their time.

The figures were most likely cast by the lost wax method. Wax shapes melt out and leave a mold for the bronze. That method lets even complex forms be cast with ease. Oliva uses two neutron tools to peer inside the bronze. Diffraction reads the mix and strain of the metal. Tomography builds a 3D view of the inner form. Both tools leave the rare piece whole and unharmed.
arxiv-2601-11388:
An approach to theoretical spectroscopy is set out in this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. Theoretical spectroscopy models how matter takes and gives light. It rests on electronic-structure theory, a broad and strong field.

Such theory can capture the many-body life of materials. It spans ground-state traits and lattice excitations in solids. It also spans light-matter interaction of many kinds. Time-resolved forms track change as it unfolds after a pulse. Modern codes each carry a few or several of these methods. The work argues for an approach that excites, in both senses. It aims at codes that cover more of the field at once.
arxiv-2601-11688:
Vedant Nipane, Pulkit Agrawal, and Amit Singh link datasheets to code with agents. Their 2026 preprint presents SpecMap, a hierarchical LLM agent. Traceability joins spec documents to the code that implements them. In embedded systems, that mapping is a fundamental challenge.

Manual mapping fails on large code repositories at scale. Old recovery methods lean on lexical similarity alone. Information retrieval tricks miss semantic and structural links. Symbol-level ties in low-level software also escape them. SpecMap uses a hierarchy of LLM agents for the task. Agents can read datasheets and code with meaning in mind. Recovered links aid audits, updates, and safety checks.
arxiv-2601-11988:
Wenyi Wang, Sousuke Noda, and Taishi Katsuragawa study light from clouds of scalar fields round spinning black holes. Scalar-tensor theories add a scalar field to gravity. Round a Kerr black hole, such a cloud can grow by superradiance, which pulls spin energy out.

They show that induced decay of the cloud makes light signals that could be seen. The cloud growth in this theory is unlike that of other boson fields. It rests on how matter round the hole is spread, through a chameleon effect. Seen signals would test this form of gravity.
arxiv-2601-12088:
Salvatore Capozziello, Maurizio Capriolo, and Gaetano Lambiase derive an energy-momentum form for a modified gravity theory. The theory, called f(Q) gravity, extends a flat, torsion-free form of general relativity. It is based on non-metricity, a measure of how lengths change under transport.

They build the affine tensor for the energy and momentum of both gravity and matter fields. That joined form is the complex pseudo-tensor for this theory. Such forms are needed to track energy flow in cosmology. The work puts energy bookkeeping for f(Q) on a firm base.
arxiv-2601-12188:
Aditi Singh, Bogumiła Jezierska, Subrata Jana, and Szymon Śmiga give a simpler way to tune range separation for many-body calculations. One-shot GW and Bethe-Salpeter runs rest much on their start point, got from mean-field theory. A range-separated hybrid start can lift skill a lot if tuned well.

Full tuning is costly, so a simple start helps. Their method gives a practical first tune with less work. Better starts mean better spectra and gaps at the same cost. The work aims at real use in materials and molecule codes.  A cheap first tune can save days of compute time.
arxiv-2601-12388:
Amartya Goswami and Joseph Israel Zelezniak study ideals in commutative rings. Their focus is on strongly hollow ideals and a stricter class that adds the word completely. They work with no finiteness assumptions, which keeps the results broad. Ideals are core objects in ring theory, so new classes draw close study.

The pair set out basic structural facts about these ideals. They look at maximality and at what holds under quotients and surjective maps. They give several ways to test when an ideal is completely strongly hollow. One key result links the two classes through the Jacobson radical. If a strongly hollow ideal is not inside that radical, it must be of the stricter kind.
arxiv-2601-13088:
Harry Huang, Talia Xu, and Marco Zuniga Zamalloa look at how light can aid tiny flying craft. Small air craft now do tasks from stock checks to air sensing. Their short flight time and weak sense of place in GPS free zones hold them back.

Craft that are lighter than air offer a swap. A helium skin gives lift, so hover takes near zero power and flights can run far longer. The snag is how to steer and stay on course with so light a craft. The team tests how light can be used both to boost flight length and to guide the craft. For indoor and calm air tasks, the work points to a low power path.
arxiv-2601-13188:
Patrick Yung Kang Lee and a large team study how people form ties with ChatGPT as a companion. Folks now turn to broad chat bots for company, not just to play apps built for that role. Yet little is known about how they see and run such ties.

The team asks how outer forces shape those ties. Friends, press, and norms may push how a tie is kept or hid. They also ask what tricks users use to keep the tie as they want it. The study fills a gap in how AI company is lived day to day. For teams that build chat bots, the finds show care points for health and trust.
arxiv-2601-13288:
Gonzalo Ariel Meyoyan and Luciano Del Corro reuse a live model's own maths to tag text in the same pass. Big served models often call split small models for safety and tag tasks. Each split call adds lag, memory load, and ops bulk.

Their swap is to train light probes on the served model's hid states. The probes read states the model has paid to make for its main text task. Tags then come out in the same pass as the text, with no split call. The probes can pick which tokens and which layers to read. For teams that serve models at scale, the trick cuts cost while it keeps the tag step.
arxiv-2601-13388:
Sasha Ronaghi, Prerit Choudhary, David H. Rehkopf, and Bryant Lin pull diabetes risk clues from free text in health files. Social facts of health, such as home, food, and work strain, sway type two diabetes care. Yet they are oft absent from the neat fields of a health file. Most such facts are caught by fixed forms, which miss the nuance of each clinic's crowd.

Free text in notes holds a rich store of such facts. The team uses large language models to draw them out in a firm form. That form then feeds a risk guess for each patient. For clinics, the route may catch risks that fixed forms leave blank.
arxiv-2601-13488:
Peter J. Forrester and Fei Wei note a set of results on high order equations for unitary matrix sums. The note gives the back tale and spur for a joint paper. It then maps the main finds of that work for a fast read.

The finds link matrix and scalar equations of high order. The sums at stake are Hankel and Toeplitz determinants built from I-Bessel functions. Such sums are the same as set unitary matrix sums. The note puts that link in a wider frame. For maths physics readers, a short map of a dense work plus its wider place has clear worth.
arxiv-2601-13988:
Laura Monk and Frédéric Naud review progress on spectral gaps of large hyperbolic surfaces in 2026. This expository paper surveys the history and recent breakthroughs in the field. The focus is the first non-trivial eigenvalue, called lambda-one. That value sets the spectral gap, a key trait of the surface's vibrations.

They ask how lambda-one can behave as surface volume grows large. The story runs from Selberg to Mirzakhani, two giants of the field. Spectral gaps link geometry, number theory, and quantum chaos. A clear review helps new researchers enter a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2601-14088:
Maria Abu-Sini and Reinhard Heckel build codes for data torn into pieces with typos in 2026. The adversarial torn paper channel models a word that is first edited, then broken. At most a set number of edit errors hit the word: insertions, deletions, and substitutions. The word then breaks into fragments at arbitrary positions.

DNA storage systems and 3D fingerprinting motivate this channel. The team studies near optimal code construction for it. A good code lets the receiver rebuild the message from torn, flawed pieces. Such codes guard data stored in fragile physical media.
arxiv-2601-14688:
Timothy D. Brandt derives statistical formulas for companion hunting in this 2026 paper. Astronomers often detect a companion only through a trend: a radial velocity or astrometric acceleration of its host star. Brandt derives the statistical relationship between that trend, a companion's mass, and its projected separation. The relationships are expressed as probability density functions.

The formulas are analytic and hold independent of all Keplerian orbital elements, so long as orbits are randomly oriented in space. In plain terms, a measured drift can be turned into odds on mass and distance without knowing the orbit's shape. The math is short and closed. No large code run is used, which makes the tool fast to use at a desk. Readers get closed-form relations for a common detection problem in exoplanet and binary star work.
arxiv-2601-14788:
Yifei Liu, Changxing Ding, Ling Guo, Huaiguang Jiang, and Qiong Cao generate human motion from text in this 2026 paper. Diffusion models have seen widespread adoption for text-driven human motion generation. Their generative capabilities and flexibility are impressive. Current motion diffusion models face two major limitations, though.

One is a representational gap. Pre-trained text encoders lack motion-specific information, so prompts are read with the wrong nuance. The other is error propagation during the iterative denoising process. Small slips compound across steps. Their model is reconstruction-anchored, using reconstruction to hold the motion on track. The aim is faith. A wave of an arm should look like the words asked for it, start to end. Readers get a text-to-motion design that fights drift in both meaning and movement.
arxiv-2601-15088:
Arnab Priya Saha and Aninda Sinha study how five particles scatter, one piece at a time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with five-point tree amplitudes, the basic terms in a scattering process. All five external particles are identical scalars.

The team expands the residues of the amplitude in partial waves. They check the build in two ways. One uses massive spinor-helicity building blocks. The other matches the five-point Veneziano amplitude at fixed mass levels. The work also brings in splitting constraints and the hidden zeros of the full five-point scattering amplitude.
arxiv-2601-15588:
A team signing as Alibaba-AAIG presents a safety guardrail model in a 2026 arXiv paper. The model is called YuFeng-XGuard. As language models spread into real products, guardrails must do more than coarse filtering. They need to judge risk in fine detail. They also need to explain their calls and adapt to new policies. Existing tools often fall short on one of these counts.

Many current guards classify fast but stay opaque. Others rely on fixed rules added after the fact. Inference cost can also block deployment at scale. XGuard is described as reasoning-centric, interpretable, and flexible. It reasons about risk rather than just matching patterns. For builders, a guard that shows its reasoning is easier to audit. That matters when a wrong block or a missed risk carries real cost.
arxiv-2601-15688:
Zhixuan Liang, Xingyu Zeng, Rui Zhao, and Ping Luo improve active learning for object detection in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active learning trains strong models with minimal labeling effort. It picks the most informative examples for humans to annotate. Most methods judge informativeness by data distribution or content alone. That judgment does not directly track downstream performance. In detection, the score that matters is mean average precision.

The authors propose performance-guided reinforced active learning, per the title. The guide is the task metric itself, not a proxy. Reinforcement learning steers which images get picked for labeling. If picks track real gains, annotation budgets stretch further. Labeling images for detection is slow and costly. A smarter picker saves money on every training round.
arxiv-2601-15888:
An unsigned 2026 arXiv paper asks why vision foundation models transfer unevenly. Foundation models pretrain on huge data to capture broad knowledge. In language tasks, that pretraining generalizes well. Vision foundation models behave differently. Despite heavy compute, their gains vary sharply across downstream tasks. One task leaps forward while another barely moves.

The authors postulate a cause: a mismatch between pretraining objectives and what downstream vision tasks demand. Pretraining may teach features the tasks cannot use well. The paper studies these transfer limits directly. For labs spending heavily on vision pretraining, knowing the limits guides where the next dollar of compute should go.
arxiv-2601-15988:
Kalyan Banerjee links two classic objects in number theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. On one side stand elliptic curves, whose rank counts independent rational points. On the other stand class groups of real quadratic fields. Class groups measure how badly unique factorization fails in those fields. Banerjee proves a relation between the two. The link ties curve ranks to the nontriviality of class groups. The connection runs across infinitely many real quadratic fields, he states.

Bridges like this are prized in arithmetic geometry. A fact about curves becomes a fact about fields, and back. Each side has its own tools, so a bridge doubles the attack on hard questions. The abstract states the claim in brief terms. Specialists will look to the proof for the exact shape of the relation.
arxiv-2601-16088:
Abhinav Jangir and Anees Ahmed study how pulse form shapes pair birth in strong fields. Their 2026 preprint looks at birth of electron and positron pairs from void space. A time based field that is not the same on each side drives the birth. The team solves the quantum Vlasov maths for this case. They vary both the phase at the pulse heart and the pulse shape.

The pair track how each change shifts the yield of new pairs. Shape and phase can raise or cut the count in clear ways. Such links help labs plan strong laser tests of pair birth. They also test if maths matches what labs will see. The work stays close to the field maths and its terms.
arxiv-2601-16188:
Sebastián Donoso, Sovanlal Mondal and Vicente Saavedra-Araya extend mean sum results along return times. Their 2026 preprint sits in the maths of long run means. Return times are the times a path comes back to a small mark. Means can be taken along those sparse times in their place of all times. Past work showed such means settle in fast mix systems.

The team widens those results to groups of acts that commute. They also use marks that shrink as time grows. The work part fills gaps left by the first author, Maass and the third author. Sparse means that still settle have use in chance and flow maths. The proof joins mix speed to mean acts.
arxiv-2601-16288:
Van Weeren and coauthors share new MeerKAT views of two star groups, Abell 1775 and Abell 1795. Their 2026 preprint deals with huge radio glows in such groups. Big glows mark groups in clash, while small glows mark cool core groups. Both trace fast grains in the thin gas in the group. Late views hint the two glow types may not split clean.

The new views span a wide band from the MeerKAT scopes. They test if the small glow in one group is of the big type. Glow type tells of past clashes and gas acts in the group. Clear views help sort glow birth tales. The work adds fine radio maps of two key groups.
arxiv-2601-16388:
Hironori Yamaguchi and coauthors find magnet order that Kondo acts help to build. Their 2026 preprint deals with a chain model called the Kondo necklace. Kondo acts pair a free spin with a held spin in a singlet. Such pairs were long thought to kill magnet order. Late work hints Kondo acts can in some cases aid order.

The team shows Néel order, a flip flop spin line, can grow with Kondo aid. That growth flips the old tale for this model class. It widens where teams should look for such order. Real stuff may show the same aid in its spin acts. The work joins two themes long set as foes.
arxiv-2601-16788:
Xuewei Li, Xinghan Bao, Zhimin Chen, and Xi Li sort wide-view street shots into named zones. A full round view shows roads, cars, folks, and sky at once. Tools must tag each point in that wide span. Depth cues help split near from far in the shot. Past tools used depth in raw or plain forms. Their 2026 preprint builds a depth code fit for round views.

Their code reshapes depth to match the round warp of the shot. A fusion step then joins depth with the color view. Sharper tags aid self-drive cars and guide bots. Such tools need the full round scene read right.
arxiv-2601-17488:
Quinn M. Gallagher and four co-authors seek a local key to sort amorphous ices. Amorphous solids lack the neat unit cells of crystals. Yet ice phases with unlike traits must differ in local structure. The authors look for a structural basis at that local scale. Such a basis would do for glasses what space groups do for crystals.

A clear basis lets labs name and sort ice forms with proof. It can show which local motifs drive trait shifts. Water ice is a model for glasses at large. Its lessons reach drugs, foods, and planetary science. The work builds a language for forms that look alike at first glance. That language is a step to control them.
arxiv-2601-17588:
Marcus Ma and Shrikanth Narayanan argue that intelligence needs grounding, not embodiment. Recent language model gains revived an old debate. Must a mind have a body to be intelligent? The authors define intelligence by four properties. They list motivation, predictive ability, and understanding among them. Grounding links symbols to the world they mean.

Embodiment entails grounding, they argue, but grounding can arise without a body. That split reshapes what builders must give AI systems. It shifts focus from robot bodies to world linkage. The debate guides research funds and design choices. A clear stance helps labs test claims about machine minds. The paper stakes that stance with care.
arxiv-2601-17688:
Sudhanva Joshi and Sunil Kumar Mishra study traversability in a wormhole-inspired teleportation protocol. The protocol uses coupled Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev systems. They are prepared in a thermofield double state with a bath. The authors add PT-symmetric non-unitary deformations. PT symmetry pairs parity and time reversal. They ask how those deformations change traversability dynamics.

Traversability marks if a signal can pass through the wormhole analogue. SYK models are a lab for holography ideas. Deformations test how robust the effect is. Results guide both theory and quantum simulation design. Teams can build SYK-like systems on quantum hardware. Knowing which knobs help or harm passage matters for those builds.
arxiv-2601-17988:
Nachi Avraham-Re'em and Emmanuel Roy prove a mixing result for a broad class of random processes. Their 2026 preprint studies infinitely divisible stationary processes indexed by a group. Stationary means the statistics do not shift over the index. Infinitely divisible means each piece can be split into like parts. The authors show that if such a process is ergodic and separable in probability, then it is weakly mixing.

Weak mixing is a stronger form of long-run independence. The result holds for any indexing group at all. It removes group assumptions that older work needed. As with Gaussian processes, ergodicity alone forces mixing here. Clean results like this anchor the theory of random processes.
arxiv-2601-18188:
Weiye Zhu and co-authors present NaVIDA, a navigation agent that learns how its own actions change the world. Their 2026 preprint deals with vision-and-language navigation. An agent reads a natural language instruction and acts on it inside a rich visual scene. Most methods learn reactive links from state to action. They do not model how an action causally reshapes the scene, so errors can compound step by step.

NaVIDA adds inverse dynamics augmentation to the training. Inverse dynamics asks which action could have caused a seen change. That signal teaches cause and effect, not just correlation. Agents that grasp it should follow routes with fewer wrong turns.
arxiv-2601-18288:
S.C. İnan probes the electromagnetic traits of the tau lepton in lead-lead collisions at a future collider. His 2026 preprint studies pairs of tau leptons made in PbPb collisions at the FCC-hh. Two numbers are in view: the anomalous magnetic moment of the tau, and its electric dipole moment. The authors report 95 percent confidence exclusion limits, plus sensitivity limits at three and five sigma. Such limits say how small a deviation the collider could detect or rule out.

The tau is the heaviest lepton, so its moments are prized probes of new physics. A dipole moment would signal a deep asymmetry in nature. Future collider studies of this kind set targets for machine design.
arxiv-2601-18488:
Alice Bernard and five colleagues study how the split of an atom's core can vary from split to split. When a heavy core splits, the two parts fly off with traits that can be counted, such as spin and mass. Math based on energy maps can give the odds for each trait. New tools add those odds up with care.

Still, a mean count can hide how wide the spread runs. The team use a dice-roll math trick to chart that spread in full. Each roll picks a split by the odds, and many rolls build the whole range. That range tells labs what a real test should see, miss by miss. It also shows which counts are firm and which ones swing a lot. Such maps help plan tests on cores that are hard to make.
arxiv-2601-19088:
Saba Alimadadi and Golnaz Gharachorlu blend two styles of mutation testing for Python code. Mutation testing grades a test suite by seeding small fake faults and seeing how many the tests catch. Old tools miss many fault types that are common in a loose typed language like Python.

Their hybrid method is driven by real fault patterns, not just simple code swaps. Python's dynamic typing breeds faults that stiff mutation rules never plant. A suite graded against realistic faults gives a truer read on whether the tests would catch the bugs that truly slip into Python projects.
arxiv-2601-19388:
Yimin Tang, Sven Koenig, and Erdem Bıyık tidy the paths of robot fleets after a planner has done its job. Multi agent path finding is a hard problem with uses in warehouses and robot coordination. Learning based solvers are fast and scale well, but their feasible plans often include wasteful or wobbly moves.

Their layer, Judgelight, post optimizes each trajectory by collapsing closed subwalks, loops that return to their start. Cutting dead loops keeps the plan valid while making it shorter and cleaner. A cheap cleanup step can lift any solver's output, which makes it a handy add on.
arxiv-2601-19488:
Yizhao Han and nine co-authors sample video frames with an eye on entropy to keep long clips coherent. Autoregressive models build video step by step, as language models build text. In language, picking from a small top candidate set works well because tokens are dense with meaning and low in redundancy.

Video tokens behave otherwise, so fixed candidate sets falter over long horizons. Their entropy guided k-guard sampling adjusts the guard by how unsure the model is at each step. Long, stable video generation is the prize, since drift and decay grow with every extra second.
arxiv-2601-19988:
Xuankai Zhou and colleagues build quantum sensors that sit directly on a material's surface. Optically addressable spins can sense magnetic fields with atomic resolution and quantum-limited sensitivity. Realising them at surfaces has been a long-standing ambition. The obstacle is depth: stable quantum spins usually must sit some distance below the surface, blunting their sensitivity to what lies above.

The team demonstrates a hybrid molecular and two-dimensional architecture. It places working spin sensors right on top of the surface. Surface placement maximises contact with the sample being measured. Such sensors could image magnetism and currents in new materials at the smallest scales. The work removes a depth limit that constrained the field.
arxiv-2601-20088:
Meng Xin and colleagues distil large models into aggressively compressed versions. Their technical report presents quantization-aware distillation for models squeezed to the NVFP4 format, a four-bit number format. Quantization alone usually costs accuracy. Distillation trains the compressed student to imitate a full-precision teacher, recovering much of the loss.

The report covers both language models and vision-language models. It shares best practices the team found for the recovery process. The distillation loss is a KL divergence between teacher and student outputs. Four-bit inference slashes memory and energy costs for serving models. A reliable recipe for recovering accuracy makes such deployment realistic. The report is written for practitioners facing the same squeeze.
arxiv-2601-20988:
Gabor Lippner and Arturo Ortiz San Miguel ask which regular graphs hold the most copies of a given pattern. Their 2026 paper studies subgraph counts in regular graphs. A regular graph gives every vertex the same number of edges. For a fixed pattern graph H, some regular graphs pack in more H-shaped copies than others. The authors seek the graphs with the highest H-density.

They reframe the hunt as a continuous optimization problem. The new frame runs through the eigenvalues of the graph. Counts of injective homomorphisms link to counts from quotient graphs of H. That link turns a discrete search into smooth math. The result gives extremal graph theory a fresh handle. It may help design networks with chosen pattern densities.
arxiv-2601-21088:
Thomas Blommel and four co-authors compare rival ways to simulate driven quantum systems. Their 2026 paper benchmarks the real-time Dyson expansion against Green's function approaches. Driven, interacting quantum systems are hard to simulate. The team focuses on density matrix dynamics and time-off-diagonal Green's functions. They also study time-resolved photoemission spectra. Those spectra show how a material responds right after a pulse.

Two themes run through the comparison. One is Markovianity: how much the system remembers its past. The other is self-consistency in the calculation. The rivals include Kadanoff-Baym equations, their generalized ansatz, and exact diagonalization for small systems. Second-order perturbation theory supplies the interaction treatment. The study tells simulators which tool to trust for driven materials. It is a careful methods audit for non-equilibrium physics.
arxiv-2601-21388:
Mingyi Wang and Dongling Wang build high-order numerical schemes for a fractional diffusion operator. The tempered fractional Laplacian models spread that is heavier-tailed than normal diffusion but still fades at long range. Accurate schemes for it are hard to design.

The authors base their framework on new generating functions drawn from the discrete symbols. For smooth functions, the schemes reach high orders of accuracy. A general frame matters because each new application otherwise needs its own scheme. Their approach gives later work a ready path to accurate, fast solvers for this class of problems.
arxiv-2601-21788:
C. J. K. Larkin and co-authors ask how one unusual pair of massive stars came to be. Wolf-Rayet stars are hot, stripped stars, and how they form at the Sun's metal content is still unclear. Simple single-star paths are hard to square with the orbit patterns seen in different Wolf-Rayet pairs.

Their 2026 study focuses on Wd1-72, a Wolf-Rayet plus O-star binary inside the young massive cluster Westerlund 1. The pair sits inside the shared wind of the whole cluster. The title poses the question the evidence must answer: is this system a recent case where the two stars interacted and exchanged material? The answer would help pin down how often binary interaction, not solo aging, makes Wolf-Rayet stars.
arxiv-2601-21888:
Alexander Fel'shtyn and Mateusz Slomiany introduce a new object in dynamical systems: the synchronization zeta function. It is attached to a pair of self-maps of a topological space, functions that send the space into itself. Zeta functions in dynamics package counting data about repeating behavior into one analytic object.

The authors also define the growth rate of synchronization points, places where the two maps agree in step. And derive an explicit formula for it in the setting of endomorphisms of compact, connected Abelian groups. Their 2026 preprint then studies congruences and asymptotics tied to the new function. Work like this extends a classic toolkit, Reidemeister theory and dynamical zeta functions, into two-map territory.
arxiv-2601-22088:
Levin Maier puts a young set of equations on firm ground. The set is called the magnetic two-part Hunter-Saxton system. It was first drawn from a path law on a space with no end. That first work sketched the shape of the set and a flow that lasts for all time.

What was missed was a proof from the side of hard sums. Maier gives that proof. He studies weak forms of the law: forms that may grow sharp points yet still hold in a mean sense. Such ground work counts, since kin of this set model liquid glass, thin seas, and magnets. Those fields need laws that can be shown to hold, not just laws that look right on a screen.
arxiv-2601-22288:
Mario Truss presents PersonaCite, a tool that ties fake research users to real proof. Their 2026 work notes that model-made personas can sound sure yet hide where their claims come from. Design teams use such personas to test products and plans.

PersonaCite lets a user ask the persona direct questions in a chat. Each reply stays bound to source proof that can be checked. The tool frames personas as research aids, not as stand-ins for real people. That bound can make fake-user tests more honest and more safe to use. It also shows its work on demand.
arxiv-2601-22388:
Monica Rincon-Ramirez and five co-authors ask if a simple heat rule picks the black hole left after two black holes merge. Their 2026 preprint notes that big simulations predict the final hole with great care. Yet a plain rule from within relativity may do the same job.

They test a maximum entropy claim: the merger settles on the state with the most disorder allowed. If true, the rule would give a fast way to call the outcome. It would also tie black hole physics to heat physics in a deep way. The work checks the claim against known cases.
arxiv-2601-22588:
Zhuochun Li and a large team ask if a small model can judge as well as a large one by reading inner states. Large models are widely used as scorers, but they are costly, opaque, and prompt-sensitive. Their 2026 preprint tests small models that judge from internal representations, not from written verdicts.

The claim rests on a gap in semantic capacity between judge and judged. If it holds, judging gets cheaper and more stable. It could also make scores easier to audit. The work rethinks a costly habit of the field. Small, sharp judges would change many pipelines.
arxiv-2601-22688:
Doyoung Kim, Jaehyeok Doo, and Minjoon Seo let a language model branch its reasoning like a tree, in one pass. Models now reason in a single line, which traps dead-end paths inside the chain. Their 2026 preprint, TSLM, uses special tokens to mark branches in the text itself.

The model can grow several paths and expand only the live ones. Tree search in one pass saves the cost of many full runs. It suits puzzles where the first path often fails. The work rethinks the shape of machine thought. Branches, pruned well, beat a single line.
arxiv-2601-22788:
Jana Gonnermann-Müller and a team built FACET, a multi-agent AI that helps teachers tailor lessons to a mixed class. Classrooms now span wide gaps in skill, drive, language, and learning needs such as dyslexia and ADHD. Their 2026 preprint notes that teachers back tailored teaching, yet workload blocks it.

FACET's agents draft varied materials at scale, under the teacher's hand. That help could make tailored learning a daily fact, not an ideal. The work targets a kind bottleneck in schools. It keeps the teacher as the judge. Scale serves care, here.
arxiv-2601-22988:
Di Zhang and a team at Tongji University teach robots to see scenes in three dimensions. Real manipulation needs a steady grasp of space, even when cameras move to new viewpoints. Policies trained from one angle often fail when the view changes.

Their method learns visual representations grounded in geometry, so scenes read consistently across views. A robot that understands shape, not just pixels, can pick and place objects more reliably. View-proof vision is a step toward helpers that work in messy, real rooms. Robust spatial understanding is the stated requirement, because a manipulation policy must know where things are, not just what they look like.
arxiv-2601-23088:
Zhixiang Zhang and four co-authors attack the semantic caches that speed up language model services. Big providers cache answers by meaning, using embedding vectors as fuzzy keys for similar queries. That saves latency and compute on repeated questions.

Treating cache keys as fuzzy hashes, the authors craft collisions that make the cache serve wrong answers. A poisoned cache can mislead many users from a single planted entry. The work tells providers to harden a component many treated as harmless plumbing. Major providers already deploy semantic caching widely, so a key collision weakness reaches production systems, not just prototypes.
arxiv-2601-23188:
Zhongxiang Sun and five co-authors give deep search agents a way to watch their own thinking. These agents handle multi-step retrieval and long tasks well. Their failures often come from having no mechanism to monitor reasoning and retrieval as the job evolves.

Drawing on cognitive neuroscience, the authors add hierarchical meta-cognitive monitoring. Higher levels check the state of lower-level search and correct course when it drifts. Self-monitoring agents should be more reliable for research, law, and other long-horizon work. Meta-cognitive monitoring is hierarchical, so oversight itself is layered rather than a single checker watching a single process.
arxiv-2604-01188:

The team builds the network and its proof of strength at one time. The proof is a formal pledge that the closed loop will hold up. They train with attacks, where each failed case guides the next round. A failed case shows just where the pledge breaks, so training can fix it. This joins learning with proof in a single loop of work. It gives engineers a path to learned control with proof in hand.

Honoré de Balzac wrote Cousin Bette in French, and James Waring made the first English version in 1888. Balzac's dark late masterpiece turns on envy and revenge inside one Paris family. He wrote it fast, in months, near the end of his vast career of fiction.

Lisbeth Fischer, plain and poor, nurses lifelong envy of her fair cousin Adeline. She helps the rake Valmont ruin Adeline's husband, the vain old Baron Hulot, by plots. Debt, disgrace, and theft spread through the Hulot house as Bette pulls her strings. A Polish exile, Wenceslas, stands at the center of love, art, and betrayal in Paris. The book is Balzac at his most pitiless, swift, and hard to put down.
bellamy-looking-backward-1888:
Edward Bellamy imagined the year 2000 in Looking Backward, published in 1888. His hero, Julian West, sleeps in 1887 Boston and wakes in the Boston of 2000. That future city runs on socialist lines he could not have dreamed. A guide explains the new order of work, pay, and goods.

An industrial army organizes labor, and equal credit replaces wages and cash. Shops, music, and meals all run as public services in his design. The novel sold hugely and launched clubs devoted to its program. It became the era's best known utopian classic. Readers still visit its future to test their own hopes. The frame tale stays charming.
blavatsky-secret-doctrine-vol1-1888:
Helena Petrovna Blavatsky published Volume 1 of The Secret Doctrine in 1888, with the subtitle Cosmogenesis. Blavatsky, a cofounder of the Theosophical Society, claimed the book rested on an ancient hidden text, the Stanzas of Dzyan. Volume 1 treats the birth and order of the universe.

Blavatsky described worlds forming in great cycles, guided by spiritual beings, long before human life appears. She set Hindu, Buddhist, and other teachings beside the science of her day and claimed they agreed. Critics attacked her sources, but readers flocked to the system. The volume became the founding text of modern Theosophy and shaped occult thought far beyond her society.
blavatsky-secret-doctrine-vol2-1888:
Volume 2 of Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine, Anthropogenesis, also appeared in 1888. Where Volume 1 treated the cosmos, Volume 2 treated humankind. Blavatsky again built on the Stanzas of Dzyan, which she said held a secret record of human origins.

She described root races, early human forms said to arise on lost lands such as Lemuria and Atlantis. Apes, in her account, came from humans rather than the other way round, a direct clash with Darwin. She mixed myth, geology, and scripture into one vast scheme. The volume completed the work that made Theosophy a world movement and fed later lost-race and ancient-astronaut lore.
boas-central-eskimo-1888:
Franz Boas based this study on his stay on Baffin Land in the far north, and it came out in 1888. He worked for the Bureau of Ethnology in the United States. The book deals with the Inuit groups of the central Arctic coast.

Boas set down food, homes, tools, and trade, then turned to belief. He gave the first full account of the angakok, the Inuit shaman, and of taboos and views of the world. The work helped launch the modern study of peoples as a strict field craft. It is still read by all who study the Arctic past.
bosanquet-logic-vol1-1888:
Bernard Bosanquet's Logic, or The Morphology of Knowledge, from 1888, opens with volume one here. Morphology is the study of forms, and Bosanquet studies the forms of thought itself: how judgment and inference grow, stage by stage. He wrote as a British idealist, in the wake of Hegel, against the dry formal logic of the schools.

For Bosanquet, a judgment is not a label pasted on the world but the mind building its world into a system. Inference, likewise, is the self-development of knowledge toward a coherent whole. Volume one lays that living account of thought from its roots upward. The work remains a summit of idealist logic, exacting and rich.
bosanquet-logic-vol2-1888:
Volume two completes Bernard Bosanquet's Logic, or The Morphology of Knowledge, of 1888. Bosanquet, the British idealist, treats logic not as a rule book for arguments but as the anatomy of knowledge in growth. The two volumes together form his fullest statement on how thought builds a world.

The second volume carries the account of judgment and inference toward the system that all knowledge seeks. Each form of thought, for Bosanquet, corrects the one before it and points beyond itself. Truth lives in the coherence of the finished whole, not in single, severed claims. Readers who finish the Logic hold the British idealist theory of knowledge at its most developed.
brazilian-constitution-1988:
Brazil promulgated its present constitution in October 1988, closing twenty-one years of military rule. A freely elected constituent assembly wrote the text in public, hearing thousands of popular amendments from citizens' groups. Brazilians call it the citizens' constitution, a name its makers prized.

The charter restores democracy in full: direct elections, free parties, and a free press after decades of censorship. Its bill of rights is lavish in the modern Latin American style, promising health, education, and social security as duties of the state. Workers gain detailed protections, and the environment receives its own chapter. Critics call the text unwieldy; defenders answer that its promises were the point. The law of freedom regained still governs the giant of South America, the founding act of Brazil's New Republic.
