The title gives no place and names no victims, so the item's weight sits in whatever detail its pages carry. Killings on this scale were the civil war's darkest feature, and each one entered the files that later told the story.
cia-0000049188: A chronology of events surrounding the murder of the Jesuit priests at the Central American University fills a CIA item from 1990. Chronologies were the case's skeleton: hour by hour, who moved, who called, who arrived too late. This one survives in the Truth Commission files, where timelines tested every witness.
cia-0000049288:
The threat from the right in El Salvador is assessed in a CIA paper from 1983, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. The threat ran two ways at once: the right's violence against the country, and its power to wreck any government that crossed it. The paper weighs that double danger mid-war.

Inside, the right is read as a political force with armed hands, able to block reforms, frighten presidents, and kill with cover. Assessments like this one warned Washington that its client government sat beside the danger, not above it. The paper survives as a measure of how plainly the risk was stated at the time.
cia-0000096488: Violence and disruptive effects on the Cultural Revolution in the eastern provinces, in shortened heading form, fill declassified CIA document 0000096488, dated June 4, 1967. The title is cut short in the catalog at the province wording. Readers get a short declassified account of disorder in China, one of many such items filed that summer.
cia-0000105888: Dated February 4, 1965, declassified CIA document 0000105888 carries instructions from Sukarno for harassment of official Americans. Its heading misspells the word as Harrassment and breaks off at Induci. What the pressure was meant to induce is lost where the heading ends. The stated means is harassment itself, aimed at Americans serving in official posts there. The brief record preserves the misspelling and the ending as released.
cia-0000107288: Ambassador Says Living U.s. Mias Unlikely is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107288, dated June 5, 1991. The title attributes the same unlikely judgment to an ambassador, unnamed in the heading. A companion item with a near matching title is dated the same day. The brief record is a diplomatic comment item in the MIA cluster as released.
cia-0000108488: Dated January 1, 1982, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000108488 concerns an American priest murdered in Guatemala. Its catalog heading notes the title itself was deleted, then gives this subject. The priest is not named in the surviving heading text itself. The brief record preserves the deletion note with the estimated date as released.
cia-0000119588:
An August 1966 CIA document covers plans for a Czechoslovak government delegation to travel to North Vietnam. Prague was one of Hanoi's generous backers inside the communist bloc. A visit at that level was both a show of support and a working trip.

Delegation visits carried aid pledges, trade talks, and public signals of unity. The agency tracked such trips to gauge how deeply each bloc state was committed to Hanoi's war. The document follows the visit as it took shape in planning. For readers, it is a reminder that the Vietnam War drew in governments far from Southeast Asia. One was a Central European state with its own troubles at home.
cia-0000126888: Dated January 1968, this CIA report relays a Soviet official's comments on the possible renewal of Arab-Israeli fighting. Seven months after the Six-Day War, a new round was already being feared. The paper preserves Moscow's private reading of the tension as reported to the agency. Soviet officials spoke carefully in such settings, and a relayed remark was weighed in Washington as a clue to whether Moscow wanted calm or advantage next.
cia-0000132188: Situation report 505, from January 1991, records Moscow denying that it had military advisers in Iraq, the heading breaking off. The denial itself was the news, marking how far Moscow had moved from Baghdad. The report sets the denial down as issued. Denials from Moscow were printed and parsed like battlefield reports, because each one redrew the line between Iraq's old patron and its new isolation.
cia-0000132288: Situation Report 597 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 5, 1991, records political developments under a headline that breaks off after the words Iraq responds to. What Baghdad was responding to is lost with the missing part of the title. Even so, the short report preserves the fact of an Iraqi response at a tense point in the Gulf crisis.
cia-0000132488: Cuba building closer ties with Communist China fills a CIA document dated April 2, 1960. Beijing offered Havana a second patron besides Moscow. The split between the two communist giants was Cuba's chance to avoid total dependence on either one. The short document tracks the growing ties between the two revolutionary states that spring.
cia-0000132588: Moscow trying to exploit the Cuban situation fills a CIA document dated September 5, 1960. The Kremlin saw an opening in America's own backyard and moved to use it. That same month Khrushchev embraced Castro in public at the United Nations. The short document tracks Soviet efforts to profit from the quarrel between Washington and Havana.
cia-0000135688: This Spanish-language record, dated 1 November 1960, comes from the papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile unit the CIA prepared for the Bay of Pigs invasion. It shares its date with at least one other document in the release. The catalog supplies no subject for either. The item is therefore identified by date, language, and collection only: a piece of declassified exile paperwork in Spanish, held as the agency released it.
cia-0000135888: 2 May 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about a compromise of PBSUCCESS reported in May, the cover of the operation cracking near the end. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136088: A CIA cable from 6 March 1954, now declassified, deals with black flights, the secret air missions of the operation, in a cable addressed to Lugton. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136188: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 6 May 1954, covers air raid warnings, word that the bombs were coming as the air war turned real. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136288: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 2 May 1954, covers the case for broad authority to direct the work, argued in a cable from Lincoln in May. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136688: Dated 1 January 1961, this Spanish document opens the year's records in the declassified 2506 Brigade files. The brigade had one winter of training left before the Bay of Pigs. The catalog names no subject for the item, and several brigade records share its New Year date. It survives in Spanish as released by the CIA, part of the archive the exile force left behind.
cia-06052388: A contract got amended in this CIA file. The solicitation's terms changed, the procurement paperwork. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. This declassified document is preserved. The record is kept, the file remains, the document lasts.
collection-des-anciens-alchimistes-grecs: Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs, 1888. The Greek alchemists, first series. This book preserves that collection. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.

French scholars gathered Greece's old alchemists in this second volume. The ancient texts, translated and edited. The Hellenistic science, recovered. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This book preserves that scholarly collection. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.

Collection des Anciens Alchimistes Grecs, troisième livraison, 1888. The third volume. This book preserves that collection. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
craniognomy-1888: Craniognomy, 1888. The skull science. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
das-geheimnis-aller-geheimnisse-ex-macro: Das Geheimnis aller Geheimnisse, 1788. The secret of secrets. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
davenport-death-blow-spiritualism-1888:
Margaret Fox Kane confessed her fraud to reporter Reuben Briggs Davenport, and his 1888 book told the world. The Fox sisters' rappings of 1848 had launched modern spiritualism. Kane, one of the sisters, now described how the knocks were made. Davenport, of the New York World, shaped her confession into The Death-Blow to Spiritualism.

The book gives the true story of the sisters, in her account, trick by trick. Toe joints, she said, made the famous rapping sounds. Believers fought the confession, and Kane later withdrew it. Historians still treat the volume as a key insider record. It broke the founding story of spiritualism open.
dellon-history-of-the-inquisition-at-goa:
Charles Dellon, a French doctor, fell into the hands of the Inquisition at Goa and lived to write the tale. His Relation de l'Inquisition de Goa appeared in French in 1687, and this English version followed in 1688. Dellon had spent his youth traveling in India when the Holy Office seized him in 1673.

He tells of the secret arrest, the cells, and the long silence. The charges against him were never shown. At last he walked in the auto-da-fé of 1676 in the procession of the condemned. His book carried the horror of Goa across Protestant Europe. It fixed the Inquisition's image in the English mind for two centuries. Few eyewitness tales of the tribunal match it.
demille-strange-manuscript-copper-cylind:
James De Mille wrote A Strange Manuscript Found in a Copper Cylinder in the 1880s. The book came out in 1888, after his death. Four yachtsmen fish a copper case from the sea. In it lies the tale of Adam More, a castaway of the far south.

More tells of a warm land near the pole and its folk, the Kosekin. Their creed turns our world on its head: they court death and scorn wealth and love. More weds a Kosekin maid and flees with her at great cost. The tale is the chief lost race book of its land, Canada.
donnelly-great-cryptogram-1888:
Ignatius Donnelly turned from lost lands to a lost author in 1888. The Great Cryptogram argues that Francis Bacon hid a cipher in the plays called Shakespeare's, proving Bacon wrote them. The book runs to two fat volumes of counts, tables, and claims.

Donnelly counts words by page and line and draws out a hidden tale of Bacon's life at court. His cipher made him the star of the Baconian cause and a target for its foes. Scholars reject the method, but the book's craft made it hard to ignore. It stands as the founding text of cipher hunting in the plays.
dream-days-pg1288: Kenneth Grahame's 1898 companion to The Golden Age: five dreamy stories of childhood, including the first appearance of "The Reluctant Dragon." Told with exquisite nostalgia, they capture the secret world of children, half real and half imagined. The most poetic of all Victorian childhood books.
europmc-pmc10163288:
Bennett and a large team show how deep learning can improve the design of new protein binders, in a 2023 study. Designing proteins that grip a chosen target is a core skill in drug and sensor development. Energy-based design methods worked, but their success rate was low, so most designs failed in the lab.

The team added deep learning steps to sharpen the design process. Their tests show higher success in making binders that hold their targets as planned. Better design tools mean faster routes to new medicines and research tools.
europmc-pmc10216288:
Clemente-Suárez and colleagues review adipokines in health and disease in a 2023 paper. Adipokines are signaling proteins released by fat tissue. Far from being inert storage, fat acts as an organ that talks to the brain, liver, and immune system, and its signals are tied to low-grade inflammation and many diseases.

The review sorts the main adipokines and what each one does. It traces their roles in obesity, diabetes, heart disease, and joint problems. It also weighs their promise as markers and drug targets. The paper shows fat tissue in a new light.
europmc-pmc10379988:
Thang, Chien, and Cuong reviewed polymer-based hydrogels for drug delivery in 2023. A hydrogel is a net of water-loving chains that can hold much water. Such gels can store a drug and let it out slowly in the body. They are soft, body-friendly, and easy to tune.

New designs release drugs when a trigger fires, such as heat, acid level, or an enzyme. Thang notes that this aim can cut harm to the rest of the body. Some gels can be injected as a liquid and then set in place. Tiny nano gels may load and aim drugs still better. The review sees gels tuned to one patient as a growth path for care.
europmc-pmc10406888:
Bernardi gathered top experts in 2023 to settle a long fight over a pore in cell power units. The pore sits in the wall of mitochondria, the parts of a cell that make energy. When calcium floods in, the pore can open and let small bits pass. If it stays open, the unit swells and the cell may die.

Two parts have each been blamed as the pore itself. One is a mover of fuel bits, called ANT. The other is the cell's energy-making machine, ATP synthase. Bernardi weighs proof for both and seeks points of shared ground. Brief pore openings may be normal and useful, aiding energy balance and calcium flow. Long openings drive injury, such as after a blocked blood vessel reopens.
europmc-pmc10776388:
How much should scientists trust a shape guessed by AI? Terwilliger and co-authors take up that question in this 2024 paper. AlphaFold, a leading AI tool, has changed how biologists study proteins, which are the working parts inside cells. Yet its guesses vary in quality and leave out factors such as small bound molecules and cell conditions.

The team checked AlphaFold outputs against maps from lab tests that use X-ray beams on crystals. Many guesses matched the maps very closely. Others, even some rated as highly sure, were bent or placed whole sections in the wrong spot. The authors urge readers to treat each guess as a strong lead, not proof, and to test key details in the lab.
europmc-pmc11047988:
Maleki Varnosfaderani and Forouzanfar assess how AI is changing hospitals and clinics in this 2024 review. Health systems face rising costs, limited access, and growing demand for care tailored to each patient. AI is cast as a key force that could ease all three pressures. The authors set out to judge where it truly helps today.

Case studies cover four domains: clinical decisions, hospital operations, medical image reading, and patient monitoring through wearable devices. Each domain shows gains and leftover hurdles, the review finds. The authors also cover how to evaluate AI tools before use. Ethical risks get a full treatment, above all data privacy and bias in the data. They call for joint work among researchers, clinicians, and technologists to deploy AI responsibly.
europmc-pmc1112588:
Rastogi and Liberles model what happens to spare gene copies after duplication in this 2005 study. Gene duplication is a key source of new traits in evolution. One fate, called neofunctionalization, gives one copy a wholly new job. Another, subfunctionalization, splits the old job between the two copies. Which fate dominates was unclear.

The authors built lattice model genes, simple simulated proteins that fold and bind two targets. Each gene was duplicated in a small simulated population with no mixing of genes. Models that allowed job splitting reached new functions through it, they found. Job splitting acted as a transition state toward a new function, not as a final fate. No pressure kept both copies identical, they note. The result reframes how duplicated genes are retained.
europmc-pmc1247388:
Whyatt and colleagues measured prenatal insecticide exposure in New York City in 2004. Minority women faced wide insecticide exposure during pregnancy there. An earlier report tied cord blood chlorpyrifos to lower birth weight. The expanded study covered 314 mother and newborn pairs.

Air samples during pregnancy showed no link to birth size. Cord blood told a different story for chlorpyrifos. Each log unit rise cut birth weight by about 43 grams. Birth length fell by 0.24 cm per log unit. Combined chlorpyrifos and diazinon measures showed similar links. Whyatt separates air exposure from blood dose. Head size at birth showed no such link.
europmc-pmc1334188:
Hellens and co-authors built plant gene test vectors for fast experiments in 2005. The vectors use Agrobacterium bacteria to deliver genes into tobacco leaves. New pGreenII vectors were stripped of parts needed only for stable transforms. That trimming suits short-term expression tests.

One test expressed a P450 enzyme to prove the system works. Dual luciferase vectors measure promoter strength and gene regulation. Transcription factors were paired with target promoters to test control. Hairpin vectors probed how silencing constructs should be designed. Hellens gives plant labs a compact functional genomics toolkit.
europmc-pmc1462988:
Bacteria carry odd DNA arrays of short repeats, called CRISPR, next to a set of linked genes. Makarova and co-authors asked in 2006 what this system does. Past work guessed it fixed DNA damage. The tight link between the repeats and the genes hinted at a shared task instead.

Sorting the linked proteins into about 25 families, Makarova saw a pattern. The parts mirror, in role, the RNA interference system that guards complex cells from viruses. She proposes the arrays act as an immune system. Stored bits of invader DNA guide attacks on matching germs and plasmids, small DNA rings. The idea recast CRISPR as defense, not repair.
europmc-pmc1621088:
Treating culture as a checklist for clinicians can backfire. Kleinman and Benson made that argument in 2006, examining cultural competency, a popular approach in medicine. It trains doctors in supposed beliefs of ethnic groups, as in the Mexican patient or the Chinese patient.

Anthropology, where the culture concept began, rejects such fixed group portraits as stereotyping. Culture is not a synonym for ethnicity or language. Kleinman notes culture is not always at the heart of a case, and leaning on it can block a practical grasp of a patient's real problem. They propose fixing the approach rather than teaching lists of do's and don'ts.
europmc-pmc1849888:
Chen, Roos and colleagues ran a head-to-head test in 2007 of programs that find orthologs, genes in different species descended from one ancestral gene. Spotting orthologs underpins gene annotation and genome comparison. No gold-standard dataset existed at genome scale, so the methods had never been fairly graded.

The team used latent class analysis, a statistical trick that infers accuracy from agreement and disagreement between methods, without a truth set. A clear trade-off emerged on the eukaryotic data tested. Methods built on BLAST searches caught more true pairs but admitted more errors, while tree-based methods were stricter and missed more. Two tools balanced best, with sensitivity and specificity both above 80 percent: INPARANOID for pairs of species, and OrthoMCL for grouping many species at once.
europmc-pmc1852588:
Zhang, Jacobsen and co-authors mapped in 2007 a silencing mark across the whole genome of the plant Arabidopsis thaliana. The mark is three methyl tags on one spot of histone H3, a spool protein that DNA wraps around. In animals the mark is vital for development, but its plant reach was unknown.

Using a dense tiling chip that covers the genome, they found the mark on about 4,400 genes. That makes it a major silencing system in plants. Its upkeep proved largely independent of DNA methylation and RNA interference, two other silencing routes. Unlike animals, where the mark spans huge regions, plant marks were confined to the transcribed part of single genes. They also avoided the low-density DNA packaging zones seen in animal genomes.
europmc-pmc2025288:
Hayward and co-authors proposed in 1977 a shared system for judging treatment response in advanced breast cancer. The project came from the International Union Against Cancer, known as the UICC. Different centres were using different evaluation methods, making published results hard to compare. A single uniform system promised fair comparison across trials. Breast cancer was chosen first because agreement seemed within reach.

A draft document was circulated widely to workers in the field for comment. It was then revised before final publication. The guidelines serve trials that assess objective response in locally advanced or spreading breast cancer. Subjective response, how a patient feels, is not covered. Eligibility requires tissue proof of breast cancer available for review. The British Breast Group accepted the system, replacing its earlier method.
europmc-pmc2125288: A medical paper studying Barlow's disease produced in fetal and newborn guinea pigs. The scurvy model. This article preserves that nutrition research. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2126288: A medical paper with a report on antimeningitis vaccination and observations on agglutinins. The meningitis shot. This article preserves that immunology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128088: A medical paper on measurement of the growth of tissues in vitro. The measured growth. This article preserves that cell biology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
europmc-pmc2128188: A medical paper on the effect of induced cellular reaction on cancer grafts' fate. The grafts, rejected. This article preserves that oncology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128288: A medical paper on epinephrine content of the suprarenal glands in anaphylaxis. The shock glands. This article preserves that endocrinology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
europmc-pmc2128388: A medical paper on leucocytic secretions. The white cells' output. This article preserves that immunology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128488: A medical paper on measurement of the inherent growth energy of tissues. The tissues' vigor. This article preserves that cell biology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2128588: A medical paper with studies on oxidation by pneumococcus, oxidation of enzymes. The germ's rust again. This article preserves that biochemistry. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2131088: A medical paper with studies on tumor susceptibility and heredity. The inherited cancers. This article preserves that oncology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131488: A medical paper on the transfer of rat anemia to normal animals. The passed anemia. This article preserves that hematology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2140088:
Pinkas, Strop, Brunger and Khosla solved the active structure in 2007 of human transglutaminase 2, an enzyme that crosslinks proteins. Called TG2, it shapes tissue matrix and drives the gluten reaction in celiac disease. Earlier structures of related enzymes all showed closed forms with hidden active sites. The team trapped TG2 with an inhibitor mimicking inflammatory gluten peptides, then read its structure by X-ray crystallography at fine resolution.

The trapped enzyme sat in an extended shape, dramatically different from earlier structures. Its active site was exposed, revealing a tunnel where the reaction happens. Two tryptophan residues bridge the tunnel and stabilise the reaction steps. Mutations on one side shifted the enzyme toward breaking down rather than crosslinking. The structure grounds new work on TG2's roles and on the celiac autoantibody response.
europmc-pmc2199288:
Calafat and colleagues measured two industrial chemicals in urine from a national United States survey in 2008. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is used in polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins. The second chemical, tOP, is used in surfactants. The team analysed urine from 2,517 participants aged six and older in the 2003-2004 survey, using sensitive mass spectrometry methods.

BPA was detected in 92.6 percent of people, and tOP in 57.4 percent of them. Exposure was near-universal across the general population in the United States. The sample was nationally representative and covered children and adults during the survey years. Children carried higher BPA levels than adolescents, who carried more than adults. Females had higher levels than males. Mexican Americans had lower levels than non-Hispanic black or white participants. Levels were lowest in the highest income group.
europmc-pmc2246288:
Blenkiron and co-workers profiled microRNA expression in human breast cancer in 2007, seeking markers of tumour subtype. MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression. The team profiled 99 primary tumours, five normal breast samples and 33 cancer cell lines with a bead-based platform covering 309 human microRNAs. They combined expression data with genomic changes measured in the same tumours.

The platform detected 133 microRNAs expressed in normal breast or tumours, out of 137 found overall. Results proved reproducible and matched independent PCR checks for a subset. Integrated analysis of microRNA expression and genomic changes classified tumours into their subtypes. The authors present the combined approach as a way to find new subtype markers. Such markers could sharpen diagnosis and point to subtype-specific biology in breast cancer.
europmc-pmc2374988:
Teschendorff and co-authors sorted a hard-to-treat breast cancer group into subtypes in 2007. These cancers lack the estrogen receptor, a hormone sensor, so hormone drugs do not work on them. The team used a feature selection method, a computer routine that picks the most telling genes, across three large gene activity data sets.

Their analysis showed this cancer group is not one disease. It holds at least four main subtypes with distinct gene patterns. One subtype stood out: its tumors carried a strong immune response gene module, meaning a set of immune genes switched on together. Patients with that immune-rich subtype had a good prognosis, a better outlook than the others. The authors presented the module as a marker that could guide how hard to treat these patients.
europmc-pmc2396288:
Eddy tackles a hidden cost in DNA database searches in this 2008 theory paper. Searching compares a query pattern against millions of sequences and scores each match. Judging whether a score could arise by chance needs a statistical formula, and one key constant in it used to require slow computer simulations to pin down.

Eddy proposed that with full probabilistic scoring, the constant takes a simple fixed value: the natural log of 2. He argued the best-match scores then follow a known bell-like curve for extremes, called a Gumbel distribution. The total-evidence scores, called Forward scores, should fade off in a matching simple pattern. Simulations across 9,318 protein family models from the Pfam database backed both claims. The result makes significance values fast and accurate to compute for both score types.
europmc-pmc2491588:
O'Brien and colleagues showed that a hormone receptor inside bone's buried cells controls bone mass in 2008. Osteocytes are former bone-building cells trapped inside the bone itself, long suspected of directing remodelling. Parathyroid hormone, PTH, drives remodelling but can add or remove bone. Whether it acts through osteocytes was unknown.

The team engineered mice whose osteocytes carry an always-on PTH receptor. These mice built higher bone mass with faster remodelling: more bone-eating and bone-building cells, and fewer builder cells dying. Their osteocytes made less sclerostin, a protein that blocks the Wnt growth signal, so Wnt signalling rose. Removing the Wnt partner receptor LRP5 blunted the extra mass but not the faster remodelling. The study splits PTH's osteocyte effects into two routes, one needing LRP5 for mass and one driving turnover without it.
europmc-pmc2553488:
Hotez and colleagues mapped the overlooked diseases of the tropics in Latin America and the Caribbean in this 2008 review. These diseases afflict the region's poorest people. Many patients are indigenous or of African descent. The authors gathered burden data, meaning case counts and healthy years lost, to rank the diseases and chart where they cluster.

Hookworm and other gut worm infections, plus Chagas disease, carried the heaviest burden, ahead of better-known threats in total impact. Then came dengue, schistosomiasis, and leishmaniasis. Trachoma, leprosy, and lymphatic filariasis followed. The diseases cluster in 11 sub-regions with distinct ecologies. The authors judge that schistosomiasis could be eliminated from the Caribbean, while the biggest burdens first need scaled-up resources or new control tools.
europmc-pmc2575188:
Jensen, Jørgensen, Binderup, and Kjaer compared in 2008 three ways of measuring tumour size in cancer drug studies on mice. Researchers judge treatments by tumour volume, usually measured with external calipers, a technique prone to error. The team implanted human breast cancer cells under the skin of 20 mice. They measured each tumour three ways: by caliper, by microCT scanning, and by PET imaging. Then they weighed the true volume after removal.

All three methods tracked the true volume, but microCT showed no systematic bias while calipers and PET both did. Repeated measurements by one observer varied by 7 percent with microCT. With calipers the figure was 14 percent. Two observers also agreed more closely with the scanner. The authors judge PET unsuitable for sizing and recommend microCT over calipers.
europmc-pmc2613888:
Oñate-Sánchez and Vicente-Carbajosa published streamlined protocols in 2008 for extracting pure, DNA-free RNA from the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Gene expression measurement by quantitative PCR demands RNA with no contaminating DNA, yet standard protocols are laborious, use toxic chemicals, and still need an enzyme cleanup step. Seeds and seed pods are especially awkward tissues.

Their two protocols use simple, non-toxic buffers for most tissues. They reserve organic extraction for seeds and siliques, the seed pods. Contaminating DNA is removed before the final precipitation step, skipping extra purification. Starting material can be as small as 10 to 20 milligrams without losing quality. Tests on genes with known expression patterns confirmed the RNA works reliably, and the low cost suits high-throughput work.
europmc-pmc2614188:
Nilsson, Kristiansson, Ryberg, Hallenberg, and Larsson measured in 2008 how much the standard fungal barcode region varies within species across the whole fungal kingdom. The region, called ITS, is the most popular locus for identifying fungi from DNA, and automated identifiers assume variation within a species stays clearly below variation between species. The team mined the international sequence databases for all fungi with enough data.

They found substantial differences across the kingdom that did not track taxonomy or lifestyle in any simple way. Some groups varied little within species, others a great deal. No single ceiling, including the canonical 3 percent threshold, separated within-species from between-species variation throughout the fungi. The authors caution against simplified automated identifications and stress that translating sequences into species names still needs taxonomic expertise.
europmc-pmc2631488:
Langfelder and Horvath published the WGCNA software package in 2008, implementing weighted gene co-expression network analysis in the R language. The method groups genes by how similarly they behave across samples, forming correlation networks whose clusters, or modules, often share a biological job. Earlier descriptions of the method were scattered across papers, leaving users without a single consistent tool.

The package covers the whole workflow. It builds networks and detects modules. It summarises each module by its eigengene, a representative activity profile. It also relates modules to each other and to outside traits such as disease state. It also computes module membership scores, simulates data, and draws visualisations. Applications already span cancer, mouse and yeast genetics, and brain imaging. The package and tutorials are freely available online.
europmc-pmc2845588:
Park, Chyun, Kim, Line, and Chew ran a controlled trial in 2010 of astaxanthin, the red pigment that colors salmon and shrimp shells, in young healthy women. Cell and rodent studies had cast it as a strong antioxidant that calms inflammation and perks up immunity, but human data were missing. Forty-two women took zero, two, or eight milligrams daily for eight weeks.

Blood levels of the pigment rose with dose. A DNA damage marker fell by week four, and an inflammation marker dropped in the low-dose group by week eight. Immune tests improved: killer cell activity rose, lymphocyte growth after stimulation rose, and skin test responses strengthened in the low-dose group. Two immune signals also rose at the high dose, rounding out a broad immune lift.
europmc-pmc2873288:
Diaz de Leon and colleagues studied in 2010 families whose faulty telomerase gene leads to scarred lungs in middle age. Telomerase rebuilds telomeres, the DNA caps that shorten each time a cell divides. Faults in its protein part, TERT, had turned up in some patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, lung scarring without a clear cause.

Across twenty-one families and one hundred thirty-four carriers, cap length shrank with age and shortened further in each new generation. Relatives without the faulty gene still had shorter caps than normal, showing caps themselves are inherited as well. Lung scarring never appeared before age forty but struck about sixty percent of carriers past that age, making the condition a slow countdown written into chromosome ends.
europmc-pmc2876988:
Schultz reviewed in 2010 what single dopamine neurons in the midbrain actually signal about reward, drawing on recordings from awake monkeys. Dopamine cells were long cast as pure pleasure signals based on lesion and drug studies. Fine-grained recordings during behavior tasks reveal a much more precise code.

The cells fire in brief bursts that report reward value compared with what was expected, a prediction error signal that learning theory requires for teaching. The burst size scales with value and probability combined into expected value, and it is measured against the spread of recent outcomes. Far fewer cells respond to punishers or merely startling events, so the signal is not general arousal. Some cells also flag risk, giving the brain a compact value-and-risk report for choices.
europmc-pmc2892488:
Darling, Mau, and Perna released in 2010 progressiveMauve, a program that aligns whole genomes even after evolution has shuffled, gained, and lost large chunks. Simple aligners assume the same parts in the same order, but real genomes rearrange, duplicate segments, and drop genes, leaving a mosaic of shared blocks. Their method finds blocks conserved in only some of the genomes, a case earlier tools missed.

A new scoring rule judges candidate breakpoints, the joints where shuffling happened, and a probability filter strips out chance matches between unrelated stretches. Fresh accuracy metrics measure breakpoint and gap calls separately. On simulated and real bacterial genomes with heavy reshuffling, accuracy stayed high. The tool became a workhorse for comparing pathogen genomes during outbreak tracing.
europmc-pmc2920088:
Steenland, Fletcher, and Savitz reviewed in 2010 the human evidence on PFOA, the persistent chemical once essential to nonstick coatings. It does not occur naturally, yet it sits in the blood of nearly everyone in industrialized countries, with a typical United States level near four nanograms per milliliter. The body does not break it down, and clearing half takes about three years.

Animal studies tie it to tumors and to immune, liver, and hormone effects. Human studies, mostly snapshots that cannot prove direction, most consistently link higher PFOA with higher cholesterol and uric acid, though the cholesterol pattern shifts oddly across exposure levels. Liver enzyme links were weaker and less consistent. Drinking water drives exposure in some communities, but general sources remain poorly mapped.
europmc-pmc2944788:
Hayes and co-authors compared how gene effects are spread for three cattle traits in 2010, asking what that spread means for predicting breeding worth from DNA markers. Holstein cows supplied the test traits: black coat share, milk fat share, and an overall body score.

Coat colour rested on three known loci explaining about a quarter of variation, plus many tiny effects elsewhere. Milk fat had one large-effect locus and a swarm of small ones. The body score showed only small effects throughout. These contrasts, measured over chromosome chunks, explain why DNA prediction accuracy differs between traits.
europmc-pmc2945788:
Goecks, Nekrutenko, and Taylor presented Galaxy, a free web platform for genome analysis, in a 2010 article with the Galaxy Team. Computer-heavy biology raised worries that results were hard for others to repeat or even to run.

Galaxy records where every dataset came from and the exact steps applied, so analyses can be shared, rerun, and checked. Its Pages feature lets authors publish a full analysis as an interactive document mixing data, tools, and explanation. The design targets researchers without programming training who still need careful, transparent computing for sequencing and other large-scale data.
europmc-pmc3103488:
Shahedur Rahman and Rezuanul Islam wrote a 2011 review in Cell Communication and Signaling about Sirt1, a protein found in mammals. Sirt1 removes small chemical tags from other proteins and needs a common cell fuel to do so. Their article gathers what was known about its many jobs in the body.

The review covers Sirt1 in fat tissue, the liver, the heart, and the brain, and links it to weight gain, cancer, aging, and cell wear over time. It also treats stress responses, early growth, and survival of placental cells. For readers, the paper offers a single map of a protein tied to diet, lifespan, and disease.
europmc-pmc3125288:
Cyril Vidau and colleagues tested combined stresses on honey bees in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Bee numbers are falling worldwide, and both gut parasites and farm insecticides are suspects. The team infected young bees with a common gut parasite, then fed some of them very low, non-lethal doses of two widely used insecticides.

Infected bees exposed to either insecticide died at clearly higher rates than bees facing only one stress. Oddly, the two chemicals pushed parasite spore output in opposite directions. Infection did raise activity of one detox enzyme in gut and fat tissue, so simple detox failure does not explain the deaths. The authors argue that parasite spread plus chemical traces in hives together help drive colony losses.
europmc-pmc3125388:
Sandra Thygesen and colleagues checked hospital coding accuracy in Denmark in a 2011 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Researchers often use a standard index of nineteen long-term diseases to adjust hospital studies, trusting that registry codes match real diagnoses. The team audited that trust against patient records.

They reviewed discharge papers and charts for fifty hospital contacts per disease, drawn from a decade of northern Danish admissions. Nearly every coded diagnosis was confirmed on review. Twelve of the nineteen diseases scored perfectly, and the weakest, diabetes with complications, still scored well above four fifths correct. The authors conclude the registry codes are reliable enough for comorbidity adjustment in research, at least in this Danish setting.
europmc-pmc3155788:
Maura Lodovici and Elisabetta Bigagli reviewed how polluted air harms the body through oxidative stress in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Toxicology. Dirty air is tied to more heart and lung disease and death, and the leading explanation runs through unstable oxygen chemicals that inflame and kill cells. The review gathers the evidence pollutant by pollutant.

Fine and ultrafine particles, ozone, nitrogen gases, and metals in particles can all generate those chemicals directly or provoke cells to make them. Traffic exhaust is a major source of the smallest particles, which reach deep into lungs and can enter the blood. How much harm follows depends partly on how well each organ can raise its own protective scavenging systems. The authors stress that particle mix, not just particle amount, shapes the health impact.
europmc-pmc3203188:
Eric Feeley and colleagues investigated how the protein IFITM3 blocks influenza A virus, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. IFITM3 is switched on by interferon, the alarm signal cells release during infection, and it was known to restrict several viruses in the lab. The team wanted to pin down exactly where it stops the virus.

They showed that interferon prevents viral genomes from escaping the cell's endosomal compartments, and that this block needs IFITM3, which by itself can produce it. Test particles could not deliver their contents into the cell interior when IFITM3 was present. The protein sits in late endosomes and lysosomes, right in the path of incoming viruses, which explains why viruses that fuse there are vulnerable while surface-entering ones may slip past.
europmc-pmc3231888:
Laura Lamberti and colleagues pooled the evidence that breastfeeding protects babies and toddlers from diarrhea, in this 2011 review in BMC Public Health. Diarrhea remains a major killer of young children in poorer countries, and feeding practices in the first two years shape the risk. The team systematically gathered studies published over three decades.

Across eighteen studies, breastfeeding protected against diarrhea illness, prevalence, hospital admission, and death, with the strongest protection from exclusive breastfeeding in the first six months and from any breastfeeding thereafter. Not breastfeeding at all carried a many-fold higher risk of diarrhea death for young infants compared with exclusive breastfeeding. The authors say the results back the World Health Organization recommendation of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months as a key child-survival measure.
europmc-pmc3282688:
Shangong Wu and colleagues catalogued the bacteria living in the grass carp's intestine, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. The gut community matters for managing farmed animals, yet basic information for many species is thin. Using gene sequencing of intestinal contents and of the fish's culture environment, the team asked what lives in the gut and where it comes from.

The intestine harbored many cellulose-digesting bacteria, fitting the fish's plant diet, and its most abundant members were tied to feed digestion. Potential pathogens and probiotics were both present as important members. A core community of three bacterial phyla ran through the samples. The gut community resembled those of the culture water and sediment most closely, marking them as major sources, though feed also significantly shaped what lived in the fish.
europmc-pmc3375788:
Van Tu and colleagues investigated hand, foot, and mouth disease in southern Vietnam in 2007, focusing on the 2005 season. The illness brings a few days of fever plus sores in the mouth and a rash on hands, feet, and buttocks. Several related enteroviruses can cause it, but one stood out as dangerous.

Enterovirus 71, the team found, was strongly tied to acute brain and nerve disease, while coxsackievirus A16 was not. Young children under five faced the greatest risk of lasting harm or death. Brain inflammation in the region was shifting toward younger children, which had prompted the study. The results argue for close virus tracking during outbreaks.
europmc-pmc3410788:
Wen, Shen, Shi, and Tang built a software platform in 2012 for tracing how microRNAs evolve across species. These tiny RNAs steer many body processes, and deep sequencing now finds them by the thousand in plants and animals. Few tools, though, could follow their sequence and activity changes across species at once.

Their platform, miREvo, combines three jobs behind a graphical interface. It discovers new microRNAs in sequencing data, finds their counterparts in other species using whole-genome alignments and measures their distances, and profiles how strongly each is expressed in each species. Tests on fruit fly and plant data showed the pipeline working end to end. The free tool targets evolutionary studies of small RNAs.
europmc-pmc3458588:
Gänzle and Follador reviewed in 2012 how lactobacilli, the lactic acid bacteria of food and gut, eat short sugar chains and starch. These chains, built of a few sugar units, are staple food in the bacteria's habitats and central to their ecological success. Two-sugar metabolism is well understood; longer chains had drawn less study until interest in gut ecology and prebiotic foods arrived.

The review walks through five chain families plus starch, using data on where each enzyme sits in the cell and what the transporters accept. Pathways for two-unit sugars often stretch to three and four units too. But nearly all the cutting enzymes stay inside the cell, so import is the choke point. That single constraint, the authors note, sets lactobacilli apart from gut specialists that digest outside.

french-chemists-essai-phlogistique-1788:
In 1788 the lead chemists of France took Kirwan's defense of phlogiston and turned it into French, with notes that hit back at each claim. The team held Guyton de Morveau, Lavoisier, Laplace, Monge, Berthollet, and Fourcroy. It was a joint strike by the new school in one book.

Page by page, their notes show where Kirwan's scheme fails the test of weight and trial. Kirwan read the notes, gave up his old scheme, and joined the new camp in time. French in tongue, the book is the death writ of the old chemistry.
frus-1861-d188:
On 29 April 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Mr. King as part of his first great round of orders. The letter is document 188 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The record heading gives King no post, so the letter stands on its date and its writer. April 1861 was the month Seward stocked the whole service with fresh orders. His note to King joins the first great round of direction that followed the fall of Sumter. April rounds like this one show the service being manned for war at full speed. Full speed in April set a pace the service kept through the whole year.
frus-1861-d288:
Mr. Morgan reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 6 April 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 288 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the month the Civil War began, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d88:
Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 September 1861. It is document 88 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two reports in one day suggest a post dealing with more than one live point. Adams kept his files as clean as Seward kept his. The second letter rounds out a dense month in the fullest correspondence of the 1861 record. The double report closes a month in which the London file grew by a third. A third more paper in one month shows the post at full wartime stretch.
frus-1862-d188:
The fourth Seward letter of 10 November 1862 closes the set as Document 188 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like the other three, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London.

A four-letter mail shows how much business one legation could carry: talks with ministers, shipyard reports, press reaction, and cases of detained ships or men. No one letter tells that whole story. Preserved together, the set lets readers see the London post's full load in a single week of November 1862. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d288:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 20 June 1862, and the first is Document 288 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Seward wrote a week before Lee's counterstroke drove McClellan from Richmond, at the last moment of the spring's optimism. His instructions in this pair carried the Department's line into a summer that would test it hard. Reading them now, with the sequel known, shows how much wartime policy was written in honest uncertainty. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d388:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg on 13 August 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 388 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-August 1862 brought the opening of the campaign that ended at Bull Run, though no one could know its result when Seward wrote. His letters to Russia that summer carried the Union's case to its friendliest hearing in Europe. This dispatch shows the Department cultivating that friendship deliberately, even while its attention was consumed by Britain and France. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d488:
On 15 March 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The instruction is Document 488 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Mid-March found Union forces advancing on several fronts, and Seward's letters abroad pressed the theme that the rebellion was losing ground. At The Hague the practical questions were maritime: Dutch ports, Dutch colonies, and the rules belligerent ships must obey. Pike's value to Washington lay in his blunt, newsman's grasp of Dutch opinion. An instruction like this one set the points he was to make. It even set the order he was to make them in. He would use them at his next meeting with Dutch officials.
frus-1862-d588:
On 28 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Thomas Corwin, the American minister in Mexico. The instruction is Document 588 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

By late May the French were advancing into Mexico's interior and the question for Washington was how far protest could safely go. Seward's orders to Corwin kept the American position clear. The United States wished Mexico well. It opposed the European enterprise. It would not be drawn into a second war. Corwin's own instincts ran hotter, which made exact instructions necessary. The dispatch shows the leash and the trust between a secretary and a distinguished minister in the hemisphere's hardest post.

frus-1863p1-d388:
