Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d488:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 2 May 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d588:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington addressed a formal note to Secretary William H. Seward on 16 July 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d688:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, on 11 November 1863. It appears as document 688 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, the State Department's printed record of its wartime mail.

The day after his 10 November notes, Seward wrote again, which shows how fast matters could move. Union and British officials clashed at times over seized ships and Southern agents in British ports. Short notes like this one kept those clashes from growing. The reader gets a close look at the craft of calm words. Each line was meant to hold a line without giving offense.
frus-1863p1-d88:
Charles Francis Adams closed his mail day with this third dispatch of 19 February 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 88 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three sheets in a day was no rare thing at the London post in 1863. The work spanned talks with Lord Russell, the temper of Parliament, and word on ships built for the South. This letter ends the day's set. Filed with the rest, it is part of the great run that makes this volume the chief printed source. That source tells the Union's fight to keep Britain neutral.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d188:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 4 November 1943 in telegram number 407, a short secret message sent from Washington. It settles the American position on Turkey just after the Moscow foreign ministers' conference, where the Soviet Union had pushed hard for Turkey to join the war.

Roosevelt agrees that the United States will join Britain and the Soviet Union in demanding Turkish air bases at once. He also agrees to press Turkey to enter the war before the end of the year. One condition is attached: no British or American forces needed for Overlord, the planned invasion of France, or for the fighting in Italy may be diverted to the eastern Mediterranean.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d288:
A United States delegation memorandum at Cairo on 23 November 1943 answers reports that Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek feared the Soviet Union meant to back the Chinese Communists against his regime. Preserved in the Hopkins Papers, the paper was probably written by Harry Hopkins, with a final sentence added by Ambassador Harriman.

Its reading of Moscow is reassuring. The Soviet government, it says, wants peace inside China under a strong central government. It knows that can come only through the Generalissimo. It holds no ambitions for Chinese territory in general, as its pullout from Sinkiang shows. It will press Chiang toward a more liberal policy, and toward some settlement with the Communists, as a party or inside his government. Korea might win independence under a four-power trusteeship.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d388:
President Roosevelt handed Marshal Stalin a secret paper at Tehran on 29 November 1943 on advance planning for air operations in the northwestern Pacific. Like its companion papers of that day, it looks past Germany's defeat to the war against Japan.

Bombing Japan from the Soviet Maritime Provinces, Roosevelt argues, would be of the utmost importance, Roosevelt argues. That importance would come once war between the Soviet Union and Japan began. Allied bombers could then destroy Japanese military and industrial centers. He asks Stalin to have his military mission in Moscow given the facts on airports, housing, supplies, communications, and weather in that region and on the route from Alaska. The aim is to base the largest bomber force the facilities allow, That could run anywhere from one hundred to a thousand four-engined bombers. Surveys are to be kept to a very few men, in the utmost secrecy.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d488:
Harry Hopkins wrote to British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden on December 5, 1943, and Eden's reply is printed with the message. The exchange took place during the Second Cairo Conference, where Eden attended with Churchill. The State Department preserved both sides in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Printing a message together with its answer lets the reader watch a piece of business open and close. Hopkins, who held no cabinet post, dealt directly with Britain's foreign secretary as Roosevelt's personal agent. The exchange shows foreign policy being handled by the leaders' inner circles at a summit, rather than through the normal exchange of notes between capitals.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d88: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on November 2, 1943, one of several messages between the capitals that day. It is Document 88 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. By early November the Cairo and Tehran plans were fixed in outline and argued in detail, and the correspondence thickened. The catalog record supplies the date and the two names. The text in the Foreign Relations series is the source for its errand.
frus-1944-quebec-d188: An editors' note marks a meeting in the Quebec Conference record whose substance is entirely lost. No record has been found of what was discussed. The time of the meeting and the names of the American and British participants come from the President's Log. Mackenzie King's presence is noted from the New York Times of September 15, 1944. The note stands in the volume so that the gap is visible rather than silent.
frus-1944-quebec-d288:
The communiqué issued at Quebec on September 16, 1944, is the conference's public face. It announces that the president, the prime minister, and the Combined Chiefs had discussed all aspects of the war against Germany and Japan. In a very short space of time, it says, they reached decisions on all points. These covered completing the European war, now approaching its final stages. They also covered the destruction of "the barbarians of the Pacific."

Its best-known sentence came from Marshall's suggestion, drafted by Ismay. The most serious difficulty confronting the conference, the communiqué declares, had been finding room and opportunity for marshalling against Japan the massive forces every nation concerned was ardent to engage. The line turned a logistics problem into a boast.
frus-1944-quebec-d88:
McCloy wrote again to Matthews on September 6, 1944. John J. McCloy served as Assistant Secretary of War. H. Freeman Matthews held a senior post in European affairs. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume.

Repeated letters between the same aides show working ties, not ceremony. War and State officials traded drafts and views on Europe daily. The Quebec Conference opened six days after this message. For readers, the letter captures preparation at the level where policy forms. Two experienced officials aligned their departments before the summit began. Their exchange is printed in the conference volume.
frus-1945-50-intel-d188:
A memorandum dated 28 February 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Acheson). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 188 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d288:
A text titled "Note by the Executive Secretary (Souers) to the National Security Council" bears the date 15 June 1948. It survives in print as document 288 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Such a note often marks the end of a chain: the talk is over, the choice is made, and this page says so. A short memo for the record can settle who knew what, and when, better than a long report written months later. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d388:
Dated 15 July 1949, this letter runs from Attorney General Clark to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). It is document 388 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Two years into the CIA's life, the question in these papers is less how to build it than how to fix it.

The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. Letters like this one let a reader follow a debate between two offices in their own words. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d88:
Russell wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 18 April 1946, returning to the intelligence office's affairs in the spring of transfers. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By April, the Central Intelligence Group was standing up under its first director, and the State office's analysts were being counted for moves. Russell's paper to the secretary belongs to that reckoning. Readers can follow the administration thread to its end here. The office that the department had housed since September was being fitted into a smaller, durable shape. The tone of such papers, careful and unsentimental, is the sound of a government keeping what it needs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d188:
Two short texts close the Italy quarrel in this exchange of 9 December 1944. Lord Halifax writes to Stettinius from Washington, forwarding a personal message from Anthony Eden. Both are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Halifax has just received the telegram from London and passes Eden's words on at once. Eden thanks Stettinius warmly for the helpful and understanding message that reached him through Winant. His keen desire, he writes, is that the two should work close together. After a week of hurt statements, the exchange marks the deliberate repair of a personal tie. The quarrel had run over Count Sforza and the Italian cabinet.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d288:
Harriman's reading of the Soviet press reached the President on 12 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew's covering memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, encloses the ambassador's ninth interpretive report on Soviet policy. It covers the period from 13 October to 31 December 1944.

The report's summary draws a clear picture. A relative lull on the Eastern Front has given the Soviet Union the chance to pursue its political aims in the lands its army has freed. As a result, the pattern of Soviet tactics in Eastern Europe and the Balkans has taken shape. The nature of Soviet aims, Harriman concludes, has been clarified in the process. Grew urges the President to read at least the opening paragraphs before he meets Stalin.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d388:
Genealogy of a draft fills Stettinius's cable to Grew of February 8, 1945. The text Grew had asked about, Stettinius explained, was a British redraft of a Soviet redraft. In origin it was a headquarters paper from Eisenhower's command. The British had since made a few changes, which Stettinius felt could be accepted without reservation.

London was most anxious to put the draft to the Russians that day. The Joint Chiefs were in full agreement, and Stettinius had authorized talks on its basis. He noted the draft left out points Washington had embodied in its note. The cable untangles who wrote what in the prisoner agreement.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d488:
Ambassador Patrick Hurley proposed a summit of his own in this top secret cable to the President, sent February 8, 1945. It had been suggested, he wrote, that Roosevelt and Churchill visit Delhi. The Generalissimo and his staff would be invited to meet them there. Such a meeting would be a great morale builder in the China theater.

It would also let the leaders clarify policies and strategy. Delhi was suggested over any place in China for two reasons: security and accommodations. The meeting might even make a proposed Washington conference by General Wedemeyer unnecessary. Hurley asked for the President's earliest word. Nothing came of the plan, but the cable shows every theater bidding for the travelers.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d88:
Gromyko asked for a second meeting, and on 13 January 1945 he and Pasvolsky talked for over two and a half hours. Pasvolsky's record is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The talk ranged across the whole Dumbarton Oaks plan for a world organization.

The ambassador opened by saying he had thought hard about their earlier discussion and re-read the President's proposal. One paragraph still puzzled him, the one on regional bodies and peaceful settlement. Pasvolsky explained that it asked whether the Council should encourage a regional group to settle a local dispute. Gromyko thought that logical within the general formula. He wanted one more talk before leaving for Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d188:
Ambassador Lord Halifax delivered a British warning on Poland in an extract dated July 5, 1945. The extract is document 188 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full note, addressed to Secretary Byrnes, appears later in the volume.

Britain is going ahead with recognizing the new Polish Government of National Unity, Halifax reports. But the Foreign Office is by no means satisfied with the assurances given. Those assurances concerned letting the recognized Polish parties take part in the promised elections. The British ambassador in Moscow has been told to inform the Soviet government at once. He is to say that the Prime Minister reserves the right to raise the matter. He would raise it at the meeting of the three heads of state. The point, Halifax stresses, goes to whether the Crimea decisions are carried out.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d288:
A background paper laid out Romania's armistice and politics, dated July 5, 1945. The paper is document 288 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is the briefing book's country study of the largest of the former satellite states.

Romania accepted armistice terms on September 12, 1944. The Allied Control Commission set up to enforce them is in practice run by its Soviet member, who interprets and enforces the terms without reference to the American and British representatives. Heavy Soviet demands and new economic agreements will likely break down Romania's economy and tie it to the Soviet Union, the paper warns. The Groza government, imposed by Moscow, represents only the leftist bloc and not the National Peasant and National Liberal parties, which American observers believe hold a large following. Washington still hopes for a three-power agreement to reorganize the government and hold free elections.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d388:
Admiral Leahy's undated note on captured German ships was kept ready only in case Stalin or Churchill raised the subject. An acute shortage of ocean tonnage, it observes, hampered the movement of troops and their equipment against Japan. That need justified a temporary transfer of captured German merchant ships to the United Maritime Authority, which the Soviet Union should join.

Once Japan surrendered or fell, Leahy proposed, the remaining captured German merchant tonnage would be divided equally among the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States. Captured German war vessels would likewise be split as equally as possible among the three, at the earliest practical date.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d488:
A British suggestion on recognizing Poland is reported in an extract of Winant's cable from London of June 25, 1945. Warner of the Foreign Office told the embassy that London was considering a proposal to Washington. When the new Warsaw government notifies the three governments, it should add a pledge in that same message. The notice would state that it has been established in conformity with the Yalta agreement.

The pledge would be to hold free elections. Winant adds a personnel note. Robert Hankey served at the British embassy in Warsaw from 1936 to 1939. He now sits in the Foreign Office's Eastern Department. When recognition is extended, he will go to Warsaw as chargé d'affaires.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d588:
Ambassador Sato weighed Moscow's silence in a very secret cable to Tokyo on July 15, 1945. It is document 588 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference, printed in translation. Stalin and Molotov had left for Berlin the night before with no answer on the Konoye mission.

Sato lists four guesses at the delay. Moscow may want to know the envoy's true task and whether concrete peace terms will come. It may doubt that Japan seeks more than a negotiated peace, which America and Britain flatly reject. It may shun any step that strains its ties with London and Washington. Or Stalin may first tell the U.S. and British leaders of Japan's request at Potsdam. The cable is a cool, clear read of Soviet motives from inside Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d688:
The State Department answered a British aide-memoire on Soviet demands on Turkey in a top secret memo of June 23, 1945. It is document 688 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. London had urged a firm joint approach to Moscow in Turkey's support.

The Department says it has studied the British paper with care. London inclines to tell Moscow early and firmly that Molotov's words to the Turkish ambassador clash with Stalin's Yalta pledges. Britain recalls Stalin agreeing that Turkey should be assured of her independence and integrity. Washington's reply is measured and cooler in tone. It stands ready, it says, to discuss the Straits at the coming summit, where Moscow will presumably present its wishes. The memo stops well short of the early protest London wanted.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d88:
Churchill proposed a press blackout for the Berlin conference in telegram number 97 to President Truman, sent June 23, 1945. The message is document 88 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Following the precedent of the Crimea conference at Yalta, he wanted the meeting closed to reporters.

His suggestion is simple: the press should not be allowed at Terminal, but photographers should be permitted. He tells Truman he has repeated the telegram to Stalin. A note records that Stalin accepted the idea four days later. The arrangement suited all three governments, which wanted to control news of the talks while still supplying the historic pictures of the leaders together.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1088:
The British Embassy in Washington sent this aide-mémoire extract to the State Department on July 16, 1945. It concerns the timing of an Italian peace treaty. London is as anxious as Washington, it says, to conclude that treaty as soon as possible. A joint public statement at Potsdam, favoring an early treaty, would do good in Italy.

The warning is against acting alone. Any such statement must speak in the names of all three governments. A one-sided statement by any single power would be most unfortunate, London argues. It hopes Washington will hold back all further action until the question is discussed at the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1188:
The British Embassy in Washington wrote to the State Department on 26 July 1945. That was the day the election results changed Britain's government. Notes between an embassy and the host foreign ministry were the formal channel for business between the two capitals.

This one went out as Churchill fell and Attlee rose. Governments changed; the channel kept working, papers moving in the usual forms. The message shows Whitehall's Washington outpost doing business on a day of upheaval at home. It is a small sign of how states run: the forms hold steady while the names at the top change overnight.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1288:
On 16 July 1945, the day before the summit opened, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. It is the staff-level writing behind the headline choices to come. The chiefs set their house's view on paper before the team left for the talks.

An eve-of-summit paper fixes the starting brief. Everything the staff wrote later at Potsdam built on groundwork of this kind. This memorandum belongs to that base layer. It shows the American military staff at its desks, thinking ahead of the leaders, on the last day before the conference made its own weather.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1388:
Mikołajczyk set down a fourth memorandum on 27 July 1945, keeping up his near-daily pace of writing during the Potsdam Conference. By then the conference had settled much of the Polish border question in draft. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Four papers in four days mark a campaign, not a correspondence. Mikołajczyk was fighting for free elections and for Poland's place among the victors rather than the spoils. Readers can track how his tone and asks shift as word of the leaders' choices reached him. The file stands as a record of how the weakest party at a great settlement makes its case: often, late, and in writing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-88: Among the unnumbered pieces placed after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume sits this note from the volume's editors. The Foreign Relations series adds such notes where the bare papers would leave a reader lost. They can supply a missing date, name a file's source, or send the reader to a linked document. This one serves that quiet guide role inside the dense July 1945 record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d788:
James Dunn, Assistant Secretary of State, wrote to Byrnes at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. Document 788 brings a senior home officer's voice into the closing days. Dunn had long handled European and political work. His letter reached the Secretary as the final texts took shape. It entered the second Potsdam volume.

A letter from Dunn carried institutional weight. He spoke for the Department's senior career staff. Readers see Washington's center advising its travelers at the climax. The document shows the home office neither idle nor shy: it pressed its views to the last. That pressure is part of how the American line was formed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d888: Britain's delegation put the paper, titled The First Charge, before the Potsdam talks on July 30, 1945. It asks that one sentence join the Economic Principles. Paying for approved imports into Germany would be a first charge on proceeds from exports of current goods and stocks. The paper notes this matches what Molotov said on July 23. Approved means approved by the Control Council. If the council blocked imports one government deemed vital, the four governments would face a new situation.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d988:
The United States delegation issued this memorandum at Babelsberg on July 22, 1945. It urges a joint declaration on German external assets. The occupying powers and the Control Council, it argues, should claim jurisdiction over those assets, acting through their own diplomats abroad. France should be invited to join the statement.

The attached draft declaration speaks in the name of the heads of state at Potsdam. It calls on every country holding German assets to place them at the disposal of the occupying powers. Their diplomats would act to gain control of the assets, for security and other Allied aims. If France holds back, the paper says, the three conferring powers should issue the declaration alone.
gao-gaoreports-b-295888: Merck took its May 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296988: Specialty Marine took its October 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298588: Sealift took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Shipping deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298888: World Wide Technology took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Big names get the same full hearing as the small ones.
gao-gaoreports-b-299088: Alutiiq Global Solutions doubled its February 2007 protest — two case numbers, one services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299888: Accent Service Company took its contract dispute to GAO in 2007, and this ruling settles it for good. The firm challenged the agency's award as unfair; the call weighs the protest point by point and rules. Quiet, workmanlike, binding — the everyday machinery of keeping federal buying fair for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-400088: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Advanced Seal Technology, Inc. The July 14, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-388: The FBI's health fraud funding oversight was weak in 2005, and GAO's report says accountability over the HIPAA money was inadequate. The review calls out the loose watch. The fraud fighters deserved the oversight. The accountability had to improve. The fraud fighters deserved the oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-488: Space station logistics alternatives needed more study in 2005, and GAO's report says more knowledge was required to pick the best options. The findings demand the research. The report warns that the orbiting lab deserved sound supply. The knowledge had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-888: The new homeland agency's training needed a game plan in 2005, and GAO's report says the prep work had to be steered well. The findings demand the planning. The report warns that the new department's people deserved preparation. The new department's people deserved preparation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-388: Nuclear plants had upgraded security in 2006, and GAO's report says efforts had been made, though the design basis threat needed work. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the reactors deserved relentless vigilance. The threat basis had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-488: Tsunami reconstruction was underway in 2006, and GAO's report says USAID had begun rebuilding in Indonesia and Sri Lanka, though key projects might exceed budgets. The findings balance the start and the warning. The report cautions that the wave's ruins needed careful rebuilding. The projects had to stay on budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-788: Iraq's rebuild needed a real strategy in 2006, and GAO's report says a more comprehensive national approach was required to achieve the goals. The findings demand the blueprint. The report warns that the billions needed a plan, not just spending. The strategy had to be comprehensive.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-88: Depot maintenance funding data was unreliable in 2005, and GAO's report says persistent deficiencies limited the accuracy of allocation data. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the repair dollars deserved honest counting. The data had to be accurate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-988: Americans at the UN needed a boost in 2006, and GAO's report says more effort was required to increase U.S. employment at the agencies. The findings press for action. The report warns that the world body's American voice needed strengthening. The hiring had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-388: The Pentagon's weapons shopping needed a portfolio brain in 2007 — GAO's report says managing the investments as one portfolio would sharpen the buying. The findings make the business case. The report's pitch: run the arsenal like a fund, not a flea market.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-88: Housing the next catastrophe's victims needed a plan in 2007, and GAO's report says better planning was essential for sheltering the displaced. The findings demand the playbook. The report warns that the tents and trailers should not be improvised again. The next storm would not wait for the plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-888: Hanford's toxic billions needed a tighter leash in 2007 — GAO's report says the Energy Department had to toughen its watch over contractor payouts at the waste plant. The findings target the money valves of the priciest cleanup on earth. When the bill runs to the billions, the report argues, the purse strings cannot dangle.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-188: The Government Accountability Office dug into the Democratic Republic of the Congo: Systematic Assessment Is Needed to Determine Agencies' Progress toward US Policy Objectives in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-288: The Government Accountability Office dug into army Corps of Engineers: Known Performance Issues with New Orleans Drainage Canal Pumps Have Been Addressed, but Guidance on Future Contracts Is Needed in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-388: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at joint Strike Fighter: Recent Decisions by DOD Add to Program Risks. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-588: The Government Accountability Office dug into cyber Analysis and Warning: DHS Faces Challenges in Establishing a Comprehensive National Capability in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-88: This 2007 GAO report finds the anthrax shot program repeating its own mistakes — shaky buys of a new vaccine and sloppy care of the licensed stock on hand. The nation's germ-defense shelves deserved better buying discipline, GAO argues. The report is a plea to run biodefense like lives depend on it, because they do.
geheime-figuren-rosenkreuzer-1785-1788:
Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer, printed at Altona from 1785 to 1788, is the emblem book of the Gold- und Rosenkreuzer order. The German title means the secret figures of the Rosicrucians, drawn from the 1500s and 1600s. The order that issued it was the leading Rosicrucian body of its century.

Sixteen engraved plates carry the book, each plate a dense symbolic image. Around the plates runs the order's own commentary, steeped in alchemy and theosophy, two paths to hidden knowledge of God and nature. The volume became the order's most famous printed work. Its plates still shape how the Rose Cross is pictured today.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-4-1788:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 4 of his Decline and Fall in 1788. Attention turns east to Justinian and the Byzantine Empire. Belisarius, Justinian's great general, reconquers parts of Italy and Africa from the Goths and Vandals. Law receives its classic code under Justinian's direction.

The plague that struck the empire in the 540s gets a chilling account. Gibbon also surveys Persia and the early state of Arabia before Muhammad. His irony spares neither monks nor emperors. The volume shows the History's true scope: a whole civilization's world. Readers admire its learning on law, war, and faith alike.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-5-1788:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 5 of his Decline and Fall in 1788. Muhammad and the Arab conquests enter the narrative in this volume. Gibbon gives a long account of Arabia, the Prophet's life, and the Koran. Arab armies then sweep Persia, Syria, Egypt, and Spain with stunning speed.

Later chapters treat the iconoclast emperors, the Bulgarians, and the state of the Eastern Empire. Gibbon's treatment of Islam was unusually fair for his age. His irony returns in full for monks and relic cults. The volume carries the story to the eve of the Crusades. Its breadth shows why the History is called a world in itself.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-6-1788:
Edward Gibbon completed his Decline and Fall with Volume 6 in 1788. The final volume covers the Crusades, the Mongols, and the last centuries of Byzantium. It ends with the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453. Gibbon closes by surveying the ruins of Rome itself.

His last pages reflect on the whole arc from empire's height to ruin. The siege of 1453 is told with grim grandeur. Gibbon finished the work in Lausanne and recalled sitting in the Capitol as a young man when the idea first struck him. The six volumes form the greatest history ever written in English, by wide consent.
giraldus-cambrensis-topography-of-irelan:
Giraldus Cambrensis tells of wolf priests in The Topography of Ireland, writ near 1188, here in Thomas Forester's English. Giraldus was a Welsh priest who rode with Prince John to Ireland. His book maps the land, its beasts, its saints, and its marvels. One part stands out: a priest in Ossory meets a pair who turn wolf by a curse, and who beg rites for a mate at death's door.

The tale is the first great wolf text of Ireland. It blends awe, faith, and doubt in a rare mix. The whole book is a rich store of that age.
golden-dawn-book-t-tarot-1888:
Hands in the Golden Dawn wrote down their tarot lore in Book T, a set of drafts from near 1888. The Golden Dawn was a small band of mages in London. Their drafts fix what each card means, how cards link to stars and signs, and how to lay a spread for fate.

Waite drew on these drafts for his famed pack of cards. Most packs since then still use their scheme. Few short drafts have shaped an art so much. Here is the source text, plain and terse, that all those packs rest on. The drafts are terse, oft in code and brief hand notes. Waite and his peers fleshed them out in their own packs and books soon past.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-1-1888:
George Grote published his History of Greece in twelve volumes from 1846, here in Murray's 1888 edition. This first volume of the ten-volume 1888 set opens the foundational modern history of ancient Greece in English. Grote, a London banker and radical MP, rewrote Greek history from a democratic point of view.

Volume One treats the legendary age, geography, and early peoples of the Greek world in careful detail. Grote sifts myth from fact, telling the tales while marking them as tales, not sober history of Greece. His preface defends Athens and democracy against the aristocratic bias of earlier English histories of the Greeks. The scale is vast, the style clear, and the learning worn with unusual ease for readers. Later volumes carry the story from early states to Alexander and his successors in turn.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-10-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this tenth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume closes the long work in full. Grote ends with Alexander and the generation of his successors, as his preface promised his readers there.

Alexander's conquests scatter Greek speech and cities from Egypt to the Indus in one brief lifetime. Grote treats the conqueror with respect and reserve, weighing the cost to the free city-states of Greece. The volume also surveys Greek Sicily and the western colonies, completing his wide Mediterranean canvas of Hellenic life. His last chapters take stock of what the Greek experiment in self-government left the modern world as legacy. The ten volumes stand as Victorian scholarship's monument to Greece, still readable and still argued.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-2-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this second volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume presses into early times. Grote writes as a scholar and a democrat, keen to do justice to the Greek people.

The early volumes trace Greece from legend toward record, state by state and colony by colony. Constitutions, lawgivers, and tyrants take shape as scattered tribes grow into the classic city-states of Greece. Grote's method weighs sources openly, so readers see doubt handled rather than hidden in the history's pages. His sympathy for popular government sets the tone that made the work a liberal landmark in England. Read in sequence, the volumes build one vast arc from myth to empire.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-3-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this third volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, retold for the democratic age in England. Each volume advances the long story while keeping Grote's clear style and open weighing of sources.

As the history moves toward the classic age, Persia looms and the Greek states arm and league. Grote gives constitutions and colonies the same care he gives battles and famous men of Greece. His Athens rises in these volumes from one city among many toward the head of a league. The narrative pace quickens as record replaces legend and the great wars come into view at last. Scholars used Grote for a century, and general readers still find him lucid.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-4-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this fourth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and its middle volumes reach the great wars. Grote's democratic reading of Athens was a rebuke to the Tory histories that came before him.

Persian invasion, Athenian sea power, and Spartan land might collide in the world these volumes survey in depth. Grote lingers on institutions as much as battles, for he thinks constitutions make the fate of states. His Marathon and Salamis stand beside his accounts of law, finance, and the Athenian assembly at work. The prose stays measured even as the scale of events swells toward the classic age's height in Greece. For Victorian readers this was Greece made modern, rational, and politically alive again.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-5-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this fifth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume stands near its classic center. Grote brings a banker's head for finance and a radical's heart for the Athenian demos to it.

Athens at her height, empire, tribute, and the building age of Pericles fill volumes of this scope. Grote defends the Athenian empire's energy while he faults its coercion of subject allies in the Aegean world. Sophists, orators, and generals move through a narrative that never loses the thread of institutions and laws. His judgments are argued, not asserted, and readers can follow his evidence page by documented page. The History's fame rests on this union of learning, clarity, and political sympathy.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-6-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this sixth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and by this volume war dominates the tale. Grote wrote with the Peloponnesian War's long shadow over Athens and Sparta in full view here.

The rival leagues harden, speeches sharpen, and the great war grinds the Greek world down year by year. Grote follows campaigns and constitutions together, since in Greece the two were never truly apart in practice. His account honors Thucydides while it checks him against the fuller record available to modern scholarship in London. Readers get plague, faction, and the slow ruin of the Athenian empire as one connected story of power. Few English histories match its patience with causes over the long haul of war.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-7-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this seventh volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume nears the war's grim end. Grote's sympathy for Athens is tested by her crimes and follies, which he does not spare.

Sicily draws Athens to her great disaster, and the tale turns on error, pride, and chance. Grote weighs commanders and assemblies alike, asking who truly chose the fatal course at each hard turn. The narrative keeps its clarity even as expeditions, sieges, and sea fights crowd the Aegean and Sicilian coasts. His democratic faith survives the wreck, for he blames men and systems, not the demos alone, here. In sequence the volume forms the History's tragic center, Greece consuming her own strength.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-8-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this eighth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume covers the war's aftermath. Grote treats defeat and recovery with the same care he gave Athens in her imperial prime years.

Oligarch coups, Spartan victory, and the slow rebuilding of walls and fleets fill these postwar chapters in Greece. Xenophon and the march of the Ten Thousand carry Greek arms deep into the Persian empire's heartland. Grote follows the shifting leagues and the rise of Thebes as Sparta's grip weakens across the Greek world. His interest in constitutions sharpens as democracies and oligarchies trade places in city after Greek city. The volume shows Greece inventing new balances after hegemony's first great collapse.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-9-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this ninth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume nears the Macedonian age in Greece. Grote's narrative slows for philosophy and oratory as the city-state world begins to fail around them.

Demosthenes thunders against Philip of Macedon while Athens debates, delays, and arms too late for her freedom. Thebes rises and falls at Leuctra and Mantinea, and Sparta fades from the first rank of powers. Grote gives the orators and the courts their due as engines of the late democratic city at Athens. His liberal reading finds dignity in Athens' last stand for self-government against a rising military monarchy in Macedon. The volume sets the stage for the History's close in Alexander's vast and brief career.
guyton-de-morveau-method-chymical-nomenc:
Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau led the team that gave chemistry a new set of names in 1787. Their scheme came out in English in 1788 with this title. Old names for stuffs were a mess of trade terms and false hints. One stuff might bear six names, and one name might serve for three stuffs.

The new names tell what a stuff is made of, in a clear scheme of roots and ends. Sulfates, oxides, and acids each fall in their own class by rule. The reform gave the new chemistry the tongue it still speaks, from school rooms to labs.
hartmann-secret-symbols-rosicrucians-188:
Franz Hartmann, a German doctor turned Theosophist, published Secret Symbols of the Rosicrucians at Boston in 1888. The book collects plates from a rare German work of the 1780s, with Hartmann's commentary for modern readers. Through it, the nineteenth-century occult revival received the Rosicrucian emblem tradition in visual form.

Alchemical diagrams, cosmic wheels, and symbolic figures fill the large plates. Hartmann explains each in the revival's own mystical idiom. The source-book shaped how the Golden Dawn generation pictured the old fraternity. Its images have been reprinted ever since, often without credit. Readers who want the visual language of Rosicrucianism, as the revival learned it, start with Hartmann's plates.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol8-1888:
Eight years separated Volume VIII of the Guiding Symptoms from the first, and it arrived in 1888. The delay shows in the care of the editing, as Hering's students worked through boxes of proving notes. Remedies still march in alphabetical order, their symptoms filed under body regions.

Few books in the school carry this much raw clinical memory. A prescriber chasing an odd, precise symptom, the kind that names one remedy alone, would search here first. The marks of rank beside each line keep the search short. Volume VIII keeps the promise of the title: guidance, not mere bulk.
hinton-new-era-thought-1888:
Charles Howard Hinton was a math man who gave the fourth dimension its name in print. His A New Era of Thought came out in 1888. He taught readers to think past length, breadth, and height. The book laid the base of what fans call hyperspace thought.

Cube drills train the mind to picture a form with a fourth reach. Hinton asks what such a space would mean for the soul and for fact. He gives plain steps that a keen reader can work through at home. The book made talk of a fourth reach a set field of thought.
home-d-d-home-life-mission-1888:
Mme. Dunglas Home guards her man's name in D. D. Home: His Life and Mission, out in 1888. Home had died two years past. His wife prints his notes, tales of guests, and words of praise from lords and sages who sat with him. Arthur Conan Doyle adds a warm word at the book's front in her aid.

The tale runs from his youth in the United States to fame in the courts of Europe. She aims to fix his fame as a true seer, not a trick hand. The book is the set life of the age's top seer.
hopkins-scientific-christian-mental-prac:
Emma Curtis Hopkins earned the name teacher of teachers, and Scientific Christian Mental Practice, from 1888, is her textbook. Hopkins trained Charles Fillmore and a generation of New Thought ministers in her Chicago classrooms. Her course builds from a Statement of Being through denials and affirmations, step by ordered step.

Students learn to deny error's power and affirm the good they claim as real. The method is mental, yet Hopkins gives it the shape of a strict spiritual discipline. Her book systematized New Thought teaching, and its structure shaped the movement's churches and classes for decades.
hugo-hunchback-of-notre-dame-hapgood-188:
Victor Hugo wrote Notre-Dame de Paris in French, and Isabel Florence Hapgood made it English in 1888. Hugo's great Gothic novel of medieval Paris stars the cathedral itself as hero. He wrote it in part to save the church from decay and clumsy repair work.

Quasimodo, the deaf bell-ringer, loves the dancer Esmeralda from his tower heights. Archdeacon Frollo's lust for her drives plots of kidnap, trial, and false witchcraft charges. Hugo fills the book with crowds, gargoyles, and a famous bird's-eye view of Paris. The end is grim for nearly all, yet the cathedral stands above their fates. The tale revived care for Gothic art across France and far beyond it.
hutton-theory-of-earth-1788:
James Hutton presented his Theory of the Earth paper in 1788 to the Royal Society of Edinburgh, in its Transactions. Hutton, a Scottish farmer and naturalist, argued that the Earth's features are the work of slow forces still at work today. That claim opened the door to deep time.

Rocks, Hutton said, are worn down, laid down in seas, hardened, lifted, and worn again in an endless cycle. At sites such as Siccar Point, tilted layers under flat ones proved to him a past far longer than the received chronology allowed. His famous line found no vestige of a beginning. The paper is the founding document of modern geology.
judge-epitome-of-theosophy-1888:
William Q. Judge boiled his creed down to its bones in An Epitome of Theosophy, a brief tract of 1888. The word means a short sum of the whole. In a few pages he states what the creed holds on God, man, death, and the fate of the soul.

The tract is like a short creed card for the faith. New fans could learn it by heart. Groups gave it out at doors and talks. Judge had a gift for plain, brief speech. This tract is that gift at its most lean. Brief as it is, the tract packs in karma, planes, and Masters. A keen fan could grasp the whole creed's frame from these few pages.
kalevala-vol1-crawford-1888:
Elias Lonnrot, a Finnish doctor, built the Kalevala from the songs of the folk of Finland and Karelia. John Martin Crawford turned it into English in 1888, the first full English form of the epic. This book is the first part of his work; the second part stands in the library too.

The songs tell of Vainamoinen, the old singer sage, and of the forging of the Sampo, a mill of wealth. Charms, births of iron and fire, and quests fill the lines in the old runo metre. The epic gave Finland its voice as a nation, and Crawford gave it to English ears.
kingsford-dreams-and-dream-stories-1888:
Anna Kingsford kept a log of her dreams, and Dreams and Dream-Stories prints it in 1888. Her friend Edward Maitland set the notes in form past her death. In sleep she met guides, saw signs, and got creeds in tale form. She held these dreams bore true light.

Some dreams read as brief fables. Some gloss her war on cruel tests on beasts, a cause she led. The log is the chief source for her signs and lore. It shows how her creed grew from night sight, not books. Some dreams warn, some teach, and some read as pure signs. Maitland adds brief notes where a dream needs a key to grasp.
kipling-plain-tales-1888:
Rudyard Kipling was a teenage newspaper reporter in India when he wrote these stories. Plain Tales from the Hills, published in 1888, was his first book for a wide audience. He wrote it at Simla, the summer capital where British officials escaped the heat.

The forty short tales show Anglo-Indian society in miniature: flirtations, feuds, pranks, and sudden tragedies. Young officers and clever widows scheme through the season while disease and distance shadow everything. Kipling's style is quick, dry, and knowing far beyond his years. The book announced a major storyteller and remains a sharp picture of the British Raj at play.
knigge-philos-endliche-erklaerung-1788:
Adolph von Knigge gave the Illuminati its shape as a working order, recruiting members and building its grades. By 1788 his partnership with founder Adam Weishaupt had collapsed in anger and mistrust. Philo's endliche Erklärung und Antwort, printed at Hannover that year, is his final public word on the break.

Writing under his order name Philo, Knigge answers the charges and questions put to him about his role. He complains that private letters and small slips were dragged into print to ruin men in public. He gives his side of the quarrel and explains why he left. Students of the order read the pamphlet as the key record of its inner split.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-3-1888:
Henry Charles Lea closed his History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages with this third volume in 1888. It turns from the map of the tribunal to special subjects that cross all lands. Lea's calm, record-based method made the set the standard work in English.

The Knights Templar and their fall, the trial of Joan of Arc, and the crimes of Gilles de Rais fill the great case studies. Lea then anatomizes the Inquisition itself: its books, its prisons, its money, and its men. He ends with the intellectual price the system charged the church. The three volumes together remain the base on which all later study builds.
lempriere-classical-dictionary-1788:
John Lemprière published his Bibliotheca Classica in 1788, a dictionary of the Greek and Roman world. Lemprière was a schoolmaster and clergyman who wanted classical learning within reach of readers without Latin and Greek. The book is better known by its short name, Lemprière's Classical Dictionary.

Thousands of entries explain gods, heroes, places, and stories from ancient myth and history. The dictionary gave poets a ready store of classical material: Keats, Byron, and Shelley all drew on it for their verse. For about a century it was the English reader's standard gateway to antiquity. Later classical dictionaries replaced it in schools, but its entries still show what educated readers of the Romantic age knew and loved.
lives-of-alchemystical-philosophers-base: Victorian scholars revisited the alchemists' lives in 1888. They built on the 1815 biographies with fresh material. The who's who of the adepts, refreshed. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This book preserves that biography for future readers.
lives-of-alchemystical-philosophers-to-w: Lives of Alchemystical Philosophers, with bibliography, 1888. The expanded lives. This book preserves that biography. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
maine-international-law-1888:
Henry Sumner Maine's International Law was published in 1888 from his Cambridge lectures of 1887. Maine, the author of Ancient Law, was the great master of the historical method in legal study. In these late lectures he turned that method on the law between nations.

Maine traces how states slowly learned to live under rules: the growth of diplomacy, the laws of war, and the treatment of neutral nations. He treats international law as a real growth from custom and treaty rather than a code handed down at once. His skepticism about grand schemes keeps the lectures grounded in practice. They were his last lectures, printed after his death in 1888. The book shows the Victorian jurist viewing world order through history's lens, and it still rewards readers who doubt easy theories of global law.
mathers-tarot-1888:
S. L. MacGregor Mathers wrote his tarot tract, Book T, in 1888. It was made for the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. Mathers led that order and set its teach in print. The tract gives the sense the order laid on each card.

Hebrew marks, star signs, and grades of the order lock to the cards. Short fate senses for each card fill the last pages. The scheme in Book T lies at the root of the Waite-Smith pack. Most new occult packs since draw on its plan in some form.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette: This Campan volume covers the infamous diamond necklace affair. A vile and senseless scandal stains the innocent queen's name unjustly. The loyal memoirist defends her mistress warmly. The dark and fateful prelude to bloody revolution.
molinos-spiritual-guide-1688:
Miguel de Molinos was a Spanish priest in Rome whose Spiritual Guide, Englished in 1688, taught the quiet way of prayer to eager readers. The book won praise across Europe and, for a time, papal approval in high places. Then Rome condemned its propositions, and Molinos died in prison.

Molinos tells the soul to lay aside effort, images, and even anxious self-examination, resting in God without grasping. Critics charged that such quiet kills moral effort and the church's sacraments alike. His fall shaped European mysticism by warning it where the line of suspicion lay. Its short chapters made it a handbook readers could carry and reread.
monluc-commentaries-cotton-1688:
Blaise de Monluc, a Gascon soldier, wrote his Commentaires in 1592 about the wars he fought under King Henri II of France. Charles Cotton's English translation, first made in 1674, appears here in the printing of 1688. Monluc rose from common soldier to marshal by wounds, daring, and a fierce will to be remembered.

His memoir is all camp and battlefield: sieges, charges, feuds, and the raw talk of men at war. King Henry IV is said to have called the book the soldier's breviary, the handbook every fighter should keep. Monluc spares no one, least of all himself, in telling how war really felt. The Commentaries remain a classic soldier's memoir of the 1500s.
morris-dream-john-ball-1888:
William Morris, the designer and poet, had become a committed socialist by the 1880s. He published A Dream of John Ball in 1888, pairing it with a shorter prose piece, A King's Lesson. The dream tale first ran in a socialist newspaper, Commonweal, which Morris helped run.

A modern socialist narrator dreams himself back to 1381, during the Peasants' Revolt led by Wat Tyler. He talks through the night with John Ball, the rebel priest who preached that things would never be well while some were masters and others servants. Morris uses the rising to ask what his own movement must learn. The book blends history, hope, and warning.
most-die-anarchie-1888: Die Anarchie, Most's 1888 anarchist work. The anarchy. This book preserves that book. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
nutt-studies-holy-grail-1888:
Alfred Nutt published Studies on the Legend of the Holy Grail in 1888, and it helped found modern Grail scholarship. Nutt was a folklorist, and he asked a bold question about the famous cup. Was the Grail a Christian relic, or something older?

Nutt pointed to Celtic tales of cauldrons of plenty that feed every guest and never empty. Behind the holy cup, he argued, stood these pagan wonders from Welsh and Irish story. His Celtic-origin case set the terms of debate for decades. Scholars still argue with this book, which is a sign of how much it started.
olympiodorus-alchemist-art-sacre-berthel:
Olympiodorus of Thebes, a scholar of the sixth century, wrote a long commentary on Zosimos and on the sayings of the old alchemists. His work On the Sacred Art is given here in the French version of Berthelot and Ruelle, from their 1888 edition of the Greek alchemists. Olympiodorus read the art through Neoplatonic thought.

He treats the metals, the egg of the philosophers, and the work of turning base stuff toward gold as signs of a deeper order. His pages carried the alchemy of Alexandria into the Byzantine world. Without such bridges, the Greek art would not have reached the Arabs or the Latin West. The commentary is dense, learned, and strange.
openalex-w1582174288: Ecosystem services got tradeoff-traded, and this ecology article covers space time trade-offs. The pages detail the trade findings. The ecologists get their paper. The trade-offs were across-Services. The paper was ecologist. The Services were Ecosystem. The Time were Space.

openalex-w2135648488: Breeders got a stats workhorse. Cruz's 2013 paper presents GENES, software for stats. The tool crunches numbers for plant and animal breeding choices — auto, at last, and free for all users today.
openalex-w2318568688: The UN's Sustainable Development Goals mention land everywhere and soil almost nowhere — an oversight this 2016 SOIL forum paper tries to correct. openalex-w2395026888: Tracking how much CO2 the oceans absorb requires stitching together decades of ship measurements. openalex-w2575837388: Cervical cancer still kills hundreds of thousands of women yearly, and its molecular wiring was incompletely mapped. openalex-w2964004288: Earthworms are soil engineers: their casts enrich nutrients, their burrows aerate and structure the ground. openalex-w4368363688: Drinkable water grows scarcer as pollution rises and treatment costs climb. This 2023 Environmental Chemistry Letters review covers methods to prepare biosorbents and magnetic sorbents for water treatment. Adsorption on cheap solids offers an effective route to cleaner water.
openalex-w4407468688: Candida species are hospitals’ leading fungal threat — deadly for the immunocompromised and critically ill. openalex-w7129093688: Lung cancer too advanced for surgery still has radiation options. openalex-w7137857988: Hunting new antibiotics starts with screening thousands of candidates fast. This paper proposes Euglena gracilis, a single-celled alga, as a high-throughput platform for antibacterial testing. The authors built the screening system. A methods study speeding the search for tomorrow's drugs.
openalex-w7162264588: Rumors fight like viruses, and this paper models the battle. openalex-w7204485688: The maker movement says students learn by building, and this article brings that spirit to biology and chemistry class. openalex-w7204635388: More children are being diagnosed on the autism spectrum, and small-town schools feel the pressure. openalex-w7204947088: Acne is often dismissed as a teen phase, but its marks run deeper than skin. openalex-w7205006588: For patients with non-ischemic heart failure, sudden cardiac death is a leading killer, and implantable defibrillators are the main defense. openalex-w7205006988: Marcelo Caetano's 2024 film Baby follows Wellington, fresh out of juvenile detention, and Ronaldo, a young sex worker, through the streets of Sao Paulo. phrenology-as-a-science-microform-a-lect: Phrenology as a Science, microform, 1888. The lecture. This book preserves that lecture. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
plos-pbio-0020288:
Steven D. Mason, Richard A. Howlett, Matthew J. Keske, and their team tested a muscle oxygen sensor in PLOS Biology in 2004. HIF-1α is a protein that reacts when oxygen runs low. The team removed it from mouse skeletal muscle and checked how the mice handled exercise.

The study helps explain why training and altitude have the effects they do. It also warns that drugs targeting HIF pathways, now in wide study, will have real effects on exercise capacity.
plos-pone-0000088:
Yi Xing, Karen Kapur, and Wing Hung Wong addressed a data problem in gene chips in PLOS ONE in 2006. The authors set out rules for probe selection and a method for computing the expression index. Faulty probes, which react to the wrong target, are a known trap in chip data. Cleaner inputs give cleaner biology. Methods papers like this one rarely make headlines, yet thousands of later studies stand on them. The exon arrays opened a window on splicing that careful math had to keep clear.
plos-pone-0000188:

A claimed rule of translation falls under direct testing here. Negative results of this sort clean up the textbook picture of how genes are read. The paper matters for anyone designing gene sequences or predicting protein output from DNA, tasks where a false rule leads to false expectations.
plos-pone-0000288:
Vanina Vergoz, Edith Roussel, Jean-Christophe Sandoz, and colleagues published this bee learning study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honeybees can be trained by smell using the sting extension reflex. In that reflex, a bee that senses a threat paired with an odor extends its sting. The authors reveal aversive learning in honeybees through this conditioning setup.

Bees were famous for learning rewards, learning which smells mean food. Showing they also learn aversively, which smells mean danger, completes the picture of their learning. The work gives bee neuroscience a second conditioning tool, useful for studying memory and its chemistry.
plos-pone-0000388:
Harish Babu and colleagues refined a way to grow brain precursor cells from adult mice, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their source was the dentate gyrus, one of the few brain regions that keeps making new neurons in adulthood. They cut out the tiny region and grew its precursor cells as a clean, enriched layer in culture.

The cultured cells went on to produce working granule cell-like neurons, the main cell type of the dentate gyrus. A reliable culture system like this gives researchers a steady supply of adult-born neurons to study. That helps work on how the adult brain adds new cells, and what those cells do for learning and memory.
plos-pone-0000488:
Adrian B. Hehl and colleagues tested a cell-death protein in an unusual host, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Giardia lamblia is a primitive intestinal parasite that lacks mitochondria, the cell's power stations. Bax is a protein that normally triggers cell death by acting on mitochondria. The team studied Bax function in the absence of mitochondria in this protozoan.

If Bax still works in a cell with no mitochondria, its killing mechanism must reach beyond them. Odd organisms make good tests for claims about how basic machinery works, because they strip away the usual context. The study probes how ancient and how flexible the cell-death program is.
plos-pone-0000588:
Georgia Panagiotakos and colleagues measured radiation's long shadow over brain stem cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Radiation therapy saves lives but can harm the developing or adult brain. The team studied the long-term impact of radiation on two cell pools in the brain. One pool holds stem cells. The other holds oligodendrocyte precursors, the cells that renew tissue and make myelin, the insulation of nerve fibers.

If precursor pools are depleted for good, later cognitive and repair problems have a cellular explanation. Long-term studies matter because patients, especially children, live decades after treatment. Findings like these inform how radiation doses are planned to spare the brain's regenerative reserves.
plos-pone-0000688:
Erin K. Hanson and Jack Ballantyne built a sharper DNA typing system for forensic work, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Forensic labs use Y chromosome short tandem repeats, markers called Y-STRs, to identify a male DNA donor. The method shines when male DNA hides in excess female DNA, as in many sexual assault investigations.

Commercial typing kits already existed, but each added marker raises the power to tell men apart. Their title promises ultra-high discrimination from one multiplex system, testing many markers at once. Better discrimination means fewer ambiguous matches in casework. For courts and labs, a stronger Y-STR panel is a practical advance, not just a technical one.
plos-pone-0000788:
Ricardo Núñez Miguel, Joyce Wong, Julian F. Westoll and colleagues modeled the working end of an immune alarm receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Toll-like receptor 4, or TLR4, sits on the surface of immune cells. It is activated by lipopolysaccharides from the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, forming part of the mammalian innate immune response. Its cytoplasmic domain, inside the cell, passes the signal onward.

Their title states that a dimer, two copies joined, of that domain provides a specific scaffold for recruiting signalling adaptor proteins. Shape explains specificity: only the paired platform fits the right adaptors. That geometry guides drug ideas for sepsis and inflammation.
plos-pone-0000888:
Yamina Seamari, Jose Narvaez, Francisco Vico and colleagues built methods to separate two states of brain cortex activity, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cortex networks fall into a slow rhythm during deep sleep and anesthesia. Cells swing between up states, active and charged, and down states, quiet and resting, less than once a second.

Telling those states apart in recordings sounds simple but is easy to get wrong. The authors offer robust ways to do it both live, as data comes in, and later, offline. Clean state labels underpin many studies of sleep and memory. Their methods give other labs a firmer base for that work.
plos-pone-0000988:
Insuk Lee, Zhihua Li and Edward Marcotte built a cleaner probabilistic gene network for baker's yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene networks merge millions of separate observations into one model of how a cell works. For yeast, such a network is a workhorse for predicting what unstudied genes do.

The catch is bias: well studied genes gather more links just because they are well studied. The authors present an improved network with that bias reduced. A fairer map gives unknown genes a better chance of being placed correctly. Yeast networks often prototype methods later used on human data, so the fix travels.
plos-pone-0001088:
Dietrich Gotzek, D. DeWayne Shoemaker and Kenneth Ross examined gene variation behind fire ant social form, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The fire ant Solenopsis invicta comes in two social forms. Some colonies have one egg laying queen; others have many. That difference reshapes colony life entirely.

A candidate gene had been implicated in regulating this social behavior. The team study molecular variation at that gene across forms. Few traits offer so direct a line from one gene region to a whole society's structure. The fire ant is also a major invasive pest, so its social genetics carry practical weight for control efforts in the southern United States.
plos-pone-0001188:
Leptospira interrogans is a corkscrew-shaped bacterium that spreads through the bloodstream and colonizes many tissues, causing leptospirosis. Brian Stevenson and colleagues examined proteins on its outer surface in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Infectious leptospires can resist killing by the complement system, part of the immune defense in blood.

The authors show that the bacterium's endostatin-like outer membrane proteins bind host fibronectin and laminin, two proteins of the tissue scaffold, plus regulators of complement. Grabbing scaffold proteins may help the bacterium attach and invade. Binding complement regulators may help it hide. Together these tricks explain part of its success as a pathogen.
plos-pone-0001288:
Animals must sense how much sugar is available and respond, and for years attention focused on glucose sensing inside cells. Emilie Stolarczyk and colleagues studied sensing outside cells instead, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They disabled GLUT2, a glucose transporter that also acts as a sugar sensor, in mice.

The authors report that loss of sugar detection by GLUT2 affects glucose homeostasis in the mice. Homeostasis is the body's balancing of blood sugar levels. Their work shows that detection at the cell surface is a real part of that balance, not a sideshow.
plos-pone-0001388:
Fredrik Vannberg and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene variant and tuberculosis. TB kills and sickens many people each year, most of all in sub Saharan Africa. A cell receptor coded by the gene CD209 can grab and take in the TB germ. Prior work had linked a variant near this gene to TB risk.

The team tested that link in their own groups of patients and controls. They asked whether the same variant raised or lowered the odds of disease. Firm checks like this sort true risk genes from false leads. The data help guide the search for host traits that shape who falls ill with TB.
plos-pone-0001488:
Yvonne Vallès, Kenneth Halanych, and Jeffrey Boore published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on mobile DNA in an animal genome. Group II introns are RNA pieces that cut themselves out of messages and can hop to new spots. They are common in germs and cell parts, but rare in animal nuclei. They are thought to be the kin of our own splicing parts.

The team found these introns in the genome of a two sided animal, a first of its kind. That find breaks the old bounds for where they can live. It hints they were once more common in animal lines. It also adds a data point to the tale of how gene splicing arose.
plos-pone-0001588:
Jeffrey Trimarchi, Michael Stadler, and Constance Cepko wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on single eye cells in mice. The retina grows from stem like cells that read cues from their world. The varied fates of those cells must in part stem from varied gene use. The team read gene use in single retinal stem cells, one by one.

Even cells of the same type and age showed wide spread in gene use. That spread may be the raw stuff from which distinct fates are picked. Single cell reads catch what pooled samples smear out. The work sets a base for how the eye builds its many cell types.
plos-pone-0001688:
Françoise Guinet, Patrick Avé, Louis Jones, and their co-authors traced the earliest events of plague infection in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, evolved recently from a gut pathogen, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis. In doing so it gained entry through the skin and extreme virulence. Which early events make it so deadly was the question.

The authors report two faults acting together. The innate immune cells that should attack first respond poorly, and the bacteria infiltrate lymph nodes in a distinctive way. The full text gives the infection time course, the cell counts, and the node pathology. These first hours decide whether plague takes hold, so they are also where new treatments would have to act fastest.
plos-pone-0001788:
Benjamin S. C. Uzochukwu and co-authors compared how mothers in town and countryside respond to childhood fever in south east Nigeria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Childhood fevers from malaria remain a major cause of illness and death among under-five children in Nigeria. How dangerous a mother judges the fever to be shapes what care she seeks.

The team surveyed rural and urban mothers on their perceptions of severity and their patterns of health care use. The full text gives the survey results and the rural-urban contrasts. Fever care often starts at home or with drug sellers. Knowing those first steps is essential for programs trying to get sick children treated in time.
plos-pone-0001888:
Ada De Luigi and colleagues tested a family of common drugs against prion disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Prions are rogue proteins that cause fatal brain ills in animals and in people, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. In past lab work, tetracycline drugs bound to the rogue protein and made it lose its tough, hard-to-break form.

The team asked whether that effect could slow real infection, both when prions enter the body and when they are placed in the brain. Past work had shown lower prion levels and longer life in hamsters dosed with these drugs. A cheap, known drug class that buys time would be a rare gain in a field with no cure.
plos-pone-0001988:
Paul Gilbert and co-authors tested a video counselor for HIV patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cutting drug use and unsafe sex among people with HIV helps their own health and lowers the chance they pass the virus on. Guidelines tell providers to screen and counsel for these risks, yet busy clinics often skip it.

The program, called Video Doctor, gives interactive counseling by computer in the clinic. As the title states, it reduced drug and sexual risk acts among HIV-positive patients in diverse clinics. A tool that counsels without staff time could fill a gap that human clinics struggle to close.
plos-pone-0002088:
Douglas Bakkum, Zenas Chao, and Steve Potter studied slow shifts in how brain networks pass signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Precise timing of nerve spikes is essential to many brain functions. From one neuron's view, the timings of incoming spikes from its partners decide whether it fires, and when.

The team grew cortical networks in the lab. Over the long term, they tracked how activity changed both the delay of spike travel and spike size. As the title states, this long-term, activity-dependent plasticity reshapes propagation itself. Wiring that retimes its own signals adds a layer to how networks learn.
plos-pone-0002188:
Christiane Dolecek, Tran Thi Phi La, Nguyen Ngoc Rang, and co-authors compared two antibiotics for typhoid fever in Vietnam, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drug-resistant typhoid is a growing clinical problem worldwide. Older fluoroquinolone drugs such as ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin, once first-line treatments, had begun to fail.

The team ran a randomized controlled trial in children and adults with uncomplicated typhoid. Patients received either gatifloxacin or azithromycin, and the researchers compared cure rates and safety. Head-to-head trials like this give doctors in high-burden regions evidence for which drug to reach for when the old standbys no longer work.
plos-pone-0002288:
Conrad Earnest and co-authors reported on six months of exercise training in inactive postmenopausal women. Their 2008 PLOS ONE paper covers how training changed heart rate variability. Heart rate variability, the small timing changes between beats, falls with age and low values predict higher mortality. Postmenopausal women have lower variability than younger women, and inactivity and obesity can push it lower still.

The data come from the DREW study, a controlled trial of exercise dose in this group. The team measured whether training raised variability over six months. Results from a large, careful trial help doctors prescribe exercise with clearer expectations for heart health.
plos-pone-0002388:
Attardo and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Alessio Attardo, Federico Calegari, Wulf Haubensak, and others. Its subject is live Imaging at the Onset of Cortical Neurogenesis Reveals Differential Appearance. The rest of the title points to the Neuronal Phenotype in Apical versus Basal Progenitor Progeny. The neurons of the mammal brain are made by progenitor cells that divide at one of two surfaces.

Some divide at the apical surface of the ventricular zone, and others divide at its basal side. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002488:
