Led by Swaddle, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from John P. Swaddle, Stavros E. Calos, and others. Its subject is increased Avian Diversity Is Associated with Lower Incidence of Human West Nile Infection: Observation of the Dilution Effect.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002588:
Research by Massacand and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Joanna C. Massacand, Patrick Kaiser, Bettina Ernst, and others. Its subject is intestinal Bacteria Condition Dendritic Cells to Promote IgA Production. Immunoglobulin (Ig) A represents the predominant antibody isotype produced at the intestinal mucosa.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002688:
Research from Abhay Kumar Thakur and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers UV-Light exposed prion protein fails to form amyloid fibrils. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Abhay Kumar Thakur, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Amyloid fibril formation involves three steps; structural perturbation, nucleation and elongation. The authors add a further point. We have investigated amyloidogenesis using prion protein as a model system and UV-light as a structural perturbant. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002788:
Work by Kamaldeen Baba and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was adenosine deaminase activity is a sensitive marker for the diagnosis of tuberculous pleuritis in patients with very low CD4 counts. The catalog record names Kamaldeen Baba first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Adenosine Deaminase Activity (ADA) is a commonly used marker for the diagnosis of tuberculous pleural effusion. The authors add a further point. There has been concern about its usefulness in immunocompromised patients, especially HIV positive patients with very low CD4 counts. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002888:
Anne-Pierre Morel, Marjory Lièvre, Clémence Thomas and colleagues linked two big cancer ideas in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One idea holds that cancer stem cells start tumors. The other holds that epithelial cells spread by first changing form, a shift called epithelial-mesenchymal transition, or EMT.

Working with a mammary tumor model, the team reports that forcing that shift can generate breast cancer stem cells. The title states that result directly. If the two processes are joined, a drug that blocks the shift might also curb the stem cells that regrow tumors after treatment.
plos-pone-0002988:
Naomi Willis, Thomas Cox, Syed Rahman-Casañs and co-authors named lamin A/C a risk marker in colorectal cancer in 2008. A-type lamins are structural proteins of the cell nucleus, coded by the LMNA gene. Faults in that gene cause several early-ageing and degenerative diseases.

Lamins also affect the retinoblastoma protein and cancer genes such as beta-catenin, both relevant to bowel cancer. The PLOS ONE study evaluates lamin A/C as a biomarker, a measurable sign of risk or outlook. A reliable marker could help sort patients by likely course and treatment need. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003088:
Marcel Kool, Jan Koster, Jens Bunt and co-authors split medulloblastoma into five subtypes by integrated genomics in 2008. Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Cure rates had improved, but predicting outcome was still a major challenge and survivors suffer serious therapy side effects.

Combining genetics, pathway signatures, and clinical features yielded five subtypes with distinct profiles, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, finer subtypes let doctors spare low-risk children the harshest treatment. The classification also gives drug research defined targets instead of one mixed disease. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003188:
Alice Hadchouel, Fabrice Decobert, Marie-Laure Franco-Montoya and colleagues link gene variants to a preterm lung disease in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Building the air sacs of the lung requires coordinated remodeling of the matrix outside cells, in which matrix metalloproteinases, or MMPs, play an important role. The team postulated that variants in MMP genes might affect MMP function in preterm lungs and alter the risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

Their title reports identification of MMP16 as a new player in lung development. Readers see a candidate gene for a serious disease of premature infants. Genetic risk clues may one day help target closer monitoring.
plos-pone-0003288:
Ming Yi and Robert M. Stephens present a pathway ranking method in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Analysis of microarray and other high throughput data often involves identification of genes consistently up or down-regulated across samples as the first step in extraction of biological meaning. This gene-level paradigm can be limited as a result of valid sample fluctuations and noise.

Their method, SLEPR, is a sample-level enrichment-based pathway ranking approach seeking biological themes through pathway-level consistency. Readers get a shift from single gene lists to whole pathway patterns. Pathway views often survive noise better and point more directly to disease processes.
plos-pone-0003388:
Chiara Begliomini and co-authors scanned human brains during grip tasks in this 2008 study. Grasping turns what the eyes see into precise hand movements. In monkeys, a known brain circuit handles that change. The team asked how the human version of the circuit behaves.

People grasped objects with the left hand or the right hand during scans. Brain activity shifted with the hand used and with the person's own handedness. Right-handed and left-handed people did not use the circuit in the same way. The study shows that hand choice shapes motor planning deep in the brain.
plos-pone-0003488:
Gita Ramjee and co-authors ran a trial of added STI protection for women in this 2008 paper. The test group used a diaphragm plus lubricant gel, with condoms. The control group used condoms alone. All women in the trial faced risk of HIV and other infections.

The trial tracked new cases of chlamydia and gonorrhea. Those are common sexually transmitted infections of the cervix. Results showed whether the added barrier gave extra protection. Such evidence guides prevention advice for women who cannot rely on condoms alone. Many women cannot count on partners to use condoms every time.
plos-pone-0003588:
A. Puppo and co-authors disturbed the egg cell's outer skeleton in this 2008 study. As eggs mature for fertilization, their inner calcium stores reorganize. That change yields a more efficient calcium response at fertilization. The actin cytoskeleton also remodels during maturation and fertilization.

Altering the cortical actin deregulated calcium signaling in the eggs. It also disrupted single-sperm fertilization and sperm entry. The skeleton is thus no passive frame but an active director. Its state helps decide whether fertilization proceeds normally. Egg quality sets the odds for in vitro fertilization in clinics worldwide. Calcium waves are one of the first signs doctors and lab staff watch for after sperm meets egg in the dish.
plos-pone-0003688:
Nyambayar Dashtsoodol, Hiroshi Watarai, Sakura Sakata, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Natural killer T cells are unusual immune cells that grow in the thymus. They were thought to come only from cells carrying both the CD4 and CD8 markers. The earliest steps of their growth stayed unclear.

The team identified precursor cells that carry neither marker, a double-negative stage. These precursors can develop into natural killer T cells as well. The extra path widens the known family tree of cells that bridge the body's fast and slow immune defenses.
plos-pone-0003788:
Annette Schneider, Dimitry Spitkovsky, Peter Riess, and colleagues published this stem cell methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Many stem cell lines must first grow alongside feeder cells to stay undifferentiated and potent. Later, those feeder cells count as contamination and must be removed. The team built a way to sort the two apart.

Their technology frees stem cells from feeder cells cleanly. As the title's fairy tale puts it: the good into the pot, the bad into the crop. Pure stem cells make later experiments and therapies safer and easier to interpret.
plos-pone-0003888:
Jennifer Waldo and Michael Scherrer described a small protein from dividing yeast cells in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Dad1p, part of the Dam1-DASH complex. That complex sits in the kinetochore, the structure linking chromosomes to the spindle. Good links let cells split their chromosomes evenly between daughter cells.

The authors produced Dad1p in the lab and gave its first detailed description. Early data on a single part helps map how the whole complex grips chromosomes. Faults in such parts can lead to cells with the wrong chromosome count. The work supports wider studies of cell division in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
plos-pone-0003988:
Thore Egeland and Antonio Salas addressed gaps in DNA haplotype databases in 2008. Forensic and disease studies often use haploid DNA, like mitochondrial DNA. Databases of normal size hold only a fraction of all haplotypes. Users still need reliable estimates for the missing types.

Their PLOS ONE article gives methods to estimate haplotype frequency and coverage. Coverage tells how much of a population a database captures. Better estimates strengthen forensic match statistics and population studies. The work helps labs state honestly what their databases miss. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004088:
Qing Chang, Wenxue Tang, Shoeb Ahmad, and co-authors studied ear gap junctions in mice in 2008. Connexin26 and connexin30 build gap junctions in the cochlea. Mutations in either are the top cause of inherited early deafness. How their loss damages hearing was not fully clear.

Their PLOS ONE article reports metabolite transfer fails without connexin30. Gap junctions pass small molecules between cochlear cells. Mice lacking connexin30 showed that transfer compromised. The finding links a hearing protein to the ear's chemical housekeeping. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004188:
Jennifer Serwanga and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some people infected with HIV stay free of symptoms for long periods without any antiretroviral therapy. Viral control, CD4 cell loss, and HIV-specific immune responses all help decide how fast the disease moves.

The team studied therapy-naive Ugandans and their HLA-B genes, which shape which virus pieces the immune system attacks. They report that T-cell recognition of the viral Gag protein across several virus clades, tied to certain HLA-B types, correlates with slow disease progression. The link points to the kind of immune response a vaccine would want to copy.
plos-pone-0004288:
Fatemeh Malekzadeh and colleagues published this pilot study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The environmental risk factors behind Crohn's disease, a chronic inflammation of the gut, remain largely unknown. A recent suggestion blamed refrigerated food, on the theory that cold-loving bacteria could be involved.

The team ran a pilot case-control study exploring the link between Crohn's disease and early exposure to domestic refrigeration. Comparing patients' early home environments with those of controls tests whether the fridge hypothesis deserves a larger study. Unusual hypotheses need small, careful tests before big ones. The study was a pilot, meant to guide a bigger one.
plos-pone-0004388:
Radiation can cause tumors, including cancers of the colon. Yet inherited traits change how strong that effect is. Eiram Elahi, Nirosha Suraweera, Emmanouil Volikos, and co-authors hunted those traits in mice. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper used Apc Min mice, a strain prone to gut growths called adenomas. They crossed that line with BALB/c mice, known to be unusually sensitive to radiation tumors.

The team counted adenomas after radiation in the crossed mice. They then mapped the DNA regions tied to higher counts. Five regions, called quantitative trait loci, controlled the outcome. Each locus is a stretch of DNA that shifts the trait. Finding them helps separate inherited risk from radiation dose itself.
plos-pone-0004488:
Air pollution breathed in by a mother before birth may leave a mark on a gene tied to asthma. Frederica Perera, Wan-yee Tang, Julie Herbstman, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study follows a group of about seven hundred children in New York City. Asthma rates there are among the highest in the United States.

Traffic fumes contain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, chemicals that cross the placenta. The team linked that exposure to DNA methylation, a chemical mark, on a gene called ACSL3 in the child. The mark is a candidate biomarker, a measurable sign of exposure. If such marks predict asthma, doctors could spot high-risk children early, and cities would have stronger evidence for cleaning traffic air.
plos-pone-0004588:
A mouse protein switched on by interferon helps resist the bacterium behind chlamydia by eating it from inside the cell. Munir Al-Zeer, Hesham Al-Younes, Peter Braun, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is Irga6. Chlamydia infection triggers gamma interferon, a central immune protector in humans and mice. In mice, the primary defense involves the interferon-induced IRG protein family.

The precise mechanisms of that defense were unclear. The team shows Irga6 mediates host resistance against Chlamydia trachomatis via autophagy, the cell's self-eating process, which can digest invaders. Human chlamydia is a major sexually transmitted infection. Understanding how mice clear it naturally may suggest ways to strengthen human defenses.
plos-pone-0004688:
Brant Peterson and colleagues showed that large genomes can help find gene control parts, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Finding the short DNA stretches that switch genes on is still a hard task. One good trick compares DNA across species and looks for parts that stay much the same over time.

That trick has found many control parts in animals with backbones. The team asked if big genomes make the search sharper. Extra DNA can act as a clean backdrop that makes kept parts stand out. If so, species with large genomes become strong tools for gene control hunts.
plos-pone-0004788:
Tina Bianco-Miotto and colleagues showed that methylation of the ABO promoter underlies loss of ABO expression in many leukemia patients, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Loss of A, B, and H blood antigens from red cells is frequent in myeloid cancers. The group had earlier reported such changes in more than half of patients with myeloid malignancies they studied.

The team tested whether promoter methylation silences the ABO gene in those cases. They found methylation does underlie loss in a significant share. The mechanism explains a long noted blood bank puzzle. It may also serve as a disease marker.
plos-pone-0004888:
Marie Bourjade, Alice de Boyer des Roches, and Martine Hausberger showed adult young ratio regulates social behavior of young horses, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adults play important roles regulating social behaviour of young individuals. Early studies suggest the share of adults in a group shapes how the young develop socially. The team tested if that share shapes aggression and bonding in young horses kept in groups of varied makeup.

More adults means calmer, better integrated youngsters. Group composition is a welfare lever in husbandry. Social learning needs adequate adult models. Horse management can apply ratios directly. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004988:
Whale sharks are the ocean's largest fish. The species is declining and poorly studied. Jennifer Schmidt and colleagues sampled their DNA across the oceans. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They compared three major ocean populations. Baseline data were badly needed for conservation planning.

They found low genetic differentiation across the three populations. The sharks mix more than their vast range suggests. Treating them as separate stocks would be a mistake. Conservation must view them as one connected population. The finding also raises questions about their migrations. These giants apparently travel far enough to keep their genes well mixed.
plos-pone-0005088:
Alzheimer's risk climbs with age. Women face higher risk than men. Lisa Placanica, Lei Zhu and Yue-Ming Li looked for a mechanism in mouse brain. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They measured gamma-secretase activity. That enzyme helps carve out the amyloid protein tied to Alzheimer's.

Activity shifted with both age and sex. The enzyme's behavior differed between male and female brains. It also changed across the lifespan. The pattern may explain part of the risk profile of sporadic Alzheimer's. Genetic mutations explain rare early cases, not the common form. This work points at an enzyme whose tuning changes with the two biggest risk factors.
plos-pone-0005188:
Interleukin-3 is a signal that tells blood-forming cells to grow and to take on set roles. It works by docking onto a receptor on those cells and starting a chain of signals inside. Dey and colleagues modeled that docking step in detail in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their model shows that two interleukin-3 molecules also interact with each other as the larger complex assembles. That cytokine to cytokine contact helps switch the receptor on. The picture adds a step that drug designers must keep in mind when they try to boost or block blood cell growth signals.
plos-pone-0005288:
The human Y chromosome carries blocks of duplicated DNA, and one region holds a puzzling patchwork segment. Schmidt and colleagues traced a gene family related to DUX4 in that region in PLOS ONE in 2009, across humans and other hominoids.

The family sits in a transition zone between the Y chromosome's active and silent parts. Its evolution proved complex, with duplications reshaping the family over time. Mapping that history helps explain how the male chromosome is built and why parts of it vary so much. The Y chromosome is hard to read, with many near-copies of the same stretch, so a clean map of one gene family there is a prize for genome work.
plos-pone-0005388:
Mechanical loading can push stem cells toward becoming bone, a fact with promise for regenerative medicine. How force is converted into that fate choice was the question for Arnsdorf and colleagues in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on Wnt signaling, a key fate pathway.

Non-canonical Wnt signaling played a role in the mechanically induced bone fate. So did beta-catenin signaling related to N-cadherin, a cell adhesion protein. Linking specific pathways to force gives tissue engineers molecular levers to pull alongside physical loading. Bone is made where force is felt most, a fact known since the days of Wolff. And this work names the gene paths that turn that felt force into new, hard bone in the end.
plos-pone-0005488:
Aleksandra Piwko-Czuchra and co-authors studied skin stem cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Skin renews itself from stem and progenitor cells in its outer layer. Grip proteins called integrins help those cells hold on and grow, but tests in dishes and in animals gave conflicting answers about their role.

The team focused on one integrin and its signals in skin progenitor cells. They found that its adhesion signals are vital for those cells to expand. Without that grip and signal, the skin cannot keep renewing itself well, which matters for wound healing and skin disease.
plos-pone-0005588:
Linda Lindström, Per Hall, and Mikael Hartman asked whether lung cancer survival runs in families, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Survival after lung cancer is poor, and patients at the same stage can fare very differently. Genes shared within families might explain part of that spread.

The team compared survival across pairs of relatives with different degrees of kinship. If close kin fare alike more than distant kin do, inherited factors are at work. Such evidence would push research toward the genes that shape outcome, not just risk. Stage of disease shapes survival strongly, so the study had to compare families within the same stage.
plos-pone-0005688:
Kelvin Wong and colleagues introduced a fast MRI method in 2009 to watch blood flow inside the beating heart. Odd flow patterns can reveal heart disease, but they are hard to measure without probes inside the body. Their method tracks fluid motion at high speed from MRI scans.

The scans yield maps of flow through each heart chamber, slice by slice. Doctors can then judge how well the heart moves blood, using the maps alone. A clear, noninvasive flow picture could help spot valve faults and weak pumping early. The team presents the method as a new kind of heart analysis built on flow itself.
plos-pone-0005788:
Munir Iqbal and co-authors reported in 2009 new types of H9N2 bird flu found in Pakistani poultry. H9N2 outbreaks in Pakistan had grown more severe than in earlier years. Every gene segment of a flu virus adds to its strength, so full genetic reading was needed.

The new viruses carry a surprise: their NS genes resemble those of the highly dangerous H7N3 and H5N1 viruses. Such mixing, called reassortment, can create fitter flu strains without warning. The finding argues for close genetic watch on poultry flu in the region. It also shows how mild and severe viruses trade parts.
plos-pone-0005888:
Casey Cook and co-authors checked in 2009 whether aging breaks the cell's protein-disposal system in mice. The ubiquitin-proteasome system tags worn proteins for shredding. Even small faults in it can disturb cell function, so an age-related decline was a natural suspect in aging itself.

Using reporter mice that reveal disposal activity, the team found no broad impairment with age. That negative result frees the field from a too-simple story. Aging may damage specific tissues or stress responses instead of the core machinery. Knowing what does not fail focuses the search for what does.
plos-pone-0005988:
Vitamin D does more than build bone, and its byproducts may calm inflamed skin. Zorica Janjetovic, Michal Zmijewski, Robert Tuckey and colleagues studied one such byproduct in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at a compound made when an enzyme called P450scc trims vitamin D3, tested in human skin cells called keratinocytes.

The compound slows cell growth and helps skin cells mature. The title adds a further effect: it cuts the activity of NF-kappaB, a master switch for inflammation, by raising levels of its blocker IkB-alpha. A vitamin byproduct that brakes inflammation in skin cells could interest teams hunting gentler treatments for inflamed skin.
plos-pone-0006088:
A copy of a cell signal can have effects its maker never planned. Judith Enyeart and John Enyeart found such a case in adrenal cells in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies an analog of cAMP built to activate Epac proteins, and asks how it drives cortisol synthesis in adrenocortical cells, the cells that make the stress hormone cortisol.

The analog's breakdown products, not the analog itself, drive the cortisol rise, and they do it by a path that skips cAMP entirely. Assuming a probe drug acts as designed is risky, as this result shows. The finding also reveals a fresh route by which the adrenal gland can be told to make its hormone.
plos-pone-0006188:
Some staph bacteria release a toxin that overexcites the immune system at tiny doses. Kedar Narayan and colleagues studied that toxin, called enterotoxin A, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Lab work with loose proteins had suggested the toxin grabs its immune target with two hands at once.

On real B cells, the toxin drew its target, HLA-DR1, into small clusters on the cell surface. Watching intact cells shows a side of the meeting that test-tube work missed. Clustering may be part of how the toxin triggers such a strong response. The detail could inform drugs that block toxin action during severe infections.
plos-pone-0006288:
A stretched, weak heart muscle, called dilated cardiomyopathy, is a leading cause of heart failure. Wenliang Zhu, Lei Yang, and Zhimin Du layered gene expression data onto protein interaction networks in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of failing hearts. Earlier work showed such integrative analysis can expose hidden disease mechanisms.

Their layered functional network analysis hunts for protein teams whose joint behaviour breaks down. Single bad genes explain only part of this disease. Network layers may reveal the modules that fail together. Those modules are candidate targets for future heart failure drugs.
plos-pone-0006388:
The tiger mosquito spreads disease to people and animals, and the germs inside it can change how it acts. Karima Zouache and her team mapped two kinds of inner germs in Aedes albopictus for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They looked in the parts used for breeding and in the rest of the body.

One inner germ, Wolbachia, stays in the mosquito for life, and other germs that can be grown in labs live there too. These lodgers can shift how the host breeds, bites, and spreads disease. Maps of who lives where are a first step to using germs against the mosquito itself.
plos-pone-0006488:
Jane Aspell, Bigna Lenggenhager, and Olaf Blanke probed the feeling of owning one's body in PLOS ONE in 2009. The unity between self and body can be disrupted with conflicting input from sight and touch. Such setups let researchers study bodily self-consciousness in healthy people. Neurological patients with disturbed body sense offer further clues.

The authors explore multisensory mechanisms that keep people in touch with themselves. Vision, touch, and body position signals must agree for the self to feel located in the body. When they clash, illusions arise that reveal the brain's rules. The work links lab illusions to real disorders of body awareness.
plos-pone-0006588:
Zheng Sun, Zheping Huang, and Donna Zhang studied modification of an antioxidant master switch in PLOS ONE in 2009. Nrf2 is a transcription factor that has emerged as a pivotal regulator of intracellular redox homeostasis. It controls expression of many endogenous antioxidants and phase II enzymes. Kinases called MAPKs can phosphorylate Nrf2 at multiple sites.

Their title reports that this phosphorylation has a limited contribution in modulating Nrf2-dependent responses. A plausible regulation turns out to be minor. Clearing away minor mechanisms focuses the field on major ones. Nrf2 matters for cancer prevention and stress defense, so its true controls are worth pinning down.
plos-pone-0006688:
Alwin Scharstuhl and co-authors studied how curcumin kills fibroblast cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Curcumin is the yellow compound found in turmeric. The group had earlier found that it strongly triggers fibroblast death. That effect could be useful against hypertrophic scars, which involve excess fibroblasts. Here they asked which inner machinery carries out the death.

The dying cells released a factor called AIF from their mitochondria. Caspase blockers could not stop the process, pointing to a different route. The molecules VDAC, Bax, and ceramides all took part in the release. Mapping that pathway explains how curcumin-driven death proceeds. It also suggests targets for future scar treatments based on controlled cell death.
plos-pone-0006788:
Jasmin Dischinger and her team found a new two-part germ killer made by a Bacillus strain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The killer class is the lantibiotics, small chains built by microbes. They hold rare sulfur links in their chains. Each starts as a dull draft chain. Steps in the cell then rework the draft into the sharp drug.

The strain Bacillus licheniformis DSM 13 makes the drug lichenicidin. Lichenicidin is rare in that it takes two chains to work. The team showed how the strain makes it. Two-chain drugs grow the known set of these killers. They also draw drug hunters who need fresh arms against tough germs.
plos-pone-0006888:
Raymond C. Wadlow and colleagues modeled the two-way conversation between cancer cells and fibroblasts in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer cells interact with surrounding stromal fibroblasts during tumor growth. The molecular rules of that interaction remain poorly understood. Poor understanding hinders treatments aimed at the cancer stroma. The authors took a mathematical, systems-level approach.

Their model organizes known interactions into a working framework. It can predict how disturbing one signal affects the rest. Such predictions prioritize laboratory experiments on the stroma. Targeting fibroblast support is a growing cancer strategy. A systems model helps choose which support lines to cut.
plos-pone-0006988:
Paul Carlson, Katherine Carr, Brian Janes, and colleagues starved anthrax bacteria of iron in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inside a host, free iron is hard for bacteria to get. Coping with iron starvation helps a pathogen copy itself during infection. The team used the Sterne strain of Bacillus anthracis, the anthrax agent.

They recorded which genes the bacteria switched on or off without iron. That response map shows how anthrax adapts to the host environment. Iron uptake systems are attractive drug targets. A treatment that locks iron away could weaken the bacteria without classic antibiotics.
plos-pone-0007088:
Traver Hart, Alice Zhao, Ankit Garg, and colleagues adapted microarray tech for living cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA microarrays print thousands of tiny spots for parallel tests. The team borrowed that spotting idea for human cells. Their goal was to read cell state across whole arrays at once.

Cells are grown and treated under standard culture conditions. They are then fixed and printed onto replicate glass slides. Thousands of mini-experiments can be stained and imaged side by side. The chips promise cheaper screens of drugs and gene knockdowns than plate-based methods.
plos-pone-0007188:
Shai Shaham introduced a software tool called galign in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. New sequencing machines could read DNA on a huge scale by then. Yet custom software to analyze the data had fallen behind the machines themselves, leaving researchers to write their own programs.

Galign is designed for rapid discovery of genome polymorphisms, the small DNA differences between individuals. Shaham describes how the tool aligns sequence data to find those variants. Geneticists working with large parallel sequencing runs get a practical method for turning raw reads into lists of differences.
plos-pone-0007288:
Ewan D. S. Wolff, Steven W. Salisbury, John R. Horner, and colleagues diagnosed a jaw disease in tyrant dinosaurs in 2009. Tyrannosaurus rex fossils often show smooth-edged holes through the jaw bone. The famous specimen known as Sue shows such lesions, on one or both sides of the mandible.

The authors compare these erosive lesions with diseases in living birds. They argue a common avian infection plagued the tyrant dinosaurs. Their diagnosis links a modern bird parasite disease to extinct predators. Paleontologists get a rare case where a fossil lesion matches a specific infection.
plos-pone-0007388:
Otto O. Yang proposed candidate HIV vaccine sequences in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A likely reason cytotoxic T cell vaccines failed is immune dominance of variable regions. The immune system focuses on epitopes that vary widely, raising the chance of mismatch with the challenge strain a vaccinated person actually meets in real exposure.

Yang addresses variation within and between HIV-1 clades, the major viral families. He presents candidate vaccine sequences designed to represent that variation. Better representation could make T cell responses match circulating viruses more often. The paper contributes design principles for a vaccine against a highly variable virus.
plos-pone-0007488:
Glenn Manthey, Nilan Naik, and Adam Bailis published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on DNA repair in baker's yeast. Breaks across both strands of DNA are dangerous lesions. Repair gone wrong can fuse chromosomes together, a change often seen in tumors. One repair route, single-strand annealing, must trim loose ends at the break. The team studied how that trimming is controlled.

They found that a protein called Msh2 blocks an alternative route for removing those loose ends. Without Msh2's restraint, the backup mechanism steps in and trims differently. That difference matters because repair choices shape whether chromosomes fuse abnormally. The study reveals a safeguard built into the repair system. Understanding such safeguards in yeast informs how scientists think about genome stability in human cells too.
plos-pone-0007588:
Patrick Meybohm and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on protecting the heart after cardiac arrest. Mild cooling after resuscitation is known to protect the brain. The heart muscle itself often falters after restart, though, and cooling's effect there was unclear. The team tested hypothermia, alone and with a protective drug strategy called postconditioning, in resuscitated animals. They measured cardiac dysfunction and its drivers afterward.

The treatments reduced heart dysfunction after resuscitation. They worked by modulating inflammation, limiting apoptosis, and slowing harmful remodeling of the heart. That extends cooling's known benefits beyond the brain. A therapy that guards two organs at once is doubly valuable in the chaos after arrest. The study maps the mechanisms, which helps clinicians use the protection wisely.
plos-pone-0007688:
Troy Lund and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns the zebrafish, a small fish widely used in labs. Zebrafish can regrow lost fins, and they keep an enzyme called telomerase active in adult life. In humans, that enzyme mostly falls quiet with age.

The team measured telomerase and the length of telomeres, the caps on chromosome ends. They found that neither age nor the regrowth of a limb changed those measures in the fish. The result helps explain why zebrafish age and heal in ways that differ from mammals.
plos-pone-0007788:
Gallen Triana-Baltzer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a drug candidate against the new pandemic flu strain of that year. The novel influenza A(H1N1) virus spread worldwide with alarming speed. Resistance to standard antiviral drugs was a standing worry.

The candidate, DAS181, is a fusion protein with a sialidase enzyme attached. It strips the receptors flu needs from airway cells, rather than attacking the virus directly. In tests, it potently inhibited the pandemic viruses. A host-targeted drug is harder for flu to evade. The work supported DAS181 as a backup for future outbreaks.
plos-pone-0007888:
David Lopez Herraez and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It scans nearly one million DNA markers across worldwide human populations. Genome-wide scans had already found new variants tied to common diseases. They also reveal the genetic structure and relationships of populations.

The authors searched that huge dataset for signs of recent positive selection. Such signs mark genes that helped people adapt to local conditions. Their evidence spans populations across the globe. The catalogue of selected regions helps explain human diversity. It also warns medical studies that background variation differs by ancestry.
plos-pone-0007988:
Kasmintan Schrader and colleagues surveyed many tumor kinds for one rare mutation in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mutation sits in FOXL2, a gene that helps build the ovary. It shows up in nearly every case of one uncommon ovarian cancer, adult granulosa-cell tumors.

Across a wide range of other solid tumors, the mutation stayed scarce. That tight pattern makes it a strong fingerprint: find it, and the rare ovarian cancer is a prime suspect. A test for a single change could help doctors name a hard case fast and choose care with more confidence.
plos-pone-0008088:
Rachel Ochola and colleagues timed how long a mother's flu-like shield lasts in Kenyan babies in PLOS ONE in 2009. The virus is RSV, the top cause of lung infection in infants. Babies are born carrying their mother's antibodies, blood proteins that fight the virus.

In Kilifi, the team measured those antibodies in cord blood and watched them fade month by month. The fading curve shows when babies lose cover and face the virus alone. Vaccine makers need that date: a shot given while the mother's shield still rules may fail, while one given too late leaves a gap.
plos-pone-0008188:
Souta Hidaka, Yuko Manaka, and Wataru Teramoto studied sound and vision in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Hearing gives useful cues about motion, though vision usually gives the clearest signal. Past work showed that adapting to moving sights can shift how loud a steady sound seems. The authors asked whether sound changes can also bend what the eyes see.

They found that alternating a sound's location makes a still object look like it moves. Sound alone thus shaped visual motion perception in their tests. The result shows the senses do not work in isolation. It helps explain how the brain merges sight and sound into one scene.
plos-pone-0008288:
Safdar Jawaid and colleagues characterized a bacterial enzyme in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Outbreaks of infectious disease, natural or deliberate, demand effective drugs and vaccines. Antibiotic-resistant strains add urgency to that need. The enzyme studied comes from Francisella tularensis, a dangerous pathogen. It is part of a pathway bacteria use to build key molecules.

The enzyme, called MEP synthase, was measured for how it works and is regulated. Phosphorylation, adding a phosphate group, appears to control it. Blocking such enzymes is a strategy for new antibiotics. The characterization supports drug design against this pathogen.
plos-pone-0008488:
Shu Lin and co-authors trace how a hormone cuts appetite in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The hormone is pancreatic polypeptide, or PP. It is a potent anti-obesity agent that lowers food intake. It does so without causing nausea. Yet the path by which it acts was unknown. The team focus on a brain region called the arcuate nucleus.

They show PP fails to cut intake in mice lacking Y4 receptors. Y4 receptors in the arcuate nucleus are thus required. The melanocortin system, a known appetite circuit, also plays a part. The chain from PP to Y4 to that circuit explains the effect.
plos-pone-0008588:
Naozumi Ishimaru and co-authors watch regulatory T cells in tissue in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Migration of T cells into lymph organs is controlled by chemokines and adhesion molecules. How regulatory T cells use those cues to prevent organ-specific autoimmunity was unclear. Autoimmune exocrinopathy attacks glands such as salivary and tear glands. It models Sjogren syndrome in humans. The team track regulatory T cells patrolling in situ, meaning in place in the tissue.

They find that in situ patrolling is essential for protection. Regulatory cells must actively move through glands to suppress attacks. Without that patrol, autoimmune damage proceeds unchecked. The work shows suppression is a dynamic, on-site activity, not a passive presence.
plos-pone-0008688:
Maria Teresa Cencioni, Valerio Chiurchiù, Giuseppina Catanzaro, and colleagues tested a body-made chemical on immune cells. Their study ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. The chemical, anandamide, belongs to the same family as plant cannabis compounds. It acts through two docking sites, called CB1 and CB2. T-lymphocytes help defend the body but can also drive harmful swelling.

Working with fresh human T cells, the team watched growth and signal release. Anandamide slowed cell growth and cut the release of messenger chemicals. Most of that calming ran through the CB2 docking site. The results hint at new ways to settle overactive immune responses.
plos-pone-0008788:
Christelle Anaclet, Nigel Pedersen, Patrick Fuller, and colleagues traced the brainstem wires behind sleep twitches. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. During REM sleep, most muscles go limp. Brief twitches still break through, especially in face and jaw muscles. The trigeminal nerve drives jaw muscles. Which brainstem circuits switch those twitches on was unresolved.

Recordings and tracing in animals revealed the circuit layout. A defined brainstem network gates the phasic bursts. Knowing the wiring explains how sleep paralysis is punctured safely. It may also illuminate disorders where sleep movements go wrong, like REM behavior disorder.
plos-pone-0008888:
Yun Huang, William Pastor, Yinghua Shen, and colleagues tested how a newer DNA tag behaves in the standard reading method. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells convert some methyl tags into hydroxymethylcytosine, called 5-hmC. The tag abounds in embryonic stem cells and certain brain neurons. Methylation is usually read by bisulfite sequencing, a chemical conversion method. How 5-hmC acts in that method was untested.

The team found 5-hmC reads as if it were a plain methyl tag. Standard sequencing thus cannot tell the two tags apart. Many published methylation maps may blend two different signals. Epigenetics needed, and gained, a warning about its main tool.
plos-pone-0008988:
Ilona Carneiro and co-authors pooled studies from across Africa to chart malaria's toll by age, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum hits children hardest where the disease is common. But the exact ages at risk shift with how much malaria circulates locally. Nobody had drawn the whole picture across settings in one analysis.

The review combined data from many studies in sub-Saharan Africa. Age patterns differed for mild illness, severe disease, and death. Season and transmission strength in each place reshaped the pattern further. Health programmes can target vaccines and treatment better with local age curves like these.
plos-pone-0009088:
Nadera Sweiss and co-authors counted immune cells in the blood of sarcoidosis patients, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disease that doctors poorly understand. Lymphocytes crowd into affected organs like the lungs and skin. Yet earlier reports suggested blood counts of those cells run low.

The team measured CD4, CD8, and CD19 lymphocytes in patients' blood. All three groups were significantly reduced in many patients. Deeper drops matched more severe disease in the organs. A simple blood count may help grade how hard sarcoidosis is hitting.
plos-pone-0009188:
Jean-Philippe Coppé and colleagues published this cell aging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns senescence, the state where cells stop dividing for good. Aging human cells also start releasing a mix of signaling chemicals. That release pattern can change how nearby cells behave, for better or worse.

The release pattern is called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. A key question was whether mouse cells, the usual lab stand-in, show the same pattern as human cells. The team showed that they do, but only when grown at oxygen levels like those inside the body. The finding validates mouse experiments on aging, with an oxygen warning attached.
plos-pone-0009288:
Annick Dubois and co-authors published this rose genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gardeners have bred roses for centuries, favoring color, form, and petal count. Wild roses carry just five petals. Most prized garden roses are double flowers, packed with many extra petals.

The team traced that trait to the so-called C-function genes that define flower parts. Tinkering with those genes converts organs meant to be stamens into petals instead. Their molecular frame explains how breeders, unknowingly, selected the same switch again and again. It connects centuries of gardening taste to one gene circuit.
plos-pone-0009388:
Qi-Shi Du and co-authors published this drug design study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The M2 proton channel is a doorway in the flu virus coat. Two older drugs, amantadine and rimantadine, blocked it well. Over twenty years, virus mutations robbed those drugs of most of their power, including against the 2009 swine flu.

Using the channel's known structure, the team designed new blockers in the computer. Their candidate inhibitors were shaped to fit the mutated channel. Computer design is faster than blind screening when a target keeps changing. The study offers fresh starting points for flu drugs that resistance has not yet beaten.
plos-pone-0009488:
Thorsten Stroh and co-authors presented a better way to get DNA into cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. The method uses short electric pulses to open tiny holes in the cell coat. DNA can then slip inside. How well it works depends on both the DNA and the cell type. Many cells take up DNA poorly with standard pulses.

Their approach combines pulses in a new sequence to raise success rates. It worked well in both human and mouse cells. More of the cells took up DNA and lived through the process. A more reliable method helps any lab work that needs to add or test genes in cells.
plos-pone-0009588:
Vishram Kedar and colleagues studied a brake on inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein tristetraprolin, or TTP, breaks down messengers that carry inflammatory orders. Losing TTP leads to severe inflammatory disease in mice. The team found that TTP interacts with another protein, CIN85. They asked what that meeting does to TTP itself.

Contact with CIN85 led to TTP being tagged with phosphate groups. That tagging tunes how TTP works in the cell. Fine control of a brake matters: too little braking inflames the body, and too much may blunt defense. The detail adds to our grasp of how inflammation is kept in bounds.
plos-pone-0009688:
Some single-celled algae poison shellfish and close beaches when they bloom. Ahmed Moustafa and colleagues profiled the active genes of one toxic dinoflagellate for PLOS ONE in 2010. A transcriptome profile lists every gene a cell is using at a given moment.

The cell turned out to carry a surprisingly rich set of genes for such a small organism. Bacteria living alongside the algae also seemed to shift which genes switched on. Both findings matter for predicting harmful blooms. They also show how much gene activity a single-celled protist can manage.
plos-pone-0009788:
Comparing averages across groups is a basic task in almost every science. Esther Herberich, Johannes Sikorski, and Torsten Hothorn proposed a stronger way to do it. Their procedure appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Real data rarely fit the tidy assumptions of textbook tests.

The method handles heteroscedasticity, where groups spread out by different amounts. It also handles unbalanced designs, where groups hold unequal numbers of cases. Both problems can mislead standard tests and distort conclusions. A robust procedure gives researchers fairer comparisons when data are messy. The procedure was built for everyday research data.
plos-pone-0009888:
Bird flu can jump between farms, and the routes are not all airborne. Jessica Leibler, Marco Carone, and Ellen Silbergeld weighed what company ties and social contacts add to that spread. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Between-farm transmission decides whether an outbreak stays local or goes regional. Company affiliation links farms under one firm, sharing trucks, crews, and equipment. Social contacts between workers add another bridge for the virus. Risk estimates guide where inspectors look first. Counting these human links sharpens risk estimates for poultry regions. Farms rarely stand alone in modern poultry production.
plos-pone-0009988:
Streambed surfaces that vary in shape may feed richer communities of microbes. Gabriel Singer and colleagues tested that idea in artificial stream channels. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The channels are called mesocosms, mid-sized outdoor experiments.

Biofilms are slimy layers of bacteria and other microbes coating stones. Surfaces of mixed shape and texture, called physical heterogeneity, raised biofilm resource use. Streams clean water partly through these biofilms. It also increased the biofilm's molecular diversity. Texture alone, it seems, can widen what a microbial community does. The channels sat outdoors under real weather.
plos-pone-0010088:
The authors were Ruth Waterman, Suzanne Tomchuck, Sarah Henkle, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper proposed a new way to think about stem cell therapy. Human mesenchymal stem cells can calm or stir immune responses. Signals from Toll-like receptors, which sense danger, shift how those cells behave.

From that evidence, the team described two states, named MSC1 and MSC2. One state favors inflammation, while the other suppresses immune activity. If doctors can push cells into the right state before treatment, stem cell therapy could become far more predictable. Their proposal appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010188:
The authors were Jonathan Grabowski, Erika Clesceri, Adam Baukus, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined lobster fishing in the Gulf of Maine. American lobsters are still managed mostly as a single species. Yet scientists have called for an ecosystem approach, which looks at how species and practices affect each other across the whole system.

The team tested a hypothesis about herring bait used in lobster traps. Heavy bait use might in effect farm lobsters, feeding them beyond natural food supplies. If true, bait policy becomes part of lobster management, not just a fishing detail.
plos-pone-0010288:
The authors were Xianfeng Fang, Peishuang Du, Yang Liu, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper gave immunology labs a cleaner method for collecting special T cells. NKT cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity, acting fast yet specifically. They are most abundant in the liver, so much of their biology was learned from liver isolates, gathered by a cumbersome procedure.

Their method isolates mouse liver NKT cells efficiently by perfusion, flushing the organ. A simpler, more reliable harvest gives researchers more cells with less damage. Better samples can sharpen studies of these unusual immune cells.
plos-pone-0010388:
Shahan Derkarabetian, David Steinmann and Marshal Hedin studied cave harvestmen, small spider relatives, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cave animals from separate places often end up looking oddly alike. Darkness and scarce food push them toward the same pale, long-legged forms. The team examined such harvestmen from mountain caves in western North America. They asked whether the look-alike forms evolved again and again.

Family trees built from DNA said yes: similar shapes arose repeatedly, at matching times. The timing suggests shared climate shifts drove species underground in waves. Looks alone can mislead about kinship, since caves remake bodies the same way. This study shows how to separate true kinship from copycat form. Caves, in effect, run the same experiment many times.
plos-pone-0010488:
Yougen Zhan and colleagues used the fruit fly eye to study two proteins tied to muscle and brain disease for PLOS ONE in 2010. One protein, dystroglycan, anchors cells to their surroundings. Its faults cause muscular dystrophies with brain and eye problems, including mental disability. The second protein sits in the mitochondria's ribosomes. The team altered both in the developing fly eye and watched cell differentiation.

The fly eye is a crisp test bed for how cells specialize. Both proteins proved necessary for proper differentiation there. That hints at shared ground between anchoring defects and energy machinery in disease. It also shows how a simple eye can model complex human syndromes. The study links two unlikely partners in development.
plos-pone-0010588:
Samuel Cordey and colleagues watched the common cold virus change inside infected volunteers, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rhinoviruses copy their genomes sloppily, so errors pile up fast. The team sampled virus over the course of each illness and read its full sequence.

Even within a few days, the virus population inside one person had diversified. New variants appeared while the original strain was still present. That rapid change helps explain why colds keep evading our immune memory. It also sets a hard problem for anyone hoping to build a lasting rhinovirus vaccine.
plos-pone-0010688:
David Frank and Sahotra Sarkar applied game theory to conservation choices, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Saving species takes joint choices by groups whose goals clash: farmers, officials, firms, and local people. Each side gains or loses from each plan, and no side controls the outcome alone.

The authors model those clashes as games with clear payoffs. Worked examples show when cooperation holds and when it breaks down. The models also show which side payments or rules can hold a deal together. Treating conservation as a game does not remove conflict, but it shows planners where a workable bargain can be found.
plos-pone-0010788:
Alessandra Bandera and colleagues examined the thymus of adults living with HIV, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV is famous for killing CD4 T cells in the blood. The thymus, where new T cells are born, is also attacked, but its role in adult disease stayed poorly understood. Thymus tissue from infected adults offered a rare direct look.

The infected thymus showed depleted young CD4 cells and signs of constant immune activation. It also produced an excess of regulatory T cells, the system's brakes. A gland making too few fighters and too many brakes helps explain why immunity fails to recover fully. The findings argue for protecting the thymus early in infection.
plos-pone-0010888:
George Siontis, Nikolaos Patsopoulos, Antonios Vlahos and co-authors published this study of medical publishing in PLOS ONE in 2010. Scans and X-rays carry weighty evidence in medical papers, yet no one had checked whether published images are chosen and shown fairly. A striking image could mislead readers if it is not typical of the study's patients.

The team reviewed hundreds of imaging figures from articles in twelve major journals, recording whether authors explained how images were selected and whether measurements, scales, and normal comparisons were provided. Only about one image in ten came with any note on selection, and a quarter left unclear whether the picture even came from the study being reported. Siontis and colleagues expose a quiet weakness in medical evidence: the pictures doctors trust are often presented without basic context.
plos-pone-0010988:
Sabrina Marozin, Enrico De Toni, Antonia Rizzani and co-authors published this cancer virus study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vesicular stomatitis virus, harmless to most healthy cells, selectively destroys liver cancer cells and is being developed as an anticancer agent. Earlier work blamed the cancer cells' broken antiviral alarms, and this study tested two other suspects: fast cell division and protein translation controls.

In other cell types, those factors had governed whether the virus could grow. In human liver cancer lines, however, neither cell cycle progression nor the translation initiation factors examined proved essential for the virus's killing. Marozin and colleagues narrow the explanation for the virus's selectivity in this cancer. Knowing what does not matter helps engineers focus on the defects that do, when tuning oncolytic viruses and drug combinations.
plos-pone-0011088:
Sabetta, DePetrillo, Cipriani and colleagues published a health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They asked whether blood levels of vitamin D track with how often healthy adults catch viral chest infections. Vitamin D is made in skin in sunlight and is also taken in food and pills.

The team measured a stored form of vitamin D in blood and followed infection rates. Their work tests a claimed link between nutrition and immune defense. If low levels raise risk, then simple blood checks could guide advice on supplements. The study adds careful data to a topic often driven by guesswork.
plos-pone-0011188:
Hatano, Kunert and Weisser worked with pea aphids in the field for PLOS ONE in 2010. When attacked, aphids release an alarm scent that warns neighbors. Some aphids then grow wings to flee. The team measured both the wing response and the costs of emitting that alarm under real field terms.

Both defense steps carry ecological costs for the aphids that pay them. Those trade offs shape how aphid groups evolve and respond to predators. Field evidence matters here, since lab tests can miss real costs. The findings help pest ecology predict how aphid outbreaks may shift when danger rises.
plos-pone-0011288:
Mumcuoglu, Bagislar, Yuzugullu and colleagues asked why breast tumors vary in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells within one tumor can behave very differently, which complicates treatment. The team proposed that cancer cells able to produce aged, non dividing offspring generate part of that variety.

If some cells keep spawning senescent progeny, the tumor gains a mixed population with mixed drug responses. That diversity engine helps explain why tumors resist uniform treatment. Personalized care would need to account for such internal variety. The hypothesis gives researchers a testable mechanism behind a familiar clinical frustration.
plos-pone-0011388:
Feihai Xu and co-authors evaluated in 2010 a blood test meant to catch enterovirus 71 early. The virus causes hand, foot, and mouth disease and, in some young children, dangerous brain and heart complications. Finding it early helps doctors watch high-risk children closely and act before illness turns severe.

The test looks for IgM antibodies, the first antibodies the body raises against a new infection. The team measured how well the test flagged real infections and how often it stayed negative in children without the virus. Judging that balance tells clinics whether a quick blood check can be trusted at the bedside. A dependable early test is especially valuable during outbreaks, when many sick children arrive at once and lab confirmation by slower methods falls behind.
plos-pone-0011488:
Gian Paolo Fadini and co-authors pooled data in 2010 to test whether counting repair cells in the blood sorts people by heart risk. Doctors judge cardiovascular risk with cholesterol and blood pressure, but progenitor cells that repair vessel linings offer a biological signal of the body's own maintenance state. Single studies of that signal were small and disagreed.

Combining many studies in a pooled analysis, the team asked whether circulating progenitor cell counts separate high-risk from low-risk patients. A pooled answer carries more weight than any one clinic's experience. If low counts reliably mark high risk, a blood count of repair cells could join the standard panel and flag patients whose vessels are failing to maintain themselves. The analysis shows how evidence pooling can settle a question that scattered small studies leave open.
plos-pone-0011588:
Dora Romaguera and a large team studied food habits and belly fat in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fat stored deep around the organs is strongly linked to poor health. The team used waist size adjusted for overall body mass as a stand-in measure for that deep fat, since direct scans are costly.

Following adults over time, the authors linked changes in that waist measure to what people ate and drank. Their findings single out dietary patterns tied to gaining or limiting deep belly fat. For doctors and the public, the work connects everyday food choices to the type of fat that matters most for long-term health.
plos-pone-0011688:
Hou-Sung Jung and co-authors identified a chloroplast protein plants need for efficient photosynthesis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Much of a plant's DNA encodes proteins sent into chloroplasts, where they build and run the photosynthetic machinery. Screening by imaging chlorophyll glow, the team isolated a mutant gene called proton gradient regulation 7, or PGR7.

They showed the PGR7 protein, conserved across plants, is necessary for electron transport to run efficiently during photosynthesis. Without it, the energy-harvesting chain falters. Naming this small cog helps researchers understand how plants fine-tune energy capture under changing light.
plos-pone-0011788:
Joan McIntyre Caron and co-authors treated metastatic melanoma cells with a simple sulfur compound, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer is most deadly once it becomes metastatic, and deaths from spreading melanoma had risen steadily for decades despite limited treatment options. The team used a mouse melanoma line known for aggressive spread.

Methyl sulfone induced loss of the cells' metastatic properties and brought back normal traits. Cancer cells that behave normally again suggest a gentler strategy than killing them outright. The turnaround in this cell line warrants study of whether the effect holds in living animals.
plos-pone-0011888:
Tao Wang and co-workers tested in 2010 whether a zinc-binding drug could protect brain cells after a stroke-like event. When blood flow to the brain stops briefly, excitatory nerve endings release excess zinc, and that zinc helps trigger the death of vulnerable neurons in the hippocampus. The drug clioquinol can grab and hold free zinc.

In gerbils given a short global blockage of brain blood flow, clioquinol blocked the zinc-driven activation of caspases, the enzymes that carry out cell death, in the sensitive CA1 region. Protecting that region matters because its neurons are central to forming memories. The result marks zinc control as a plausible line of defense after stroke.
plos-pone-0011988:
Pier Federico Gherardini, Gabriele Ausiello, and Manuela Helmer-Citterich presented in 2010 software for comparing protein structures piece by piece. Local comparison finds shared patches, such as enzyme active sites, even when whole proteins differ. The catch is that results depend heavily on how the structure is represented for comparison.

Their program, Superpose3D, lets users define their own structure representations instead of accepting one fixed scheme. Flexibility matters because a representation good for one question can hide the answer to another. Giving researchers control over the representation makes local comparisons a more honest tool for finding functional similarities between proteins.
plos-pone-0012088:
Bogdan Dumitriu, Pallavi Bhattaram, Peter Dy, and their co-authors published a mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on red blood cell production. Their focus is Sox6, a protein that helps control which genes are switched on in cells. The team asked whether adult mice need Sox6 to make red cells well, both in normal health and when anemia creates sudden demand for more.

Red cell output rises or falls with a hormone signal, and the authors test how much of that response depends on Sox6. Their work shows Sox6 is needed for the system to run at full strength in both calm and stressed states. That finding helps explain how the body protects its oxygen supply when blood is lost.
plos-pone-0012188:
María Llorens-Martín, Gonzalo Tejeda, and José Trejo studied new brain cells in mice raised in enriched surroundings, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A rich environment with toys and space boosts the birth of new neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, and this growth may underlie some of enrichment's calming and protective effects. The team used a two-pulse labeling method to track cells born at different times.

They found enrichment's effects on new neurons change with time rather than staying fixed, with different cell groups affected at different stages. Timing-aware results stop researchers from averaging away the real story. They also hint at when interventions might best support the aging or injured brain.
plos-pone-0012288:
Ashley Wright, Nicole Fox, and Karl Johnson built a screening toolkit from fruit fly deletion strains, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Each strain in the collection is missing a known chunk of the genome, so screening the set can locate genes behind any trait. The team defined the collection and ran it through screens for embryo defects, for partners of orphan receptors, and for genes that misplace proteins.

Their results show one shared toolkit serving many different questions at once. A screened deletion set turns gene hunting from artisanal work into an assembly line. Other researchers can order the same strains and repeat the trick for their own traits, which multiplies the paper's value.
plos-pone-0012388:
Christine Champion, Dominique Guianvarc'h, Catherine Sénamaud-Beaufort and colleagues studied how the drug zebularine jams DNA methylation enzymes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In mammals, methyl tags on DNA help control which genes stay on or off, and the enzymes that place them, called DNMTs, are targets of cancer drugs. Zebularine blocks these enzymes, but the exact grip was unclear.

The team worked out how zebularine traps the C5 class of these enzymes in a stuck state. Knowing the trap in detail helps chemists design stronger, more selective blockers. Better DNMT drugs could reactivate silenced tumor guard genes in cancer while limiting side effects on healthy cells.
plos-pone-0012488:
Maria Poulou, Donald Bell, Kostas Bozonelos and colleagues built a gene switch directly into a chromosome, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Most lab gene switches rely on foreign regulator proteins and drug-like triggers such as hormones or antibiotics. The team wanted a cleaner switch driven by a natural yeast regulator, Leu3p, and a metabolite signal.

Their integrated switch turns a gene off and on in response to the metabolite alpha-IPM, without loose plasmid copies. A stable, chromosomal switch gives steadier control for experiments and for engineered yeast in industry. Cleaner switches also reduce side effects that foreign regulators cause in cell studies.
plos-pone-0012588:
Zacariah Hildenbrand, Sudheer Molugu, Daniela Stock and colleagues identified a new part in a cellular proton pump, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. V-ATPases are molecular machines that pump protons to acidify cell compartments, which digestion, signaling, and waste handling all require. The pump's V1 head is held by stalks, and how the stalk base assembles was incompletely known.

The team characterized the C-H peripheral stalk base as a distinct component in V1 assembly. Knowing the full parts list of this machine matters beyond basic curiosity: faulty acidification underlies kidney disease, bone disorders, and some cancers. Each resolved part is a potential future drug grip.
plos-pone-0012688:
Benameur, Soleti, Porro and co-authors tested tiny cell fragments as helpers for growing new blood vessels. The fragments, called microparticles, bud off cell surfaces when cells switch on or die. Their 2010 study used particles from human T cells carrying a signal protein named Sonic hedgehog.

In mice, these particles favoured new vessel growth by way of the nitric oxide pathway. New vessels can rescue tissue starved of blood after a blocked artery. A natural particle that nudges growth could inspire safer treatments than raw growth factors. The team checked the vessel growth in living tissue, not just dishes.
plos-pone-0012788:
Rujoi, Pipalia and Maxfield screened small molecules for their effect on cholesterol handling in mutant cells. Niemann-Pick type C disease traps cholesterol inside cell storage compartments, causing wide harm. Their 2010 study used cells carrying the disease fault and tested which small molecules lower sterol build-up.

They traced the cholesterol pathways each helpful molecule actually changed. Knowing the pathway stops researchers chasing effects that look good but act elsewhere. The screen hands drug hunters a set of leads for a disease with few options.  Each hit was checked again in follow-up tests for dose effects.
plos-pone-0012888:
Fatti, Grimwood and Bock compared HIV treatment results across three levels of care in South Africa. Reports had conflicted on whether small primary clinics match hospitals at antiretroviral therapy. Their 2010 evaluation covered four South African provinces and all three tiers of treatment service.

They report better therapy outcomes at the primary healthcare level. Strong results at local clinics support moving HIV care out of crowded hospitals and closer to patients' homes. That shift became central to how South Africa scaled up treatment.  Clinics, district hospitals and referral centres were each scored.
plos-pone-0323988:
Mathew A Dittmann, Grzegorz Buczkowski, and Brock A Harpur published this 2026 study of gene silencing in the Argentine ant, a widespread invasive species. Ants are hard to engineer genetically, so feeding them interfering RNA is a practical way to test gene function. The team fed workers glowing tagged RNA and tracked it through the body, then checked gene activity and nestmate recognition behavior.

The swallowed RNA reached the antennae and dialed down the core smell receptor gene there, changing recognition behavior. Feeding can thus silence tissue-specific genes in ants, opening smell research in social insects.
plos-pone-0326588:
Neelam Yadav and colleagues present a research paper from 2026 on a new way to judge street-level air quality without fixed monitors. Their system, called PPDRTL, photographs leaves on roadside trees and treats the dirt settled on them as a record of nearby traffic pollution. The team worked across busy, medium, and quiet roads and checked their readings against official board data from Haryana in India.

Inside, the authors describe how they cleaned up leaf images with three search methods. They pulled out simple picture traits. Those traits fed a basic straight-line model that predicts an air quality score. The best version matched official readings closely in a short pilot test. For city planners, leaves could become cheap extra sensors where monitor stations are too sparse.
plos-pone-0334188:
Jackline Juma and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Set in Kisumu, Kenya, it reports a high prevalence of Plasmodium ovale wallikeri, a malaria parasite species often overlooked. The cases appear in co-infections alongside Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria species, in people carrying malaria parasites.

The comparison runs between symptomatic patients and asymptomatic carriers, people infected without feeling ill. A hidden second species matters because treatments and tests tuned to falciparum can miss ovale parasites that later relapse. Malaria programs in western Kenya are the readers who must adjust diagnosis and follow-up to this mixed picture.
plos-pone-0334488:
Ayuko Yukawa and colleagues surveyed three hundred and thirty seven school nurses in Japanese middle and high schools on mental health and suicide knowledge. School nurses are front line adults for teens in distress, yet their training gaps were barely measured. Forms probed knowledge, attitudes, planned responses, and confidence for student mental health and suicide risk.

One third wrongly believed careful listening alone can manage psychotic symptoms. Many hesitated to ask students directly about suicide plans even when risk looked clear. Over half lacked confidence to teach mental health topics. Evidence based training for school nurses, the authors urge, is a direct lever for teen suicide prevention.
plos-pone-0336088:
Mohit Neema, Peggy Nopoulos, and colleagues describe a long study of children and young adults who carry risk for Huntington's disease. Huntington's is known for brain damage that shows in midlife, yet the faulty gene is present from birth. The ChANGE-HD study asks how that gene shapes the growing brain long before symptoms start.

The plan follows about four hundred fifty people aged six to thirty across several sites for seven years. Visits gather thinking and movement tests, behavior checks, blood and saliva samples, and brain scans. A partner study covers the rarer childhood-onset form of the disease. Results are expected later, and the team hopes early markers of change could one day guide treatment trials.
plos-pone-0336888:
Sananda Saha, Ayesha Maliha Khan, and Fahim Kabir Monjurul Haque tested bottled electrolyte drinks sold in Dhaka, Bangladesh, in 2026 for germs and drug resistance. The local drinks are made without national standards approval, leaving their safety unchecked.

Forty samples from nine brands all held bacteria, and many broke international limits for total germs or faecal contamination. Each drink carried more than one species, including several that cause disease. Many isolates resisted multiple drugs. The authors present the findings as a direct case for licensing and routine testing of a product marketed for recovery from illness.
plos-pone-0339488:
Zhecheng Wang and co-authors examined how political uncertainty sends risk rippling through cryptocurrency markets. Crypto prices swing together in crises, but the timing and strength of those linkages may change when politics turns unstable. Their 2026 study split price movements into short, medium, and long horizons, then modeled how shocks pass between coins under calm and tense political conditions.

Responses were lopsided. Over medium and long horizons, most coins reacted more strongly to shocks when political uncertainty ran high, and high-uncertainty shocks widened the spillovers between coins. Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Monero consistently sent risk outward, while smaller coins like Peercoin and Namecoin mostly absorbed it. The authors offer the map as a guide for investors and regulators watching crypto stability.
plos-pone-0341988:
Zeeshan Sidiq and seven colleagues compare this 2026 PLOS One head-to-head evaluation of two rapid molecular tests for tuberculosis at a New Delhi center. Both tests are endorsed by the World Health Organization, but clinics also care about reliability, failed runs, and cost. More than six hundred people with suspected lung tuberculosis gave paired samples for the Truenat and Xpert Ultra systems, with culture as the reference.

Both tests were highly accurate. Xpert Ultra caught slightly more true cases and produced fewer failed results, while Truenat was cheaper and easier to run in small, decentralized settings, though repeat testing was needed more often. For drug resistance detection, both were perfectly specific but missed some resistant cases. The authors recommend a tiered approach that plays to each platform's strengths.
plos-pone-0342288:
Giulia Cardamone and seven colleagues watch inflammation switch on production of a little-known growth factor. Their 2026 cell study uses MCF7 breast cancer cells. The signal molecule IL-1 beta, a hallmark of inflamed tumour surroundings, was the trigger. The gene IGFL1 responded on two levels. Its transcription rose, and its translation into protein rose further. The team dissected the gene's tail region, the three-prime untranslated stretch that governs how messages get read.

That tail proved to be the control hub. Within it, one distinct guanine-rich stretch carried the inflammation response. Remove or alter that element, and the translational boost depends on it. Tumours are inflamed places, and inflammation quietly retunes which proteins cancer cells manufacture. Pinpointing the exact switch for one growth factor shows the mechanism in miniature. Such switches could someday be drugged to starve tumours of signals they currently order on demand.
plos-pone-0342888:
Homes that both use and sell electricity, called prosumers, now also run computing tasks that can be sent to nearby edge servers. Rui Xue and colleagues tackled the tangle: offloading choices burn local power, and power prices change whether offloading pays, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

They built a mathematical model maximizing long-term benefit across output, delay, and money, under server capacity and community energy balance limits. A learning agent proposes offloading decisions while a rule layer blocks any that break hard constraints. The hybrid design aims to keep the grid stable while households trade energy and computing in step.
plos-pone-0343188:
Marsophia Marcellus and Catherine Murphy present this 2026 PLOS One cell study on how breast cancer cells crawl toward a chemical signal linked to metastasis. The signal, CXCL12, guides the highly mobile triple-negative cell line they studied. Cells were placed in collagen gels of two densities with a steady signal gradient, then filmed for a day so software could track each cell's movement and shape.

The cells responded to the signal above a threshold concentration, and directed movement was clearest in the denser gel. Cells also took on a range of shapes in the gel, and shape turned out to matter: differently shaped subpopulations sensed and followed the gradient differently. The authors argue that cell shape belongs in models of how cancers spread.
plos-pone-0344388:
Louise Dewick and colleagues report that the placenta contracts on its own during healthy pregnancy. Their imaging study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The team had first described such contractions in 2020. This time they scanned thirty-six women with smooth, problem-free pregnancies. The scans took place between week twenty-nine and week forty-two.

Contractions showed in at least three-fifths of the women. They came about twice an hour on average. Every pregnancy ended with a healthy baby of good weight. No mother showed signs of placental disease. Because these events are common in normal pregnancy, knowing their pattern matters. It can stop doctors from mistaking them for warning signs.
plos-pone-0344688:
Fishing trips succeed or fail in the angler's mind long after the cooler is emptied. Caren Collins and colleagues modeled what drives trip satisfaction among Texas coastal anglers, using dockside interviews collected over more than three decades, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Instead of mailed surveys answered from fading memory, interviewers met anglers at boat ramps the same day. Catch details, how much was caught, fish size, and effort, predicted satisfaction most strongly for three favorite species. Grades rose over the years and toward the southern coast, and the drivers differed by target fish. Managers can use the results to protect the trip qualities anglers actually remember.
plos-pone-0345688:
