Kebenu Feyisa Gonfa and coauthors published a 2026 soil study in PLOS ONE on rescuing salty, sodium-damaged farmland at the Metehara sugar estate in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley. Such soils stunt crops across the region. In laboratory soil columns, the team tested phosphogypsum, a fertilizer-industry byproduct, at five doses up to double the calculated gypsum need. The doses were tested against natural gypsum and an untreated control, with several amounts of washing water.

Phosphogypsum at the full calculated dose or above, washed with three to four pore volumes of water, brought salt and sodium down to levels most crops can tolerate. The highest dose removed the largest share of soluble salts and sodium, and the byproduct matched the reclamation job well overall. The authors call phosphogypsum a promising material for this widespread problem, while insisting that greenhouse and field trials must come before any rate is recommended to farmers.
plos-pone-0346788:
Laurène Petitfour, Manuela De Allegri, and co-authors surveyed patients leaving clinics in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province to learn what actually drives satisfaction with care. Their 2026 study questioned six hundred sixty-six outpatients across more than one hundred twenty public and private facilities in four districts, distilling sixteen satisfaction questions into a single score.

Average satisfaction ran high, at about seventy-six out of a hundred, and neither the type of facility nor the district mattered. Women scored notably lower than men, while insured patients scored higher. What patients actually experienced mattered most: respected privacy lifted scores strongly, and having prescribed drugs available helped too. Spending related to satisfaction in a curve, rising then falling. The authors urge policies aimed at specific groups and at the basics of care delivery.
plos-pone-0347188:
Jolan Alsaud and colleagues survey in 2026 sleep problems and life quality across the wider public in Qassim, Saudi Arabia, where the link had not been studied before. More than a thousand people picked at random in public places completed trusted scales for sleep quality and for health related quality of life, plus background questions.

Most respondents reported poor sleep, and average scores for physical and mental life quality sat below ideal levels. After accounting for background and illness, sleep factors still predicted both kinds of quality, with a much larger share for mental health. The authors call for sleep checks inside public health work and wider awareness.
plos-pone-0347488:
Beata Gruber-Bzura and colleagues ask if flat cell cultures mislead safety tests. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Global standards test device extracts on cells grown flat. Real tissue is three-dimensional, though. So the team grew mouse cells as tiny balls, called spheroids. Both formats then faced latex extracts.

The ball cultures proved hardier than the flat ones. Toxic effects took longer to show. Older balls bounced back after long exposure. They even regrew, a recovery backed by damage tests and gene readings. Flat layers sounded the alarm sooner. The authors say round models deserve a place in device safety checks.
plos-pone-0347588:
Dongxun Jiang and Zhaocheng Li built a scoring model for how well cities in China withstand sudden natural disasters. Data on housing, infrastructure, output, and population covered twenty five districts in Changchun and Hohhot. Three yardsticks anchor the model: how fast a city responds, how well it shares resources, and how many facilities serve each person.

Expert weighting plus a ranking method scored districts by service level and exposed weak spots in each city. Short and long term investment plans followed from the gaps. Stability checks suggested the model reflects city strength fairly, though the authors note limits. City leaders get a structured way to spend scarce resilience funds where gaps bite hardest.
plos-pone-0347688:
Jiao Yan and co-workers fine-tune a road binder that mixes water-based epoxy resin into emulsified asphalt. The blend promises tougher pavement, but the asphalt can break apart before the epoxy hardens. Their 2026 study adds a curing accelerator at four doses and tests heat strength, sticking power, wear, and chemical change from the molecular level up.

A small dose, about one part in a hundred, gave the best results across the board. Rutting resistance, adhesion, and freeze-thaw durability all peaked there, and wear losses shrank. Chemical scans showed that dose helped the curing reaction finish, while triple the dose left leftover agent and interfered. The right pinch of accelerator, not more, makes the greener binder perform.
plos-pone-0347988:
Qi Wang and colleagues lay out a pilot trial of mindfulness training delivered through virtual reality headsets to people caring for relatives with dementia at home. Caregivers suffer high rates of depression and stress, and standard mindfulness courses are hard to attend. Their 2026 protocol will randomise ninety caregivers to VR sessions in calming virtual nature, audio-guided practice, or usual care for eight weeks.

Outcomes cover mood, burden, mindfulness, quality of life, and the relationship with the person cared for, with interviews probing acceptability. As a protocol, the paper reports plans, not results. The pilot's job is to learn whether the approach is feasible and worth a full trial.
plos-pone-0348088:
Mastewal Worku Lake and colleagues checked how faithfully health facilities in Ethiopia's Amhara Region follow the national malaria rule: test every suspected case before treating. Malaria has resurged sharply in the region. Their 2026 mixed-methods study scored fifty-three public and private facilities on following the guideline's steps, testing coverage, and consistency, then interviewed staff about the gaps.

Average fidelity landed at about sixty-four percent, with only two in five facilities scoring high and private clinics trailing public ones. Engaged staff, good support systems, and simpler procedures raised fidelity. Interviews blamed supply shortages, patient pressure, and skipped counselling. The authors say closing these gaps is essential while transmission climbs.
plos-pone-0348188:
Mohamed Baklola and colleagues survey medical students across ten universities in Yemen for this 2026 PLOS ONE study of research in a war-torn country. Doing research as a student builds evidence-based habits, yet students in conflict-affected, low-resource settings face broken funding, missing mentors, and crowded curricula.

The online questionnaire measured what students know about research, how they feel about it, how much they have actually done, and what blocks them. The multi-university picture is meant to replace guesswork with a shared baseline, so medical schools and outside partners can target the worst barriers first. The authors frame research capacity as part of rebuilding a health system, not a luxury extra.
plos-pone-0348288:
A K M Mominul Islam and colleagues test a head start for foxtail millet seed in this 2026 PLOS ONE field study from Bangladesh. Foxtail millet is nutritious and shrugs off harsh climates, but its seeds germinate poorly and seedlings start weak, which caps yields.

In lab and field trials across winter and summer, four varieties were soaked before sowing in water or in one of several chemical primers at two strengths. Priming improved germination, seedling vigor, and final grain yield, with the best treatments pushing germination toward nine seeds in ten. For small farmers, a cheap overnight soak is an unusually affordable way to get more from a hardy but underused grain.
plos-pone-0348588:
Sue In Choi and colleagues piloted a digital lung sound recorder meant to work at a distance, where a doctor cannot press a stethoscope to the chest. Sixty-four people took part, some healthy and some with lung diseases from asthma to pneumonia. All were examined the ordinary way while the device captured the same sounds. Three experts later classified the recordings blind and compared verdicts.

Agreement between the digital recordings and bedside listening was strong for every rater, and wheezing sounds were recognised most reliably. They found the device comfortable, and tidal breathing recordings proved usable alongside deep breathing ones. The authors conclude the recorder captures lung sounds well enough to support remote care and to feed the growing libraries that train diagnostic algorithms.
plos-pone-0348788:
Heitor Levy Ferreira Praça and co-workers map where drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment goes wrong in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Resistant cases need long, hard treatment, and many patients never finish. Their 2026 study reviews nearly a thousand cases over eight years and joins personal risk factors with a map of high-risk neighborhoods.

Close to a third of cases ended badly, most through patients dropping out of care. Dropping out clustered among men, people with low schooling, and those using alcohol or other drugs. Deaths ran higher after age forty and with the toughest resistance patterns. Three high-risk zones sat in the city's poorer north. Local support aimed at those blocks could lift completion rates.
plos-pone-0348888:
Hosain Yasemi, Khalil Momeni, and co-authors studied why patients in Iran's Ilam Province often travel outside their home area for hospital care. Such travel burdens families and signals gaps in local services. Their 2026 study first interviewed fifteen experts to name the drivers, then asked twenty-five participants to rank them using a structured comparison method.

Forty-one detailed factors fell into four groups covering doctors, patients and families, health organizations, and social culture. Late payment of doctors' claims, too few specialists, weak equipment and buildings, and advertising by hospitals in neighboring provinces stood out. Doctor-related factors ranked as the strongest influence overall, while social and cultural factors ranked weakest. The authors say fixing pay, staffing, and facilities at home would stem the outflow.
plos-pone-0349188:
Eric Wang and colleagues studied a small RNA called miR-9 inside the vessel-lining cells of the eye and heart, two places diabetes damages most. High blood sugar lowers miR-9 in both tissues, and losing it harms the lining. In heart cells the team had already found the switch behind the drop, involving a long RNA partner and chemical marks on DNA packaging.

Retinal cells told a different story: the same fall in miR-9 was controlled through different upstream routes than in heart cells. Tests with mark-blocking drugs and gene-silencing tools separated the two mechanisms. The lesson is practical: a treatment that restores miR-9 in the diabetic heart may not work in the diabetic eye, because the same problem is wired differently in each tissue.
plos-pone-0349288:
Xin Li and co-authors combined single cell and bulk gene data in 2026 to map programmed cell death in lung injury caused by sepsis. The complication is frequent and deadly, and usable gene markers for it remain few.

They scored thirteen death related gene sets, merged network and difference analyses, and trained more than a hundred model combinations to find the best classifier. They then linked the death score to immune and metabolic patterns and located the model genes in single cell data. A defined death signature could help doctors spot septic lung injury earlier and researchers pick targets with cell level precision.
plos-pone-0349388:
Maria Moreno-Druet, Nadejda A Soudzilovskaia, Frederik De Laender, and co-authors tested whether soil fungi learn from past temperatures, a question with climate stakes because warmer soils may release more carbon. If fungi acclimate, warming-driven carbon loss could soften. Their 2026 study gave seven common soil fungi different temperature histories, then grew them at test temperatures and measured growth alongside traits like pigmentation and spore load.

History barely mattered. Growth after the two-stage treatment depended little on which temperatures came first, and trait shifts did not predict which fungi would grow well. The authors conclude that thermal acclimation in these fungi is limited and idiosyncratic, varying by species without a usable pattern. For climate modelers, the message is cautionary: do not count on soil fungi adjusting their way out of warming.
plos-pone-0349588:
Could a tree ever grow on Mars? Agnieszka Wendland and colleagues treat the question seriously for a future warmed, terraformed planet, in this 2026 PLOS One thought experiment built on a detailed Martian surface energy model.

They borrow limits from Earth's hardiest high-mountain conifers: a growing season long enough, nights not too cold, days not too hot. Water, soil, oxygen, and safe carbon dioxide levels would also be needed, though those are not modeled here. The study asks where and when on Mars the temperature window alone might open. It is a planning exercise for the far future, not a prediction.
plos-pone-0349688:
Thai rice farmers work small plots under very different conditions, so one recipe for higher yields fits few. Manusnan Suriyalaksh and colleagues gathered data from more than seventeen hundred smallholders in central Thailand, covering fifty-eight farming and money variables, for this 2026 PLOS One study.

Four automated prediction systems competed, and the best forecast yields with fair accuracy. An explanation method then ranked what mattered: farmers' social networks topped the list, ahead of harvest rental and labor costs. Better-connected farmers harvested more, likely through shared know-how. Grouping farmers by profile showed different drivers per group, arguing for support tailored to each type rather than blanket advice.
plos-pone-0350088:
Shu-Xian Lin and Kuang-Sheng Yeh studied a dangerous strain of E. coli bacteria collected from pet dogs and cats treated for urinary infections at a veterinary teaching hospital in Taiwan. The strain, called ST131, spreads worldwide and resists many antibiotics in human medicine. The team examined four hundred bacterial isolates collected between 2011 and 2019.

Twenty-six isolates turned out to be ST131, and detailed checks on nineteen showed they carried many genes that help the bacteria grab iron and survive in the body. All resisted two common penicillin drugs, though all still responded to one last-line medicine. Finding this human threat strain in pets raises questions about shared bacteria between animals and their owners.
plos-pone-0350188:
Amartay Kumar Dhar, Sharmin Akther, and Farhana Akter Bina studied which factors shape whether mothers in Bangladesh get checkups after giving birth. They used a national health survey from 2022 and compared a standard statistical model with several machine learning models. A method called SHAP then ranked which factors pushed each prediction up or down.

Machine learning clearly beat the standard model at predicting who received postnatal care. Where the birth took place was the strongest factor, followed by the husband's job, living in a rural area, household wealth, and media exposure. The ranking gives health planners a short list of levers for raising care after childbirth.
plos-pone-0350288:
Obinna Ekwunife and co-authors counted what patients pay out of pocket for rapid COVID tests in Nigeria, Malawi, and Zimbabwe in 2026 work. Testing was free at the sites, yet travel, lost work, and side costs can still shut out the poor.

Adults at clinics, pharmacies, and community sites were surveyed in 2022 and 2023 about every cost tied to getting tested, from fares to lost earnings. Costs were judged against household income to find catastrophic spending. Professional and self testing routes differed by country. The accounting gives pandemic planners a fuller price tag than the test kit alone suggests.
plos-pone-0350388:
Rodney N Nagoshi, Ashley E Tessnow, and Robert L Meagher reported two new genetic markers for fall armyworm strains in 2026. The crop pest has two look-alike strains that differ in plant hosts, and naming them has rested on markers from a single gene.

Drawing on population data from across the Americas, the authors validated markers that support earlier claims about strain identity being carried mainly on one sex chromosome acting as a unit. Extra markers let researchers cross check strain calls instead of trusting one gene. Better strain tracking matters because the strains differ in spread, host use, and possibly control response.
plos-pone-0350888:
Kathryn Hirabayashi and colleagues asked whether steroids given during a child's COVID illness prevent long COVID later. They used health records from a national pediatric research network. The records began with over eight hundred fifty thousand infected children. Statistical balancing built fair treated and untreated groups. Inpatients and outpatients were judged apart. The team then watched for long COVID diagnoses in the months after infection.

Almost nothing set the groups apart. Hospitalized children on steroids showed a lower risk of one slice of long COVID, the gut kind. No other benefit appeared in any group. The plain reading is that routine steroids do not prevent long COVID in children. Families get a clear answer where habit might otherwise prescribe the drugs.
plos-pone-0350988:
Luis G Ayala and colleagues propose a new yardstick for hospital engineering capacity in Mexico: biomedical engineers per hospital bed. Engineers keep medical devices and hospital systems safe and running, yet world counts usually divide engineers by population, which hides their link to beds and gear. Counts for Mexico from 2017 to 2022 were used to test the measure.

Dividing engineers by beds ties staffing directly to the machines and wards they serve. The paper follows world guidance for building health indicators, so the measure can be tracked over time and compared across regions. A bed based count, the authors argue, gives planners a sharper view of whether hospitals can maintain modern care safely.
plos-pone-0351188:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 engineering study, pull apart rock-filled concrete to see what makes it resist splitting. This material packs large rocks into self-flowing concrete, saving cement on big projects. Its strength depends on the rock skeleton and on the thin boundary layer where rock meets cement paste. The team combined real breaking tests with a detailed computer model.

Strengthening the boundary layer raised splitting strength by more than a third before the gains leveled off. Stronger rock helped similarly, also up to a plateau. Rock size mattered in an arc: medium sizes did best, and mixing sizes, so small rocks fill gaps between large ones, beat any single size. The model let the team watch cracks grow and match the wreckage of real samples. Their guidance for builders is concrete: invest in the boundary layer and grade the rock.
plos-pone-0351688:
Inge Brouns and colleagues tested a long-standing idea about small clusters of sensing cells in the airways, called neuroepithelial bodies. The idea says these cells detect low oxygen and signal the brain through nerves to adjust breathing. Direct proof was missing, so the team watched living mouse lung slices under a microscope, tracking calcium flashes that would mark a sensing response during low oxygen.

The control tissue, from the carotid body, flashed strongly, proving the test could detect sensing. The airway clusters never flashed, at any age or oxygen pattern, though they still responded to other stimulation. Low oxygen did stir their mitochondria. The authors conclude these cells probably do not send calcium-based low-oxygen alarms to the brain, which sends researchers back to rethink what the clusters are actually for.
plos-pone-0351788:
Han and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether the so-called good cholesterol predicts recovery after surgery for a slipped lumbar disc. This cholesterol, carried in high-density particles, had already been linked to spine wear, but its value for judging outcomes was unknown. The team reviewed patients who had a common fusion operation over five years.

Nearly a thousand patients were included, and their recovery was scored by function and cost measures. Statistical screening kept cholesterol level among the factors tied to outcome. A cut point emerged: patients in the normal range recovered better than those with abnormal levels. In patients without brain or vessel disease, the pattern bent into a U shape, with a middle band of levels looking best. The authors caution that the link was modest and uneven across groups. Still, a routine blood value might one day help surgeons set expectations before operating.
plos-pone-0351988:
Broken ribs are easy to miss on chest scans of older patients, whose bones carry extra growths and thinning. Shan Xiong and co-authors tested whether a computer helper improves detection in emergency care, in a 2026 PLOS One study covering more than one thousand chest injury patients.

Six radiologists read scans alone and again with the helper, and a senior panel set the true answers. Reading alone, the doctors caught fewer fresh breaks in patients over sixty than in younger ones. With computer help, their catch rate for older patients rose to match the younger group. False alarms also fell, suggesting real value for busy emergency teams.
plos-pone-0352088:
Malalaniaina Rakotobe and colleagues examined how young brain cells connect in the developing cerebellum of mice. Older microscope work had spotted unusual links between cells in a layer where new neurons are born. The team wanted to know what those links really are, since several kinds of cell bridges can look alike under the microscope.

Using dyes, genetic labels, and live imaging in week-old pups, they separated bridges left over from cell division from other connections. Some dividing-cell bridges were present, while a second bridge type was absent. They also found thin membrane protrusions joining cells, related or not, hinting at a little-studied way cells may talk during brain growth. More work is needed to learn what those links do.
plos-pone-0352188:
Hussen Ebrahim and seven colleagues document what Ethiopian highland farmers know about local forage plants. Their 2026 study surveys three hundred twenty-three smallholders in two districts of the northeastern highlands. Livestock there feed mainly on natural pasture. Scientists have catalogued these herbaceous forages before, but implementation ignored farmers' own knowledge and failed. Interviews and rankings captured how farmers see the resource, its decline, and the obstacles to using it better.

Farmers confirmed the pasture is shrinking alarmingly. Forestland expansion took the largest share of blame, then cropland growth and resettlement. For using local forages, land shortage ranked as the top challenge. Lack of awareness and spreading eucalyptus plantations followed. Farmers had already cut animal numbers in response. The study argues that grazing science starting from this knowledge stands a chance of working. Restoration plans drawn without the people who read these pastures daily have a long record of quietly failing.
plos-pone-0352588:
Erin Wertz and six colleagues fight false claims by adding facts. Their 2026 study ran forty-eight field experiments inside Instagram ads. The targets were people who rarely read news. Short verified videos addressed climate change, vaccines, judging news, and election integrity. The ads reached nearly two and a half million accounts. Over forty thousand viewers completed follow-up assessments.

The intervention worked. Forty-six of the forty-eight tests moved results in the right direction. Forty reached statistical significance. Belief accuracy improved, and so did democratic attitudes and media literacy. Vaccination intentions budged somewhat as well. Effects did not depend on special persuasive tricks or formats. Some climate effects persisted over time. For platforms and public agencies, the study demonstrates a scalable, positive route to resilience: put good information where non-readers already scroll.
plos-pone-0352688:
Rongkang Pei, Zeyu Lyu, and Guolong Wang build an artificial intelligence model for reading social media storms. Their 2026 study tackles narrative structure in posts about public events. Such posts carry opinion, emotion, and fast-moving themes. Older tools treated sentiment, topic, and time separately. The authors fuse all three inside a transformer model built on a RoBERTa language backbone.

The combined model beat four kinds of baseline systems. It recognised narrative structure more accurately. It also classified sentiment and topics better. Performance held up across different events and in noisy, messy text. Those are exactly the conditions of real public opinion monitoring. The authors close with ethics: privacy, anonymisation, and bias all need care. The tool could help officials follow public reaction during crises, provided those safeguards hold.
plos-pone-0352788:
Lucas Souza and seven colleagues build a new blood test for cattle brucellosis in this 2026 study. Brucellosis spreads from animals to people and hurts herds worldwide. Current tests use crude bacterial extracts. Those can react falsely to other germs. The team instead predicted small protein fragments, called epitopes, that the immune system recognises. Synthetic copies became the test's targets.

Two peptides survived screening against known positive and negative cattle sera. Built into a standard laboratory test, they caught eighty-four percent of positive animals. They correctly cleared about eighty-three percent of negatives. A combined multi-epitope protein performed notably worse on both measures. The authors call the work preliminary. Still, defined synthetic targets could eventually replace messy bacterial extracts, giving veterinarians cleaner and more consistent brucellosis screening.
plos-pone-0352888:
Belachew Getnet Eneyew and Workiyie Worie Assefa investigate this 2026 PLOS One study of why wetlands in two districts of northwestern Ethiopia are being turned into farmland. The team combined satellite land-cover records spanning thirty-six years with household surveys and interviews with local experts, then modeled what shapes attitudes toward converting wetlands.

Nearly half the wetland area had become farmland over the study period. Most households and even officials favored conversion despite recognizing wetlands' benefits, and local government had handed wetlands to unemployed graduates and landless families as a jobs measure. Age, land and livestock holdings, and livelihood type all shaped the appetite to convert. The authors urge ecological checks before conversion and wider job creation so families are not forced onto wetlands.
plos-pone-0352988:
Yibo Chen and three colleagues ask, in this 2026 PLOS One study, whether large language models predict people's behavior better when they first predict emotions. The setting is deliberately narrow: personnel in high-pressure, high-stakes roles, drawn from a single cultural background so the data stay consistent. The team built a dataset linking scenarios, emotions, and behaviors, then fine-tuned a language model on it.

The emotion-first model beat both a plain baseline model and a model trained to predict behavior directly, across several accuracy measures. The authors connect this to decision theories that treat emotion as a step in choosing actions. They present the work as a bridge between artificial intelligence and behavioral science, with lessons for forecasting behavior where mistakes are costly.
plos-pone-0353288:
Yang, Wu, and Mo built a classifier for indoor radio positioning in a 2026 study. Ultra-wideband signals locate people and goods indoors, but walls block direct paths and warp the signal. Telling a blocked path from a clear one is the key first step.

Their method combines several fast tree models in parallel and reads signal patches at multiple scales across time and frequency. Tests on a public data set beat deep learning and single-tree rivals on accuracy and held up on new data, with workable computing cost. Reliable blocked-path detection could steady indoor navigation in warehouses, hospitals, and malls where satellite signals fail.
plos-pone-0353388:
Mar Riera-Pagespetit and seven colleagues ask whether sugar control still protects the kidneys after age eighty, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Spain. Doctors often relax targets in the very old to avoid dangerous low-sugar episodes, leaving the kidney question open. The team followed more than a thousand patients over eighty with type 2 diabetes and initially healthy kidneys, across five years of records.

Kidney disease appeared in over half of both groups, but clearly more often — and sooner — in those with poor sugar control. Statistical adjustment left the link standing on its own. The authors do not demand strict targets for everyone; they argue sugar control deserves a real place in individualised decisions for the oldest patients.
plos-pone-0353488:
Unahalekhaka and colleagues tracked a drug-resistant hospital germ across Thailand in a 2026 study. The germ resists a last-resort antibiotic family and causes dangerous blood infections with few treatment options. Gene sequencing covered dozens of isolates collected from hospitals nationwide between 2020 and 2024.

One global clone dominated and appeared in region after region. Resistance came mainly from one gene, with a second powerful resistance gene riding on moving DNA pieces in a subset of isolates. That moving piece matched a known carrier found in two clones. Steady gene tracking, the authors argue, is essential to catch spread early and guide hospital infection control.
plos-pone-0353688:
Dejan Mihajlovic and seven colleagues translate a questionnaire about period pain into Serbian and check that it still measures what it should, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The scale asks how much menstrual pain interferes with daily life, a burden most women experience but medicine often underrates. Three hundred and fifty female health-science students with period pain in the past year completed the Serbian version plus a standard stress questionnaire.

The translation held together excellently: items hung on a single factor, consistency scores were high, and scores rose alongside depression, anxiety, and stress scores as expected. Serbian clinicians and researchers now have a validated tool for a complaint long dismissed as normal.
plos-pone-0353788:
Rezapour compared two popular tools for finding genes that switch on or off in a 2026 study. Gene studies guide disease research, yet the tool chosen can change the gene list a team reports. Tests used real and partly simulated data from virus, bacteria, and scarring conditions, with repeated sampling at many sizes.

One tool found more changed genes when samples were few, while the two tools agreed more as samples grew. Genes found only by the other tool, though fewer, predicted outcomes better in fresh data from separate virus studies. The author advises judging tools by whether their gene lists hold up elsewhere, not by list length alone.
plos-pone-0353888:
Yanhua Xiao and six colleagues build a neural network that spots changes between satellite images taken at different times, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Their data are hyperspectral images, which record many narrow colour bands and reveal changes invisible to ordinary cameras. Standard methods compare the two images too crudely and blur fine detail.

Their design extracts deep differences layer by layer, then uses fine interpolation to recover changes smaller than a single pixel. The network is aimed at mixed-resolution image pairs, a common real-world headache. Better change detection feeds land-use monitoring, disaster assessment, and environmental watch-keeping, where missing a small change can mean missing the start of a much bigger one.
plos-pone-0354088:
Madhawi Altaib and three co-authors asked what new speech-language pathologists actually need to succeed at work, in this 2026 PLOS ONE interview study. University training is meant to prepare graduates, yet employers still report gaps. Fifteen people took part in focus groups: former students, teachers, practising clinicians, and employers who hire them.

Four themes ran through the discussions: personal qualities, working independently, solid academic grounding, and day-to-day clinical skill. Attitude, flexibility, and clear decision-making mattered as much as book knowledge. Participants wanted broader hands-on placements and more specialised teaching. Their message is that degree programmes must keep evolving if graduates are to handle varied clinics confidently from day one.
plos-pone-0354288:
Momeni Javad and colleagues map in 2026 where wind is most likely to strip soil in eastern and northeastern Iran, a dry region hit by dust storms. Ten learning models were trained on climate, soil, land shape, and rock data. Two models, a forest based one and a combined ensemble, scored best on standard accuracy checks.

Their maps put roughly a quarter to a third of the area at moderate or high risk. Sandy soil, seasonal temperature and rain patterns, height, and a wetness measure drove the pattern most. The maps can help officials target tree planting, grazing control, and other defences before land degrades further.
plos-pone-0354488:
Kangbien Park, a single author, published this 2026 paper proposing a rulebook for steering evolution in the lab. Directed evolution of creatures that reproduce without sex promises useful microbes and molecules, but experiments stumble at known points. Park sets out ten formal logics meant to handle those difficulties, then tests them in a simulation where an imaginary limb evolves toward a wing.

Simulated populations using the logics reached the target trait about two and a half times faster and with good accuracy, while those without them lagged. Park discusses what would make the approach rigorous in real experiments.
plos-pone-0354588:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, examine how a medical collagen sponge made from cow tissue affects macrophages, key immune cells that guide healing. Such sponges are widely used to stop bleeding and fill tissue, and they break down safely in the body. Their effect on immune behavior, though, was largely untested.

In cell cultures, the sponge made macrophages grow faster and eat particles more actively, and it raised their output of a signal that grows new blood vessels. Fluid from those cells then helped vessel cells form tube-like structures. The sponge mildly stirred resting immune cells, yet it calmed cells that had been provoked by a bacterial toxin, cutting their output of inflammatory signals. This two-way action, the authors suggest, helps explain how the sponge supports tissue repair: lively when healing starts, restraining when inflammation runs hot.
plos-pone-0354688:
Vera Sorin and five colleagues published this 2026 study on language models drafting the summary section of chest scan reports. Impressions guide care, but machine drafts can drift into generic wording. Using nearly twelve thousand CT lung artery reports, the team let two large models write summaries with no examples, random examples, or examples retrieved to match each case.

Matched examples won every comparison, and giving more examples at calmer settings helped further. Scores still landed in the middle range, so Sorin insists radiologists must check drafts before any clinical use. The trick is retrieval, not just model size.
plos-pone-0354888:
Liang Xu and Xiao Wu published this 2026 study of how Korean speakers and Chinese learners of Korean handle requests and refusals in conversation. Using written dialogue tasks built around twenty-four linked scenarios, they compared native speakers with intermediate and advanced learners, counting which politeness strategies each group chose and how scenario factors changed those choices.

Native speakers used a wider range of strategies than learners, though advanced learners closed much of the gap. Choices also shifted when several social factors combined. Xu and Wu propose their scenario design as a template for teaching the delicate art of saying no politely.
plos-pone-0355188:
Chaoyang Luo and Jing Bi study in 2026 heat treated coal waste in cement. They ask if it can replace part of the cement in building mixes. Two helpers were added to boost the waste. One was red mud, and the other was a silicate solution. Tests varied the mix in a set grid. Heat flow and microscope tools tracked how the paste set.

The silicate slowed the main setting stage. It also kept water being used at later stages. That points to a longer curing process. Red mud partly made up for strength lost with the waste. Using both helpers gave lower strength than silicate alone. Its inner structure was also looser and less even.
plos-pone-0355288:
Ruo-qiao Wen and colleagues compare in 2026 three ways to extract DNA from blood for finding very faint malaria infections after treatment. Finding hidden low level infections matters where malaria has been nearly wiped out, since missed cases can restart spread. The methods used a spin column, a red cell bursting route, and magnetic beads.

The bead method gave far more DNA, kept long pieces intact, and found more positive cases among faint clinical samples. It also detected the parasite at lower dilutions than the column method. The authors recommend bead extraction for surveillance screening where missing a case carries high risk.
plos-pone-0355488:
Charlotte Goodrose-Flores and Linda Björkhem-Bergman compared quality of life in Swedish women living with lipedema, a painful fat disorder. Lipedema causes abnormal fat build-up, usually in the legs, and is often missed or dismissed. Their 2026 study set women with lipedema beside healthy women and an exploratory group with advanced cancer.

Women with lipedema scored worse than healthy women on every quality-of-life dimension measured. On pain, physical function, and emotional problems, their scores matched the cancer group's. Their general health scores were lower still, and body image worries were markedly higher. They also reported more pain, fatigue, depression, and anxiety. The authors argue lipedema deserves recognition as a heavy burden, not a minor condition.
plos-pone-0355688:
Madalitso Chelenga and colleagues lay out a protocol, published in 2026, for the first global tally of Tritrichomonas foetus. This single-celled parasite has a split reputation. In cattle it is a serious cause of infertility and lost calves. In cats it causes stubborn diarrhea. In pigs it is a harmless gut passenger.

The planned review will search five databases without language limits for prevalence studies in the three hosts. It will pool the numbers by species and region. It will probe how diagnostic method and farm management shift the estimates. Duplicate screening and bias checks are built in. A trustworthy world map of this parasite would show surveillance programs where to look harder. It would also show where control efforts are actually keeping herds clean.
plos-pone-0355988:
Seyed Houtan Shahidi and three colleagues settle a practical question for runners in this 2026 study: does the standard one percent treadmill incline really reproduce outdoor running? Twelve trained male endurance runners completed identical staged workouts indoors on a treadmill and outdoors on a track, with breath-by-breath gas measurement throughout. The team compared running economy, the oxygen cost of covering a kilometer, and total energy cost across intensities.

Outdoor running cost more on every measure. Oxygen cost per kilometer was higher outside at all intensities, and the economy gap widened as effort approached the second ventilatory threshold; carbohydrate burning also rose outdoors near that intensity. The authors conclude the customary one percent grade under-corrects for the road. Athletes and coaches should not treat treadmill numbers as a perfect mirror of outdoor performance when planning training or testing.
plos-pone-0356088:
Igor Loncaric and an international team screened the mouths of Pacific marine mammals along Southern California. They hunted a group of staphylococci better known from dogs and cats. Their 2026 study sampled 452 animals across eight species. The set ran from California sea lions and elephant seals to dolphins and a pygmy sperm whale. Every isolate was then characterized with susceptibility tests and several layers of genetic typing.

They recovered forty-six isolates, mostly one species. Some were resistant to penicillin and tetracycline. A string of brand-new genetic types appeared, alongside fresh virulence genes. The diversity suggests these bacteria are established, evolving residents of marine mammals. They are not stray contaminants. The authors call for long-term monitoring of a potential bridge between wildlife, pets, and people.
plos-pone-0356388:
Benjamin Hägglund and four colleagues validate a cheap way to test pointing accuracy in clinic, in this 2026 study. Reaching precisely to a target is basic to arm function, and disorders of movement control degrade it, yet clinics lack a standardized, affordable test. Their protocol uses a small consumer hand-tracking camera and measures the average error across ten pointing attempts, with each hand, eyes open and closed.

Twenty adults performed the tests while a laboratory-grade multi-camera system recorded the same movements as a reference. With eyes closed, the cheap device's scores lined up moderately to very strongly with the reference system. With eyes open, agreement was weaker, though the average bias stayed small. The authors call the validity acceptable for clinical use and outline the further checks, reliability and sensitivity to change, still needed before routine adoption.
plos-pone-0356488:
Nhan Hien Phan and colleagues reviewed fifty patients aged eighty and over treated for bile duct stones. The treatment was a through-the-liver endoscopic laser procedure at their center in 2023 and 2024. Their 2026 retrospective study chose this route because open surgery is perilous at such ages. A scope is threaded through the liver to shatter stones with a holmium laser. The team graded clearance, complications, and hospital stay.

Every patient finished with complete or near-complete clearance. Most needed a single session, and nobody died from the procedure. About a quarter had adverse events, nearly all minor. Stones lodged both inside and outside the liver, plus active bile duct infection, predicted incomplete clearance and longer stays. The authors present the technique as a feasible lifeline for the very old.
plos-pone-0356688:
Wei Xu and Zhuxin Mao grade the feeding quality of common vetch, a legume forage. It was grown across three climate zones of western China. The zones run from cold alpine plateau to dry loess hills. Forage quality shifts with weather, and farmers need guidance on where and what to plant. Four cultivars grew in replicated plots for one season. The team measured sugars, protein, fat, and fatty acids. Then they blended the traits into a single quality score. The score was built from the data's main patterns.

Place beat cultivar: ecological zone moved most traits more than variety did. Alpine and transitional zones outscored the dry loess zone, with alpine vetch richer in sugars and healthy fats while warm dry conditions capped quality. Xu and Mao advise matching vetch planting to zone strengths when building high-quality forage supplies.
plos-pone-0356788:
Ayesha Liaqat and colleagues designed a candidate tuberculosis vaccine entirely on the computer, stitching together parts of four proteins the TB bacterium uses at different stages of infection. Their 2026 study follows the reverse vaccinology route: predicting which pieces the immune system can see, checking the stitched molecule for safety signals, and simulating how it docks onto an immune sensor.

The construct, named TetraFuVac11, passed the standard computational screens: predicted to be stable, non-allergenic, and non-toxic, and it held its grip on the immune receptor in motion simulations. The team also mapped how to build it in bacteria for laboratory production. None of this proves protection; it produces a well-vetted blueprint that now needs animal and cell experiments.
plos-pone-0356888:
Jingyi Hou and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE hunting for anti-aging compound combinations hidden inside a traditional Chinese herbal formula, Dengzhan Shengmai. Such formulas are synergistic by design, but finding which chemicals cooperate is a needle-in-haystack problem. The team built a deep learning system that fuses molecular properties, safety predictions, and network embeddings of protein interactions, then ranks pairs by whether their joint effect should exceed their separate ones.

The system scored near the top of standard accuracy measures, beating conventional baselines; protein network features carried most weight in its judgments. From thirty profiled chemicals, the three top combinations were tested in artificially aged nerve-like cells, restoring viability, calming oxidative stress, and cutting senescent cells substantially. Gene profiling showed roughly a thousand aging-related gene changes reversed across shared longevity pathways. The framework is offered as a general synergy hunter for complex traditional formulas.
plos-pone-0356988:
Fei Tong and Yinxi Cai examined whether city growth in China's Yangtze River Delta counties keeps people and land in step. They used satellite night lights, population grids, and land cover data from 2013 onward. Their 2026 study trained a deep learning model to extract urban land and population patterns. It scored how coordinated the two were in each county. It also probed which forces drove coordination in each period.

Land urbanized faster than population nearly everywhere, leaving a region-wide mismatch. Yet coordination improved steadily. It spread outward from core cities toward the east. The leading driver changed by era, with foreign investment dominating the earliest period. County-level diagnosis like this helps officials see whether new districts are filling with people or merely with pavement.
plos-pone-0357088:
Xiaoming Li and a large team studied road asphalt blended with very high shares of recycled tire rubber. The rubber made up from three tenths to half of the mix. The team also studied how heat and oxygen age such blends. Their 2026 study baked samples in laboratory aging ovens. It then probed stiffness, cold cracking behavior, and chemistry. It also tracked vapor emissions across the material's simulated life.

The richest rubber blend behaved unexpectedly well at first. Aging made its rubber network swell and cross-link. That fought the separation that plagues such mixes. It also shielded the asphalt beneath from hardening, a sacrificial protection. The trade-off arrived in deep cold, where the dense skeleton relaxed stress poorly. Late life brought peeling at the rubber and asphalt boundary. The work maps both the promise and the expiry date of tire-heavy roads.
plos-pone-0357288: Hospital pneumonias caused by drug-resistant bacteria are every doctor’s nightmare. This subgroup analysis tested imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam against hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia from imipenem-nonsusceptible pathogens. The results guide last-resort antibiotic choices when standard drugs fail.
plos-pone-0357388:
Julia Reddy leads a team of eight following substance exposed newborns who went home without a child protection report, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Hospitals may discharge such infants when no safety concern is apparent, but what happens over the following years was unknown. The study linked California births from 2018 to protection records, comparing exposed children with unexposed ones across their first five years.

Fewer than fourteen percent of exposed children were ever reported for maltreatment harm in that window. Still, exposed children were modestly more likely to be reported, and to have a report confirmed, than unexposed children, by roughly three percentage points. The same small elevation appeared even when the only exposure was cannabis. The authors suggest that families judged safe at birth may still benefit from voluntary support, rather than surveillance alone, to keep risk low.
plos-pone-0357488:
Hung-Chih Yeh and co-authors test whether lifting straps change scores on a standard full-body strength test. The test asks athletes to pull hard against a fixed bar at thigh height while standing on a force plate. Thirty men took part, half trained judo players and half students who lift weights for fitness, and each man pulled both with straps and bare-handed in random order.

Straps raised peak force, speed of force build-up, and total push across both groups, with no special extra gain for either group. Judo players still showed stronger grips in a separate squeeze test. Yeh and colleagues argue that straps let the test measure whole-body strength rather than grip limits, so labs should state clearly which way they test.
plos-pone-0357588: Starek and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on catheters steered by magnets inside the body. Doctors guide these soft tubes with outside magnets during heart procedures. In lab tests, the team measured how much force the catheter tips apply. They compared different catheters and settings head to head. The right force matters: too little fails to treat, too much can harm tissue.
plos-pone-0357788: Rico-Bolívar and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why people living with HIV end up in hospital. The records came from a large specialist hospital in Bogotá, Colombia, covering 2018 through 2024. Sorting the causes over those years shows how needs shifted, including through the pandemic. Hospitals can use such counts to plan beds, clinics, and support for this patient group.
plos-pone-0357888:
Olivia Young led a team of seven authors testing loving-kindness meditation in a randomized trial, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. This practice involves wishing well to oneself and others. The team asked whether it can ease pain and improve social well-being, two things that often worsen together in chronic illness.

Young's trial used random assignment and a control comparison, the strongest design for such a question. If a gentle, low-cost practice delivers measurable relief, it could sit beside standard care without drugs or side effects. The social side matters too: pain isolates people, and a practice aimed at connection may help on both fronts. Careful trials are how ancient practices earn, or fail to earn, a place in modern care.
plos-pone-0357988:
Abdushukur I Rakhmatullaev led a team of five authors screening Uzbek apple varieties for disease resistance, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Local apples face apple scab, powdery mildew, and fire blight, three costly orchard diseases. Instead of waiting for symptoms, the team used genetic markers to hunt resistance in local varieties.

Rakhmatullaev's marker-assisted screening speeds up the search for hardy trees adapted to Central Asian conditions. Varieties that already grow well locally, and carry resistance, are gold for breeding programs. Importing foreign varieties can fail on climate or taste; improving local stock avoids both traps. The markers found here let breeders select resistant seedlings early, cutting years from orchard development.
plos-pone-0358588:
Kunmiao Xu led a team of six authors redesigning highway guardrails, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Guardrails must stop speeding cars without becoming hazards themselves. The team designed an extra-high grade rail from a strong steel grade called 700L, aiming for a lighter rail that still holds firm after impact.

Langfelder and Horvath present WGCNA, an R package for weighted correlation network analysis. Correlation networks were becoming a common tool in bioinformatics when they wrote. Their method groups genes that rise and fall together across samples into related modules.

Inside the package, weighted analysis builds networks from microarray and similar data in a principled way. Modules can then be tied to traits such as disease state or tissue type. WGCNA gave systems biology a shared, documented toolkit, and its gene modules are now a routine starting point for hunting disease genes.
pmc-2892488:
Darling, Mau, and Perna present progressiveMauve, a method for aligning multiple whole genomes at once. Aligning genomes remains hard because related organisms differ by rearranged blocks, duplicated segments, and genes gained or lost. Those changes create a mosaic of matching and non-matching regions, even between close relatives.

ProgressiveMauve was designed to align two or more genomes while allowing for that shuffling. It finds conserved blocks and shows how their order changed. Such alignments let researchers trace how pathogens evolve, which parts of a genome stay stable, and where new genes enter.
pmc-2945788:
Goecks, Nekrutenko, Taylor, and co-authors present Galaxy, a web platform for computational research in the life sciences. As biology came to rely on computation, worries grew about whether results could be reached and repeated by others. Galaxy was built as an open, web-based home for genomic research.

The platform addresses access, reproducibility, and transparency together. Researchers can run analyses through a browser, share exact workflows, and let others rerun them. That openness helps small labs do serious genomic work and lets reviewers check how a published result was actually produced.
pmc-4202688:
Vidarsson, Dekkers, and Rispens reviewed IgG antibodies in 2014, covering their subclasses and allotypes. IgG is the most abundant antibody type in human blood serum. It comes in four subclasses that are much alike but differ in parts of their constant region, above all near the hinge.

Those small structural differences change how each subclass triggers effector functions, the actions that clear germs and infected cells. Allotypes, the inherited variants of these antibodies, add a further layer of variety. The review links structure to function across all forms. That knowledge matters for vaccines, antibody drugs, and tests that read immune responses.
pmc-5446088:
Bowden, Del Greco, Minelli, and their team wrote in 2016 on how to judge gene-based causal tests that use summary data. A method called MR-Egger had just been put forward for such tests. It can work even when some gene variants used as tools are not valid, and it can flag bias.

The paper centers on a statistic that shows how much the variant-level results vary. That value tells the user how far the MR-Egger results can be trusted for a given dataset. When the spread is too low, the bias test loses its power. The guidance helps analysts pick the right method and read its output with care.
pmc-5889788:
Andrea Cipriani, Toshi Furukawa, Georgia Salanti, and a large team compared antidepressant drugs in 2018. Major depression is common, costly, and a heavy burden worldwide. Drugs are used more often than talking therapy because services are scarce.

The team pooled hundreds of trials to compare many antidepressants head to head, even where no direct trial existed. All the drugs beat a placebo for short-term response, but they differed in side effects and dropouts. The rankings give doctors and patients a firmer base for choosing a first drug. The study is widely cited in treatment guidelines.
pmc-6912988:
Sam Kovaka, Aleksey Zimin, Geo Pertea, and coauthors presented StringTie2 for long-read RNA assembly in 2019. New sequencers read RNA in stretches thousands of letters long. Long reads can reveal full transcripts that short reads piece together poorly.

StringTie2 assembles those long reads against a reference genome with better handling of their error patterns. It also works in a mixed mode that pairs long reads with accurate short ones. Tests show cleaner transcript models and fewer false joins. Transcript studies of complex genes rely on such tools to get isoforms right.
pmc-8128288:
Nicholas Davies and colleagues modeled in 2021 how transmissible the B.1.1.7 variant of SARS-CoV-2 was in England, and what its spread would mean. This variant, first flagged in the United Kingdom, carried many mutations affecting how the virus attaches to and enters human cells. Using several kinds of statistical models and data streams, the team estimated its growth advantage over earlier forms of the virus.

Their results indicated the variant spread substantially faster, which raised the level of control measures needed to hold it back. The findings landed while the variant was sweeping England, and they informed urgent policy choices. The study also became a model for how to size up a new variant quickly.
proudhon-system-economical-contradiction:
Benjamin R Tucker published his translation of Proudhon's System of Economical Contradictions in 1888. Proudhon had issued the work in 1846 with the subtitle The Philosophy of Misery. Tucker, Proudhon's chief American champion, spread his books through his journal Liberty and its press.

Proudhon marched through the ideas of political economy, division of labor, machinery, competition, and monopoly, finding each both good and harmful. That method of paired contradictions drove Karl Marx to answer with The Poverty of Philosophy, a famous attack. The quarrel split the young socialist movement. Tucker's translation lets English readers judge Proudhon's dense, daring critique of political economy in the form that provoked Marx.
psellos-de-operatione-daemonum-greek-lat:
Michael Psellos, the brilliant Byzantine courtier of the eleventh century, wrote a dialogue on the operation of demons. This edition of 1688 prints the Greek with Latin alongside. The Renaissance had met Psellos through Ficino's Latin translation of 1497, which made Byzantine demon lore a Western classic.

In dialogue, Psellos explains how demons act on bodies and minds in the Eastern church's teaching. Their kinds, powers, and limits receive orderly treatment. The tone is curious rather than frightened. Greek and Latin on facing pages served the scholars of 1688. The book is the demon lore of Byzantium, elegantly imported westward, and it coloured occult writing for centuries.
pseudo-democritus-physica-mystica-berthe:
The Physica et Mystica, questions on nature and secret things, claims the name of Democritus, the laughing philosopher of atoms. In fact it comes from Bolos of Mendes, writing in Egypt in the first or second century. It is the oldest layer of Greek alchemy. Berthelot and Ruelle printed it in 1888, in French translation.

Recipes for making gold, silver, purple dye, and gems fill the book, mixed with spells and the lore of like acting on like. A letter to Leucippe travels with the text. The work shows alchemy at its birth, half craft and half mystery. All the later art, Greek and Arab, grows from these pages.
queiros-os-maias-1888:
Eça de Queirós published Os Maias in Portugal in 1888, and the text here is the Portuguese original. Carlos da Maia, last hope of a great Lisbon family, is raised by his grandfather Afonso after family tragedy. Carlos studies medicine, idles in high society, and falls in love with a married stranger, Maria Eduarda.

A buried secret about Maria's birth turns love into horror for them both. Around the pair, Eça paints Lisbon's politics, salons, and newspapers with amused disgust. The novel tracks the Maia family's slow decline across three generations. Portuguese readers rank Os Maias as their greatest novel. Its English translation of 1925 exists but could not be staged here.
reid-essays-active-powers-1788:
Reid's Essays on the Active Powers of Man, from 1788, turn Thomas Reid from the mind's knowing to its doing. Five essays, complete here, treat the powers that move a person to act. Will stands first, then the springs of action: appetite, desire, and affection, summed up as motives.

Morals close the work, as Reid grounds right and wrong in a moral sense open to reason. The book is his moral philosophy entire, the partner of his Essays on the Intellectual Powers of 1785. Against theories that made humans mere bundles of feeling, Reid defends free, rational agency. His calm system shaped moral teaching in Scotland and America for a century.
rhys-celtic-heathendom-1888:
John Rhys gave these talks as the Hibbert Lectures in 1888, on how faith grew among the Celtic peoples. Rhys held the chair of Celtic studies at Oxford. His theme was the old faith of Britain and Ireland before the church age. The talks drew crowds who wanted hard proof, not just old tales.

He traced gods, rites, and hero tales through Welsh and Irish texts and folk use. Druid belief holds a key place, weighed with care from the old proof. The talks stand as the first sound school study of Celtic pagan faith, still cited today.
schiller-revolt-of-the-netherlands-1788:
Schiller turned from plays to history with his History of the Revolt of the Netherlands, published in 1788. Edward Backhouse Eastwick translated the work into English in the nineteenth century. The book tells how the Dutch provinces rose against Spanish rule in the 1500s.

Schiller traces the clash of faith, taxes, and foreign rule that drove the revolt. William of Orange and the Duke of Alva stand out as the great opposed figures. The narrative gave Schiller the ground from which Don Carlos had grown. It also won him respect as a historian, not only a playwright. Readers still value its clear story of a small people's fight for its liberties.
stevenson-black-arrow-1888:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote The Black Arrow as a serial for a boys' magazine, using a pen name. It appeared in book form in 1888, after Treasure Island had made him famous. Stevenson himself thought it rather careless work, but young readers loved it.

During the Wars of the Roses, young Dick Shelton finds his father was murdered by his own guardian. He joins the outlaws of Tunstall Forest, who sign their revenge with black arrows. Battles, escapes, and a rescue-romance follow as Dick shifts sides in England's civil war. Richard of Gloucester, the future Richard III, appears as a chilling young fighter. The novel is a fast, rousing adventure of the fifteenth century.
storm-rider-white-horse-1888:
Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse in 1888, a German novella set on the Frisian coast. Hauke Haien is a bright farm boy who rises to become dike master. He dreams of a new, safer dike against the North Sea. Villagers mock his plans and fear his pride and ambition.

Storm frames the tale as a story told on a stormy night, with hints of a ghostly rider. Hauke's new dike is tested by a great flood. Family loss and local distrust deepen the gloom. The novella blends realism with legend and dread. It is Storm's last and most famous work, a classic of German fiction.
strindberg-comrades-1888:
August Strindberg wrote Comrades in 1888, a four-act naturalist comedy, here in Edith and Warner Oland's translation. The play stages an artist-marriage, Bertha and Axel, as a war of the sexes in modern dress. Strindberg called it a comedy, though its close is as cold as any of his tragedies in effect.

Bertha and Axel, painters in Paris, vow a marriage of equals, comrades without roles of sex. Her picture reaches the Salon while his is refused, and jealousy rots the pact from within fast. Friends, a doctor, and a cynical lieutenant feed the couple's doubts about art, love, and freedom in marriage. Axel engineers her fall from the pedestal, and the comradeship ends in contempt on both sides at last. The Olands' translation showed English readers Strindberg's Paris and his battle lines in wedlock.
strindberg-creditors-1888:
August Strindberg wrote Creditors in 1888, a one-act tragedy, here in Edwin Björkman's English translation in print. The play is a masterpiece of psychological vampirism, built from Tekla and her two husbands in one room. Björkman, Strindberg's great English champion, kept its talk swift, modern, and cruelly lucid for foreign readers abroad.

Gustav, Tekla's first husband, returns in disguise and coaches her present husband Adolf to doubt her love. Adolf, a painter turned sculptor, sickens as Gustav drains his faith in his art and his wife. Tekla arrives, all charm, and Gustav's revenge completes itself in a death offstage and a cold exit line. Three people, one set, and talk as a weapon: the design is flawless and pitiless in execution here. Directors rank it with Miss Julie as Strindberg's most actable and most revived one-act work.
strindberg-miss-julie-1888:
August Strindberg wrote Miss Julie in 1888, here in Edith and Warner Oland's translation, as Countess Julie. The one-act naturalist tragedy of Midsummer Eve is the most performed Strindberg play in the world today. Its preface, a manifesto of naturalist drama, is as famous as the play itself in theatre history.

Julie, a count's daughter, dances with servants at the midsummer feast and singles out Jean, the valet. Their night moves from flirtation to intimacy to a cruel contest of class, sex, and will. Kristin, the cook and Jean's fiancée, sleeps and wakes through the moral wreck around her in the kitchen. At dawn Julie, ruined in her own eyes, takes Jean's razor at his cold urging on stage. The Olands' version fixed the play's English name and text for early American stages.
synesius-alchemist-commentary-berthelot-:
An alchemist named Synesius, not the famous bishop, wrote this commentary on the book ascribed to Democritus. He casts his teaching as a dialogue with Dioscorus, a priest of Alexandria. Berthelot and Ruelle printed the text in 1888 in their edition of the Greek alchemists, in French translation.

Synesius unpacks the riddles of the master: what the divine water is, how metals are born from mercury and sulfur, and why the art hides in code. His commentary became the standard teaching text of the Greek school. Students of alchemy read Democritus through Synesius for centuries. The little dialogue is a key that still fits the oldest locks of the art.
taillepied-psychologie-apparition-esprit:
Noël Taillepied, a Norman monk, published his treatise on the apparition of spirits in French in 1588. His title calls the work a psychology, in the old sense of a study of souls. Separated souls, phantoms, and prodigies fill its chapters, mapped with a surprisingly kind hand.

Taillepied asks where souls go and how they may return to warn or comfort the living. He writes for Catholic readers who feared ghosts and sought them at once. His tone stays gentle where other demonologists thunder. The book is a French treatise of ghosts from inside the cloister. It preserves the afterlife as ordinary Norman folk imagined it, visitor by visitor.
teresa-avila-life-1588:
Teresa of Avila wrote her Life at the bid of her church guides. She was a Spanish nun who led a reform of the Carmelite order. The work dates to the 1500s, and David Lewis gave it English dress. Few books on the soul's life are read with such warmth.

Teresa tells of her sick youth, her lax years, and her slow turn to deep prayer. She tells of raptures, visions, and talks with God in plain words. She also tells how she founded strict new houses for her nuns. The book is a great life tale of the inner path.
the-history-of-australian-exploration-fr: Ernest Favenc tells the tale of a hundred years of trekking across Australia — from the first landing through Burke and Wills, Stuart, and the men who opened the vast inland. His story honors the grit and grief of the pathfinders. The best early record of how the lone continent was mapped and won.
the-man-of-letters-as-a-man-of-business-: Howells's Man of Letters as Man of Business: the writer's economics. The dean on authorship as trade. Practical and wise. Essential for writers, howells on the writer's trade, practical wisdom, essential for authors, the writer's trade.
