Medieval magicians prized the Liber Juratus Honorii, the Sworn Book of Honorius, among the oldest of their grimoires. Its writer claims the art was sworn to secrecy by a council of masters. Honorius of Thebes stands as its supposed author, though the true writer is unknown.

The goal is high: through prayer, fasting, and the use of divine names, the magician seeks a vision of God himself, the beatific vision. Angelic rites fill the long preparation. Few medieval magic books aim so far beyond common spells. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Its ambition alone secures its fame.
tob-0144-54488:
Anthropogenesis, the second volume of The Secret Doctrine, follows spirit as it descends into matter and takes human form. Blavatsky teaches that humanity passes through root races, from shadowy early forms to solid bodies. Atlantis and Lemuria enter the story as lost homes of early races.

She retells human prehistory as a spiritual epic, mixing myth, geology, and claims drawn from Eastern texts. Much of the lost-continent lore still repeated today traces back to these pages. Scientists rejected the scheme outright, yet its reach proved enormous. Occult groups, novelists, and seekers have mined volume two for over a century.
tob-10088:
Carved in cuneiform more than four thousand years ago, the Epic of Gilgamesh is the world's oldest surviving epic, presented here in an Old Babylonian version. Gilgamesh is the proud king of Uruk. His friend is Enkidu, a wild man tamed by city life, and together they seek fame through dangerous deeds.

When Enkidu dies, the story turns. Gilgamesh, terrified by death, quests for the secret of immortality and is forced toward accepting his mortal limits. Its flood story predates the Bible's account by centuries. Readers get heroic adventure joined to one of literature's earliest, plainest looks at grief and dying.
tob-10988:
A short apocalypse called the Ladder of Jacob survives in Slavonic, retelling the patriarch Jacob's famous dream. Genesis shows Jacob a ladder reaching heaven, with angels going up and down. This later text expands the dream into a full vision.

An angel guides Jacob up the ladder and explains the ages of history to come, with kings, wars, and a final deliverance. The work likely began as a Jewish text and passed through Christian hands. Small as it is, it shows how early readers turned one Bible scene into a map of all history, and it rewards students of the pseudepigrapha.
tob-4185-79588:
Religion and the heavens draw Plutarch's attention through much of volume four of Goodwin's Moralia. He writes on the oracle at Delphi and why its answers grew obscure. His long essay on Isis and Osiris remains a key source for Egyptian religion as Greeks understood it.

Another piece asks what the face seen in the moon might be, mixing story with early astronomy. Plutarch treats foreign gods and strange rites with respect rare in his age. The volume shows his mind at its most curious and open. Goodwin's translation brings these rich, learned essays to readers near the end of the complete set.
tob-4188:
E. B. Cowell edited the great English Jataka, the tales of the Buddha's former births. Five hundred forty-seven stories tell how the future Buddha lived as monkey, elephant, deer, prince, and ascetic, perfecting a virtue in each life. Monks and lay teachers across Asia have retold them for two thousand years.

A greedy jackal, a patient buffalo, a wise monkey king: the animal fables carry lessons in giving, patience, and truth. Folklore scholars rank the set among the world's oldest story collections. Verified from a pre-1930 public-domain edition, Cowell's version gathers the whole teeming menagerie, with the frame verses that state each tale's moral.
tob-9047-60688:
Metals, mining, and the arts dominate volume five of Pliny's Natural History in Bostock's version. Gold and silver come first, with frank remarks on how greed for them corrupts men. Bronze casting and iron working follow, craft by craft.

Then Pliny turns art historian. He names sculptors and painters, dates their works, and tells how masterpieces were made and moved. Much of what we know about Greek art survives only because he wrote it down. The volume reads like a tour of a vast museum that no longer exists. Rome's wealth, skill, and taste all stand on record here.
toussenel-les-juifs-rois-de-l-epoque-188:
Alphonse Toussenel, a French writer on beasts and on the world of work, first brought out this book in 1845. The text here is the full 1888 print, in French. Its title calls the Jews the kings of the age, and its theme is what he named financial feudalism.

Toussenel holds that banks and rail lines have made a new feudal class that rules France. His charge is aimed at the Rothschilds and at the whole world of high finance round them. The book founds a dark line of thought in France, and it is kept here as a record of its age.
un-sc-res-1288:
Southern Lebanon's force was renewed at the start of 2000. On 31 January 2000 the Security Council extended UNIFIL for six months, until 31 July. The Secretary-General had reported on the force that month. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and borders in full. It re-asserted the force's founding terms from 1978. All parties had to cooperate with UNIFIL so it could do its job across the south.

The Council condemned all acts of violence, above all those against the force itself. It urged the parties to end such attacks. Within five months the picture changed completely. Israel withdrew from Lebanon that May, and the renewal that followed had a new purpose.
un-sc-res-1388: As number 1388 in the Council's series, the resolution is catalogued in this library under 2002. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1488: Security Council Resolution 1488, from 2003, is held here in the official-record wording transcribed by Wikisource. A resolution is not commentary; it is the Council acting, with nine of fifteen votes needed and the five permanent members able to block. The full text lets readers judge the decision by its own exact terms.
un-sc-res-1588: An advance United Nations mission was working in Sudan in March 2005. It was preparing the ground for a larger peace operation after the north-south peace deal. On 17 March 2005 the Security Council extended that mission, UNAMIS, by one week. The new end date was 24 March 2005. The whole resolution is two sentences long. The brief pause let the Council finish work on the full mission, which it created days later.
un-sc-res-1688:
Resolution 1688 brought the trial of Charles Taylor under a formal Council decision, adopted on 16 June 2006. Taylor, the former president of Liberia, faced war crimes charges at the Special Court for Sierra Leone. He had been caught in Nigeria and handed to the court in Freetown. Holding the trial there raised fears of unrest across the region.

The Council clears the way for the trial to move to The Hague in the Netherlands. The Special Court keeps sole control of the case while sitting abroad. The International Criminal Court agreed to lend its courtroom and cells. Dutch authorities must help move Taylor, witnesses, and experts so the trial can proceed safely.
un-sc-res-1788: From 2007, Resolution 1788 records a decision of the Security Council in official form, preserved through English Wikisource. The Council's texts often do quiet work: extending a mandate, adjusting a committee, setting a date. Whatever work this one does, the entry preserves its exact instructions, which is what the officials who received them had to follow.
un-sc-res-188:
Yemen brought a complaint to the Security Council. It protested a British air attack at Harib. The attack took place on 28 March 1964. Resolution 188 was adopted on 9 April 1964. The Council heard statements on the matter. It recalled Article 2 of the Charter. That article bars attacks on other states.

The Council condemns reprisals. It says they clash with the aims of the United Nations. It deplores the British action at Harib. It also deplores all other attacks in the area. It calls on Yemen and Britain to show restraint. Both sides should avoid new incidents and restore peace. The Secretary-General is asked to help settle the issues. He would use his good offices for that task.
un-sc-res-1888:
Resolution 1888, adopted in September 2009, gave the fight against wartime sexual violence its own leadership at the UN. It created a special representative on the issue, a post meant to press governments and commanders directly. The Council acted a year after Resolution 1820's demands.

The text also calls for expert teams to deploy to conflict zones, better data on attacks, and women protection advisers inside peace missions. Its aim was machinery: named officials, reporting lines, and duties that survive news cycles. Together with 1820, it forms the core of the UN's framework on conflict-related sexual violence.
un-sc-res-1988:
Taliban sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1988, adopted on 17 June 2011. Since 1999 one list had covered both Al-Qaida and the Taliban. Peace talks in Afghanistan were gaining ground. A single list made it hard to lift names of Taliban members who laid down arms.

The Council splits the old list in two. Taliban names move to a new list run by a new committee. The asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo still apply to those listed. Names can come off for people who renounce violence and join the peace process. Kabul will be consulted and can propose removals. A companion text the same day kept Al-Qaida on its own regime.
un-sc-res-288:
Southern Rhodesia's sanctions were kept in force by the Security Council on 17 November 1970. Five years had passed since the illegal declaration of independence. Some states still defied resolutions 232 (1966), 253 (1968), and 277 (1970), against their Charter duty under Article 25. The sanctions committee had filed its third report on enforcement.

Acting under its Chapter VII decisions, the Council again condemned the illegal declaration of independence. It held Britain, as the administering power, chiefly responsible for ending the rebellion. London was called to take urgent and effective steps so Rhodesia's people could exercise self-determination. The Council decided the present sanctions would remain in force. All states were urged to apply the Rhodesia resolutions in full, and those still aiding the regime were deplored. States were further urged to grant the illegal regime no form of recognition.
un-sc-res-388:
Rhodesia's sanctions net was tightened in the spring of 1976. The sanctions committee had sent a special report that winter. On 6 April 1976 the Security Council closed two loopholes. States had to stop their nationals from insuring Rhodesian exports. Goods shipped in breach of sanctions could no longer find cover. The ban applied to exports leaving Rhodesia after the vote.

States also had to block Rhodesian firms from gaining trade names and franchises. No commercial or public body there could be granted such rights. Non-member states were urged to follow the same rules. The steps extended the sanctions of 1968 into finance and branding. They aimed to raise the cost of the illegal regime's defiance.
un-sc-res-588:
Iran and Iraq were ordered back to the Council's own plan on 8 October 1986. The war had run for six years and was growing fiercer, with heavy loss of life and damage. The Council had been seized of the question throughout. In February 1986 it had adopted resolution 582, a full plan for ending the war. Neither side had carried it out.

The Council called on Iran and Iraq to put resolution 582 (1986) into effect fully and without delay. That text demanded a cease-fire, a pullback to the recognized borders, a prisoner exchange, and talks on every open issue. The Secretary-General was asked to step up his efforts with both parties to give the plan effect. He had to report to the Council no later than 30 November 1986. The Council would then meet again on his report.
un-sc-res-688: Dated 1991 in the catalog, Resolution 688 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-88: China's new government sought a voice in the Council's Korea debate in 1950. On 8 November 1950 the Council decided to invite a representative of the Central People's Government of the People's Republic of China. The guest would be present while the Council discussed a report from the United Nations Command in Korea. The invitation rested on the Council's rules of procedure. The vote was eight to two, with one abstention. The one-sentence act came as Chinese troops were entering the Korean War.
un-sc-res-988:
Sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 988, adopted on 21 April 1995. Belgrade had closed its border with Bosnia to all goods except food, medicine, and clothing. Monitors from the international conference verified the closure. Reports told of helicopter flights crossing that border, and an inquiry was under way.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the partial suspension of sanctions in place until 5 July 1995. Flights and ferries under the suspension may not carry extra fuel beyond flight needs. Belgrade must help investigate the helicopter reports and keep the border sealed. If the closure fails, the suspension ends five working days after the report.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Lebanon asked for more time for the UN force in its south, and Resolution 1288, adopted on 31 January 2000, granted it. The force, UNIFIL, had watched the border area since 1978. The Council studied the Secretary-General's January report on the force and noted Lebanon's written request for an extension.

The mandate was renewed for six more months, until 31 July 2000. The Council restated its strong backing for Lebanon's territorial integrity and sovereignty within its recognized borders. It also pointed peacekeepers toward a newer duty of the era, welcoming UN efforts to train its personnel in preventing HIV/AIDS and other communicable diseases across peacekeeping operations. Nobody yet knew Israel's withdrawal that spring would soon change the force's work.

One piece of the sanctions on Afghanistan is lifted on 15 January 2002. The sanctions had banned flights and frozen funds linked to the Taliban. The Council now noted that Ariana Afghan Airlines was no longer owned, leased, or run by or for the Taliban.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ruled that the flight ban and asset freeze no longer applied to the airline's aircraft or funds. A related measure was ended as well. The narrow change shows sanctions being unwound piece by piece where the Taliban link was gone, while the wider regime stayed in place.

Six more months for the Golan Heights observer force are approved on 26 June 2003. UNDOF, which watches the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces, stays in place until 31 December 2003. The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. It also asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the period on developments and on measures taken toward that goal.

Seven days is all this Sudan bridge grants, and that is the point. On 17 March 2005, the Council adopted Resolution 1588 without dissent. The advance mission, UNAMIS, had gone in to pave the way for a full peace force. The north-south peace deal had ended Sudan's long civil war that January. The advance team's mandate was about to lapse.

The text simply extends UNAMIS to 24 March 2005. It recalls the chain of Sudan texts behind the step. One of them, passed a week before, had set the same end date. The Council stays seized of the matter. Days later, it swapped the advance team for the full Sudan mission, UNMIS.

The trial of former Liberian President Charles Taylor is moved out of West Africa by Resolution 1688, adopted on 16 June 2006. Taylor had been transferred to the Special Court for Sierra Leone on 29 March 2006, charged over the Sierra Leone war. The Council judged that his presence in the subregion threatened the peace of Liberia and Sierra Leone. The Netherlands had agreed to host the trial, using International Criminal Court premises.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council welcomes the Netherlands' offer and the ICC's agreement to provide its premises in The Hague. The Special Court keeps exclusive jurisdiction over Taylor in the Netherlands. All states must cooperate, including making evidence and witnesses available. The travel ban under Resolution 1521 (2003) is lifted for Taylor's trial travel and for required witnesses. The Court is asked to make the proceedings accessible to the subregion, including by video link.

The Golan Heights observer force is renewed for six months on 14 December 2007, until 30 June 2008. UNDOF keeps watch between Israeli and Syrian forces. The parties are called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The force's enforcement of the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse is welcomed. A report is asked for at the end of the period.

A British air attack at Harib in Yemen is deplored on 9 April 1964. The Yemen Arab Republic had complained about the strike of 28 March 1964 on its territory. Both sides were heard while tensions in the area ran high, with Yemen's civil war drawing in outside powers.

Reprisals are condemned as incompatible with the purposes of the United Nations. The British military action at Harib and all other attacks and incidents in the area are deplored. Yemen and the United Kingdom are called on to show the utmost restraint, avoid further incidents, and restore peace. The Secretary-General is asked to use his good offices, with both parties' agreement, to settle the outstanding issues between them.

The fight against sexual violence in armed conflict is strengthened on 30 September 2009. A July 2009 report found such violence still widespread and sometimes systematic, against women and children above all. The text follows the 2000 and 2008 resolutions on the subject and the Council's repeated, unmet demands for the abuse to stop.

All parties are demanded to take proper steps at once, including enforcing discipline and command responsibility, and to have all reports of sexual violence by their forces investigated. The Secretary-General is asked to appoint a Special Representative to lead the United Nations work on the issue. States are urged to reform laws and courts so offenders are prosecuted, and expert teams are sought to help countries where violence is worst.

The Taliban sanctions are split into their own regime in Resolution 1988, adopted on 17 June 2011. Afghanistan's reconciliation drive, backed by the 2010 Consultative Peace Jirga and the High Peace Council, was hampered by Taliban names sitting on the joint 1267 Consolidated List. The Monitoring Team had recommended treating Taliban and Al-Qaida differently.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council moves everyone designated as Taliban, and their associates, off the Consolidated List onto a new List run by a new committee. The asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo stay unchanged. Designation covers financing, supplying, or recruiting for the Taliban, including through Afghan narcotics proceeds, and ransom payments fall under the freeze. States should consult the Afghan government before proposing names, and listing comes with public narrative summaries. Delisting is tied to the reconciliation conditions: renouncing violence, breaking with Al-Qaida, and respecting the Afghan constitution, including women's rights.

Resolution 288, adopted unanimously on 17 November 1970, returns to Southern Rhodesia five years after its illegal declaration of independence. The sanctions committee's third report documented how some states kept breaching the mandatory measures of 1966 and 1968. Britain, the colonial power in law, still bore the main duty of ending the rebellion.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council restated its rejection of the outlawed independence claim. It called on Britain, as administering power, to take urgent and effective measures to end the revolt and let Rhodesians exercise self-determination under the Charter. The wording kept legal responsibility pinned on London while sanctions did the slow work of isolating the Smith regime.

Loopholes in the Rhodesia bans got plugged in 1976. Goods still slipped in and out of the banned land. Ships flew false flags. Brands and shop deals kept trade warm in the shade. A sanctions team sent its word on 15 December 1975. Resolution 388 passed with no dissent on 6 April 1976.

No one could insure goods shipped in breach of the bans. That bar hit loads sent out of Rhodesia. It hit loads sent in as well. It hit goods held on Rhodesian soil. Brand rights and franchise deals were banned too. No firm there could trade on a world name. States outside the UN were urged to fall in line. The aim was to starve the revolt of cash and cover, one clause at a time.

Resolution 588, adopted unanimously on 8 October 1986, orders Iran and Iraq to use the exit the Council had already built. The war was in its seventh year. That February the Council had adopted resolution 582, a balanced plan deploring the war's start and escalation and pointing toward a settlement. Neither capital had carried it out, while losses of life and destruction mounted.

The Council called on Iran and Iraq to implement resolution 582 fully and without delay. It asked the UN chief to press harder with both capitals toward a peaceful settlement and to keep the Council informed. The text is barely a page, which underlines its impatience: the terms existed, and only compliance was missing.

Iraq's own people came under harsh repression in the spring of 1991, just after the Gulf War. The repression fell most heavily on Kurdish areas in the north. Huge numbers of refugees fled toward the borders with Turkey and Iran. Human suffering was on a very large scale. Resolution 688 was adopted in April 1991.

The Council condemned the repression of the Iraqi civilian population. It said the effects of that repression threatened peace and security in the region. Iraq had to end the repression at once, as a contribution to removing that threat. Iraq also had to let international aid organizations reach everyone in need, anywhere in the country. Every facility for their work had to be given. The Secretary-General was told to press on with relief work and to report on the plight of the Iraqi people, above all the Kurds.

Chinese troops poured into Korea in the fall of 1950. The UN Command there sent the Council a special report. Debate on that report raised a hard point. Beijing's regime had no seat at the UN table. Resolution 88, passed on 8 November 1950, dealt with that gap. Eight members voted yes. China and Cuba voted no. Egypt held back.

The Council chose to invite a voice from Beijing. A man from the Central People's Government could sit in. He could be heard while the Korea report was debated. The tool was rule 39, which lets the Council hear outsiders. The step did not grant China the seat itself. That prize stayed with Taipei for two more decades.

Sanctions relief for Belgrade is extended by Resolution 988, adopted on 21 April 1995. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) had closed its border with Bosnia and Herzegovina to all goods except food, medicine, and essential clothing. The ICFY Mission monitoring the closure reported good cooperation. Reports of helicopter flights crossing the border were under investigation.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council suspends the restrictions named in Resolution 943 (1994) until 5 July 1995. It confirms that goods, including extra fuel, may not ride on the permitted flights and ferries without sanctions-committee approval. It demands a probe of the helicopter reports and stronger support for the ICFY Mission. The Secretary-General must report every 30 days on whether the border closure is certified as real. If he reports it is not, the suspension ends automatically on the fifth working day after his report, unless the Council decides otherwise.
waite-lives-of-alchemystical-philosopher:
Short lives of famed adepts fill A. E. Waite's Lives of Alchemystical Philosophers, his hand book of 1888. Waite gives each name a tale, a list of works, and a note on what the sage sought. Gold, long life, and a cure for the soul blend in their quests, life by life.

The book is a who's who of the great art. Waite writes with care, yet lets the odd charm of each life shine. Fans used it as their map of the field. It still serves as a first guide to the names. Some lives get a page, some get a full tale of quests. Each gloss ends with the books that sage left for fans to chase.
walker-reincarnation-forgotten-truth-188:
E. D. Walker published Reincarnation: A Study of Forgotten Truth at Boston in 1888, with Houghton Mifflin. Walker wrote the first systematic English survey of reincarnation beliefs across the world's religions. Hindu, Buddhist, Greek, early Christian, and modern witnesses file through his chapters in turn.

He gathers Plato, the Upanishads, Origen, and the theosophists of his own day into one argument. The book introduced the doctrine to the late nineteenth-century English-reading public at large. For decades it stood as the standard reference on the subject in English. Walker writes as an advocate, yet his learning is broad and his sources are named. The survey still serves readers tracing the idea's long, wandering history.
white-great-controversy-1888:
Ellen White, co-founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, published The Great Controversy Between Christ and Satan in 1888. The book tells a sweeping story of cosmic conflict, from the fall of Lucifer to the promised new earth. Adventists treat it as the movement's central prophetic history.

White follows the fight through the fall of Jerusalem, the early church, the Reformation, and the last days still to come. Each age, in her telling, turns on whether God's law and Sabbath are honored or set aside. The narrative gave her church a story of itself that still shapes Adventist reading of world events.
yeats-fairy-folk-tales-irish-peasantry-1:
W. B. Yeats, then a young Irish poet, made this hoard of Irish folk tales in 1888. He drew the tales from Croker, Carleton, and other men who had heard them from the folk. The book came at the start of the Irish revival in arts and letters.

Fairy troops, banshees, witches, and saints walk through the tales Yeats chose. The merrow tales of the sea folk hold a place of their own in the set. The book is a landmark: a great poet's first hoard of the lore of his own land.
zola-dream-1888:
Eliza Chase translated The Dream, Zola's novel of 1888, from the French Le Reve. Chapter one sets a hard winter in 1860, when the river Oise froze over. Snow buried the small city of Beaumont in Lower Picardy that Christmas.

A girl of nine shelters all night under the arch of Saint Agnes portal. Thin dress, torn silk kerchief, and huge shoes mark her as a lost foundling. Lacemakers in the cathedral town raise her, and she dreams of a prince. Love for a noble son brings the dream near truth. Yet dreams in Zola seldom survive daylight, and heartbreak follows in its purest kind.
zosimos-panopolis-oeuvres-berthelot-1888:
Zosimos of Panopolis, an Egyptian Greek who wrote around 300 CE, is the earliest alchemist whose name and works survive. Marcellin Berthelot and C. E. Ruelle printed his works in their great edition of Greek alchemy in 1888. The text here gives Zosimos in the editors' French translation.

Zosimos writes letters to a woman pupil, Theosebeia, full of visions, furnaces, and coded talk of metals turning toward gold. He quotes older masters and dreams of a divine water that frees the spirit from the body. His pages are the fountainhead of the alchemical art in the West. Every later adept, Greek, Arab, and Latin, drew from this spring.
